ProximalLangevin/Proximal.lean.title: Actual proximal minimizers and optimality
ProximalLangevin/Proximal.lean.summary:
Proximity is defined by global minimization of a convex function plus a positive quadratic penalty. Its residual is characterized by a true supporting subgradient. Monotonicity of these supports gives uniqueness and firm nonexpansiveness, while finite-dimensional compactness and a lower bound supply existence. These facts justify every subsequent use of the actual proximity map.

On a real inner product space let \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=f(p)+\|p-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\). Convexity, a lower bound, finite dimension and \(\lambda>0\) construct a true minimizer; the variational lemmas also apply to any supplied minimizer.

steps.title: Quadratic objective and global support
steps.body:
The definitions mean \(p\in\arg\min Q_{\lambda,x}\) and \(s\in\partial f(p)\) precisely when \(f(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\le f(y)\) for every \(y\). Apply the support inequalities at \((p,s)\) and \((q,t)\) to each other, add and cancel function values to obtain \(\langle s-t,p-q\rangle\ge0\). No differentiability is involved.

Formal correspondence: proxObjective : Objective minimized by the proximity mapping with parameter lam . IsProxPoint : p solves the actual unconstrained proximity minimization problem at x . IsSubgradient : The global supporting-hyperplane characterization of a convex subgradient.

The support condition is global: it compares the function at every competitor with an affine function touching at the support point. At two support points, use each point as the other's competitor. The function values cancel upon addition, leaving \(0\le\langle s-t,p-q\rangle\). This is monotonicity of the subdifferential, and it remains valid for finite convex functions with nondifferentiable corners.

steps.title: The residual characterizes the minimum
steps.body:
A vector \(s\) is a subgradient of \(g_2\) at \(p\) when \(g_2(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\le g_2(y)\) for every \(y\). The exact proximal optimality condition is

\[ p=P_\lambda(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{x-p}{\lambda}\in\partial g_2(p). \]

For necessity, compare the minimizing objective at \(p\) with its value along \(p+t(y-p)\), use convexity, and let positive \(t\) become arbitrarily small. For sufficiency, insert the supporting-hyperplane inequality into the difference of the two quadratic objectives. This proves the global minimum directly, without assuming differentiability of \(g_2\).

Apply monotonicity of subgradients to the residuals at two inputs. It gives firm nonexpansiveness,

\[ \|P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\|^2 \le\langle x-y,P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\rangle. \]

Cauchy–Schwarz gives nonexpansiveness of \(P_\lambda\). Expanding the square gives nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\) as well. Those are derived geometric facts, not premises stored in a proximal-map structure.

To see the necessity calculation explicitly, fix \(y\), put \(d=y-p\), and compare the proximal objective at \(p\) with the competitor \(p+td\), \(0<t\le1\). Convexity bounds \(f(p+td)\) by \((1-t)f(p)+tf(y)\). After expanding the square and dividing by positive \(t\), \[f(y)-f(p)\ge\left\langle\frac{x-p}{\lambda},d\right\rangle-\frac{t}{2\lambda}\|d\|^2.\] Letting \(t\downarrow0\) gives the support inequality. Thus the variational argument establishes a subgradient at the chosen minimizer without assuming differentiability.

Formal correspondence: isProxPoint_of_subgradient : A residual subgradient is sufficient for proximal optimality. subgradient_of_isProxPoint : Convex proximal minimizers satisfy the residual subgradient inequality. isProxPoint_iff_subgradient : Exact convex proximal optimality condition.

For sufficiency, expanding the quadratic difference gives \(Q_{\lambda,x}(y)-Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\ge\|y-p\|^2/(2\lambda)\) when the residual is a support at \(p\). Thus the support not only proves global optimality but quantifies the objective increase away from \(p\). Necessity is obtained by short line-segment competitors and a limit, so the equivalence does not assume a differential first-order condition for the original nonsmooth function.

steps.title: Firmness gives uniqueness and two contractions
steps.body:
Apply subgradient monotonicity to \((x-p)/\lambda\) and \((y-q)/\lambda\). Multiplying by \(\lambda\) gives \(\|p-q\|^2\le\langle x-y,p-q\rangle\). For a common input, the right side is zero, so \(p=q\). Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\|p-q\|\le\|x-y\|\). Finally expand \(\|(x-y)-(p-q)\|^2\); firmness bounds its mixed term and proves \(\|(x-p)-(y-q)\|\le\|x-y\|\).

Formal correspondence: IsProxPoint.firm : Firm nonexpansiveness follows from convex proximal optimality. IsProxPoint.nonexpansive : Proximal minimizers are nonexpansive in the input. IsProxPoint.residual_nonexpansive : The residual of the proximal mapping is also nonexpansive.

Put \(u=x-y\) and \(v=p-q\). Firmness gives \(\langle u,v\rangle\ge\|v\|^2\), hence \(\|u-v\|^2\le\|u\|^2-\|v\|^2\le\|u\|^2\). This proves contraction of the residual map \(I-P_\lambda\) with the same unit constant. If the inputs coincide, firmness forces \(v=0\), which proves uniqueness independently of the compact-attainment argument.

steps.title: Compact attainment and the chosen map
steps.body:
For \(\lambda>0\), define

\[ Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=g_2(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda},\qquad P_\lambda(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_p Q_{\lambda,x}(p). \]

A finite-valued convex function on a finite-dimensional real space is continuous. If \(g_2\ge b\), then outside a sufficiently large ball the quadratic term makes \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\) exceed \(Q_{\lambda,x}(x)=g_2(x)\). A continuous function attains its minimum on that closed ball, and the same point therefore minimizes it globally. The proof explicitly constructs a suitable radius from \(\sqrt{2\lambda(g_2(x)-b)}+1\).

The Lean definition chooses a minimizer when one exists and assigns zero outside that domain. All mathematical endpoints establish existence from convexity, the lower bound, and positive \(\lambda\); their conclusions do not depend on that fallback value. Strict convexity of the quadratic, expressed through the variational characterization below, gives uniqueness.

The existence argument first uses finite-dimensional convexity of a finite-valued function to obtain continuity. If \(f\ge b\), a radius \(R>\sqrt{2\lambda(f(x)-b)}\) ensures \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)>f(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}(x)\) whenever \(\|p-x\|>R\). A minimum on the compact closed ball is therefore global. The chosen-map theorem invokes this existence result under its explicit assumptions, then uniqueness identifies all minimizers. Consequently later occurrences of prox denote the actual unique minimizer on the positive-parameter domain.

Formal correspondence: exists_proxPoint : Existence of proximal minimizers for finite-valued convex potentials bounded below. Finite-valued convex functions are automatically continuous in finite dimensions. prox : Choice of a true proximal minimizer, with zero as a harmless value off the existence domain. prox_isProxPoint : On its mathematical domain, prox attains the quadratic minimum.

Choose a closed ball centered at \(x\) that contains every point where the objective can improve on its value at \(x\). The lower bound on the potential and positivity of the quadratic coefficient provide such a ball. Continuity gives a minimizer on this compact set; outside it the objective is larger than the known competitor value. The minimizing point is therefore global and is the unique point characterized by the residual support condition.

ProximalLangevin/Moreau.lean.title: Moreau envelope: gradient, smoothness and finite bias
ProximalLangevin/Moreau.lean.summary:
The Moreau envelope is an actual minimum value, not a formal smoothing symbol. Comparing neighboring minimizing objectives proves a two-sided quadratic remainder and identifies its gradient with the scaled proximal residual. A global value Lipschitz bound on the original potential also yields finite residual and uniform value-gap estimates, which later control smoothing bias.

Let \(f\) be finite-valued, convex and bounded below on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and \(\lambda>0\). Set \(P=P_\lambda\), \(f^\lambda(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}(P x)\), and \(r(x)=(x-Px)/\lambda\).

steps.title: Value bounds and the exact residual
steps.body:
The envelope is the objective value at the actual chosen minimizer. Testing its objective with \(p=x\) proves \(f^\lambda(x)\le f(x)\). If \(f\ge b\), the nonnegative quadratic penalty also proves \(f^\lambda\ge b\). The residual definition is at this point only a vector formula; its gradient interpretation is proved below.

Formal correspondence: moreau : Moreau envelope, evaluated at the selected true proximal point. residual : The proximal residual, which is the actual Moreau gradient on its domain. moreau_le : The Moreau envelope lies below the original potential. le_moreau : The Moreau envelope is above every common lower bound of the potential.

Testing the minimization problem with the input itself removes the quadratic penalty and gives the upper value bound. At the minimizing point, the original lower bound and nonnegative penalty give the lower value bound. These comparisons show that the envelope is finite everywhere on the positive-parameter domain. They do not yet identify its derivative; that identification requires the neighboring-objective comparison.

steps.title: Global supports and quadratic upper remainder
steps.body:
Use the residual subgradient at \(P x\), test it at \(P y\), and expand the two quadratic penalties. The remaining squared norm is nonnegative, yielding \(f^\lambda(x)+\langle r(x),y-x\rangle\le f^\lambda(y)\). Conversely use \(P x\) as a competitor in the objective at \(y\), giving an upper remainder \(\|y-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\). For \(z=ax+by\), multiply the supports at \(z\) by \(a,b\ge0\), \(a+b=1\); their linear terms cancel and prove convexity.

Formal correspondence: moreau_support : The proximal residual supports the Moreau envelope globally. moreau_upper : Quadratic upper Taylor bound for the Moreau envelope. moreau_convex : Convexity of the envelope is a consequence of its global supports.

For the lower estimate, the residual support at \(P_\lambda x\) controls the change in original potential between the two minimizers. Combining it with their quadratic penalties leaves a nonnegative square. For the upper estimate, keep the old minimizer as a competitor at the new input and expand only its quadratic penalty. The resulting remainder is bounded above by \(\|y-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\), uniformly in the choice of nearby input.

steps.title: Nonexpansiveness and the derivative
steps.body:
Define \(g_2^\lambda(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}(P_\lambda(x))\) and \(r_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-P_\lambda(x))\). The subgradient inequality at the actual minimizer proves the lower support bound, while comparison with that same minimizer in the neighboring objective proves the upper bound:

\[ 0\le g_2^\lambda(y)-g_2^\lambda(x) -\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle \le\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}. \]

The right side is little-o of \(\|y-x\|\), so the envelope is differentiable and \(\nabla g_2^\lambda=r_\lambda\). The global supports imply convexity. Nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\) then yields

\[ \|\nabla g_2^\lambda(x)-\nabla g_2^\lambda(y)\| \le\lambda^{-1}\|x-y\|. \]

The gradient is continuous, so the actual envelope is continuously differentiable. This establishes the regularity needed by the existing Langevin theorem even when the original potential has corners.

The key derivative estimate is the two-sided remainder \[0\le f^\lambda(x+h)-f^\lambda(x)-\langle r_\lambda(x),h\rangle\le\frac{\|h\|^2}{2\lambda}.\] Dividing by \(\|h\|\) makes the upper bound \(\|h\|/(2\lambda)\to0\). The declaration moreau_hasGradientAt packages this Fréchet remainder estimate, moreau_differentiable forgets the derivative value, and gradient_moreau identifies the derivative's Riesz vector with the residual. The continuity of that residual, already obtained from nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\), upgrades differentiability to \(C^1\).

Formal correspondence: prox_lipschitz : The selected proximal mapping is nonexpansive. residual_lipschitz : The actual envelope residual has the sharp 1 / lam Lipschitz constant. moreau_hasGradientAt : The Moreau envelope is differentiable, with gradient equal to its proximal residual. moreau_differentiable : Differentiability of the actual Moreau envelope. gradient_moreau : Exact formula for the actual Moreau gradient. moreau_contDiff : The envelope is continuously differentiable, even when f is nonsmooth.

With \(y=x+h\), the remainder divided by \(\|h\|\) is at most \(\|h\|/(2\lambda)\), which tends to zero. This is the Fréchet differentiability criterion with derivative \(h\mapsto\langle r_\lambda(x),h\rangle\). The residual-map contraction yields its global gradient Lipschitz constant \(1/\lambda\). Thus the envelope has the exact regularity required for a smooth Langevin step, even though the original function need not be differentiable.

steps.title: Bounded residual and a sharp uniform gap
steps.body:
Assume \(f\) is convex, bounded below and globally \(K\)-Lipschitz, with \(K\ge0\) and \(\lambda>0\). Fix an input \(x\), let \(p=P_\lambda(x)\) be its actual proximal minimizer, and write \(r=(x-p)/\lambda\). Proximal optimality gives \(r\in\partial f(p)\). Test this support at \(p+r\), then apply value Lipschitzness:

\[ \|r\|^2\le f(p+r)-f(p)\le K\|r\|. \]

If \(r=0\), the desired bound is immediate; otherwise cancel the positive norm. Thus \(\|r\|\le K\), and the identity \(x-p=\lambda r\) gives the displacement estimate \(\|x-p\|\le\lambda K\).

For the envelope value, the competitor \(p=x\) gives \(f^\lambda(x)\le f(x)\). To obtain the reverse comparison, put \(d=\|p-x\|\) and use the exact minimizing objective value:

\[ \begin{aligned} f(x)-f^\lambda(x) &=f(x)-f(p)-\frac{d^2}{2\lambda}\\ &\le Kd-\frac{d^2}{2\lambda}\\ &=\frac{\lambda K^2}{2}-\frac{(d-\lambda K)^2}{2\lambda} \le\frac{\lambda K^2}{2}. \end{aligned} \]

The completed-square remainder is nonnegative because \(\lambda>0\). Combining both comparisons yields the uniform finite gap \(0\le f(x)-f^\lambda(x)\le\lambda K^2/2\) for every input. For \(U=g_1+f\) and \(V_\lambda=g_1+f^\lambda\), the same gap gives \(V_\lambda\le U\le V_\lambda+\lambda K^2/2\). This pointwise sandwich can be exponentiated and integrated to compare the actual marginal potentials; it requires no Taylor expansion or passage of an asymptotic remainder through an integral.

Formal correspondence: residual_norm_le : The Moreau gradient has norm at most the Lipschitz constant of f . prox_displacement_le : A Lipschitz potential moves each proximal point by at most lam K . moreau_lower_of_lipschitz : Sharp uniform approximation bound for a K -Lipschitz potential. moreau_gap_of_lipschitz : The pointwise Moreau correction is nonnegative and at most lam K² / 2 .

ProximalLangevin/StrongMoreau.lean.title: Strong convexity after full Moreau smoothing
ProximalLangevin/StrongMoreau.lean.summary:
Smoothing the full strongly convex potential weakens its modulus by the exact resolvent factor \(1+m\lambda\). The proof evaluates the envelope at a convex combination of its two minimizers and combines the potential's convexity deficit with the quadratic penalty's deficit. A completed square gives the optimal coefficient for this comparison.

Smoothing an entire \(m\)-strongly convex potential changes its modulus to \(m_\lambda=m/(1+m\lambda)\). This proof needs \(m\ge0\), \(\lambda>0\), convex minimizer existence and a lower bound, without differentiability of the original function.

steps.title: Two exact quadratic identities
steps.body:
For \(a+b=1\), expand inner products to prove \(\|au+bv\|^2=a\|u\|^2+b\|v\|^2-ab\|u-v\|^2\). The needed effective modulus follows from the exact square

\[m\|u\|^2+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{\lambda}-\frac{m\|v\|^2}{1+m\lambda}=\frac{\|(1+m\lambda)u-v\|^2}{\lambda(1+m\lambda)}\ge0.\]

Formal correspondence: norm_convexCombo_sq : Exact square identity for a convex combination in a real inner product space. weighted_quadratic_lower : The quadratic infimal convolution has the sharp effective modulus.

The first identity follows by expanding every inner product and collecting the mixed term. In the second identity, the denominator \(\lambda(1+m\lambda)\) is positive because \(\lambda>0\) and \(m\ge0\). Its right side is therefore nonnegative. The inequality obtained by dropping this square transfers two separate deficits, one in proximal outputs and one in residuals, into a deficit in the original input difference.

steps.title: Compare actual minimizers
steps.body:
If \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex, its actual full Moreau envelope is

\[ m_\lambda=\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\text{-strongly convex}. \]

The proof evaluates the envelope at the convex combination of its two actual proximal minimizers, applies strong convexity to \(U\), and uses the exact square identity for that combination. The remaining comparison is the weighted quadratic inequality

\[ \frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\|v\|^2 \le m\|u\|^2+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{\lambda}. \]

Completing the square proves this inequality with the displayed sharp modulus. No differentiability of \(U\) is needed. In contrast, smoothing only \(g_2\) preserves the modulus of the unsmoothed \(g_1\); the two constructions must not share a convexity constant by notation alone.

Let \(p=P_\lambda(x)\), \(q=P_\lambda(y)\), \(z=ax+by\), and test the objective at \(ap+bq\), with \(a+b=1\). The potential contributes the deficit \(\frac{mab}{2}\|p-q\|^2\); the quadratic penalty contributes \(\frac{ab}{2\lambda}\|(p-q)-(x-y)\|^2\). The weighted quadratic inequality bounds their sum below by \(\frac{ab}{2}\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\|x-y\|^2\), proving the exact strong-convexity definition for the envelope. Positivity of \(\lambda(1+m\lambda)\) makes the completed-square remainder nonnegative.

Formal correspondence: moreau_strongConvex : The actual Moreau envelope preserves strong convexity with the exact reduced modulus.

Let \(u=p-q\) be the minimizer difference and \(v=x-y\) the input difference. The convex combination of the minimizers is an admissible competitor for the envelope at the convex combination of inputs. The two squared deficits are \(m\|u\|^2\) and \(\|u-v\|^2/\lambda\). Their lower bound is \(m\|v\|^2/(1+m\lambda)\), so the envelope obeys precisely the strong-convexity inequality with the displayed reduced modulus.

ProximalLangevin/ProximalEnergy.lean.title: The nonsmooth single-pair energy estimate
ProximalLangevin/ProximalEnergy.lean.summary:
The energy inequality compares the true proximal output with any comparator while retaining the original nonsmooth potential difference at the input. An input subgradient controls the difference between input and proximal output. Completing a square produces a forcing term proportional to the square of the proximal scale, the correct quantity for summing particle energy estimates.

For convex \(f\), a true proximal minimizer \(p=P_\eta(x)\), positive \(\eta\), and a genuine input subgradient \(s\in\partial f(x)\), proximity controls both squared distance and the original nonsmooth energy.

steps.title: Expand supports and complete a square
steps.body:
Let \(p=P_\lambda(y)\), \(s\in\partial g_2(y)\), and \(a\) be any comparator. Proximal optimality supplies the residual subgradient at \(p\). Combine its support inequality at \(a\) with the support inequality for \(s\) at \(p\), expand the squared distances, and use the nonnegative square \(\|(y-p)-\lambda s\|^2\). The result is v3 Lemma A.8:

\[ \|p-a\|^2\le\|y-a\|^2 -2\lambda\bigl(g_2(y)-g_2(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2\|s\|^2. \]

If \(\|s\|^2\le C\), replace the last term by \(\lambda^2C\). The proof works with any genuine subgradient satisfying that bound; it does not assume an energy estimate or a convergence statement. Taking the minimal section in C1 is one way to supply such a vector.

Formal correspondence: isProxPoint_energy_le : Proximity decreases squared distance and nonsmooth energy, up to the squared norm of any subgradient at the input point.

Write \(d=x-p\). The residual support at \(p\) implies \(2\eta[f(p)-f(a)]\le2\langle d,p-a\rangle\). The input support gives \(f(x)-f(p)\le\langle s,d\rangle\). Add these to the squared-distance expansion. The remaining scalar expression is \(2\eta\langle s,d\rangle-\|d\|^2\le\eta^2\|s\|^2\), obtained from \(\|d-\eta s\|^2\ge0\).

steps.title: Instantiate the chosen point and bound the forcing
steps.body:
The existence theorem proves that the chosen \(P_\eta(x)\) meets the variational premise. Substitution gives \(\|P_\eta(x)-a\|^2\le\|x-a\|^2-2\eta(f(x)-f(a))+\eta^2\|s\|^2\). If \(\|s\|^2\le C\), multiply by the nonnegative \(\eta^2\) to replace the final term by \(\eta^2 C\). The vector must satisfy the true support inequality; a merely named subgradient is insufficient.

Expand \(\|p-y\|^2=\|x-y\|^2-2\langle x-p,x-y\rangle+\|x-p\|^2\), and use the residual subgradient at \(p\) to replace its pairing with the potential difference. A supplied subgradient \(s_x\in\partial f(x)\) bounds the remaining difference \(f(x)-f(p)\) by \(\langle s_x,x-p\rangle\). Completing the square gives \(2\lambda\langle s_x,x-p\rangle-\|x-p\|^2\le\lambda^2\|s_x\|^2\). Thus a bound \(\|s_x\|^2\le C\) produces the forcing \(\lambda^2C\). This algebra is why that forcing has a squared proximal scale.

Formal correspondence: prox_energy_le : The deterministic nonsmooth energy estimate for the actual chosen minimizer of the proximal objective. prox_energy_le_of_subgradient_bound : A squared-subgradient bound supplies the forcing term in Lemma A.8.

The comparator is arbitrary, so the same deterministic inequality can later be applied with a random reference point pointwise. A bound on \(\|s\|^2\) supplies only the last forcing term; it does not replace the requirement that \(s\) be a genuine supporting subgradient. The positive scale ensures both actual minimizer existence and validity of the residual optimality characterization used in the argument.

ProximalLangevin/ParticleEnergy.lean.title: Jensen repairs the averaged pairwise energy
ProximalLangevin/ParticleEnergy.lean.summary:
The common parameter is averaged after independent pairwise proximal calculations. This averaging is generally different from minimizing one shared-state proximal objective. The valid lifted energy estimate is obtained by Jensen's inequality for the parameter output, exact scaling of latent output squares, and a sum of genuine single-pair energy inequalities.

The scaled state is \(z=(\theta,x_1/\sqrt N,\ldots,x_N/\sqrt N)\), with \(N>0\), and \(J_i z=(\theta,x_i)\). The actual algorithm averages proximal parameter outputs; this module proves its energy inequality directly.

steps.title: Averaging squares in the shared parameter
steps.body:
Cauchy–Schwarz for finite sums gives \(N(N^{-1}\sum_i b_i)^2\le\sum_i b_i^2\). Apply it separately to each parameter coordinate of the pairwise outputs. Each latent block instead satisfies an exact equality after multiplying by \(N\), since \((\sqrt N)^2=N\). Summing all coordinates yields

\[\|\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)-a\|^2\le\frac1N\sum_i\|P(J_i z)-J_i a\|^2.\]

The first declaration is the scalar Jensen inequality \(N\bar b^2\le\sum_i b_i^2\), with \(\bar b=N^{-1}\sum_i b_i\). It follows by multiplying the average-of-squares inequality by positive \(N\); hn supplies exactly that sign and the nonzero denominator.

For the state-space comparison, write \(p_i=P(A_i z)\), with \(A_i z=(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\), and let the comparison state be \(a\). In parameter coordinate \(j\), the discrepancy is the average of \(p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}\), since the common comparison parameter is the same for every pair. The local identity hid inside hθ moves that constant through the average, and scalar Jensen gives

\[N\left|\frac1N\sum_i p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}\right|^2\le\sum_i|p_{i,\theta,j}-a_{\theta,j}|^2.\]

For particle coordinate \((i,j)\), unscaling instead gives the exact identity

\[N|N^{-1/2}p_{i,x,j}-a_{i,j}|^2=|p_{i,x,j}-\sqrt N a_{i,j}|^2.\]

This is hx, using \((\sqrt N)^2=N\). Expand the two Euclidean squared norms into finite coordinate sums, exchange the parameter and particle summations, and add the parameter inequalities to the exact latent identities. The result is \(N\|\operatorname{Pair}P(z)-a\|^2\le\sum_i\|p_i-A_i a\|^2\); division by \(N>0\) proves the displayed bound. No convexity or proximal property of \(P\) is used at this geometric stage.

Formal correspondence: average_sq_le : Jensen's inequality for an average of real coordinates. pairwiseMap_sq_dist_le : Squared distance of the actual averaged output is bounded by the average of the separate pairwise squared distances. This holds for every joint map.

For vectors \(b_i\), Jensen says \(\|N^{-1}\sum_i b_i\|^2\le N^{-1}\sum_i\|b_i\|^2\). Here \(b_i\) is the parameter component of the \(i\)-th output minus the common comparator parameter. Each latent component instead contributes exactly \(N^{-1}\|p_{i,x}-\sqrt N a_i\|^2\). Adding both blocks gives the displayed inequality for completely arbitrary pair maps, independently of their convex or proximal properties.

steps.title: Sum genuine proximal energy inequalities
steps.body:
The roadmap on v3 page 19 identifies averaged pairwise proximity with the proximal map of the lifted averaged potential. Shared parameter coordinates prevent that identity in general. The needed energy conclusion can nevertheless be proved without changing the algorithm.

For arbitrary pair outputs, Jensen's inequality for their averaged parameter gives

\[ \|\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)-a\|^2 \le\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|P(J_i z)-J_i a\|^2. \]

The scaled latent-coordinate contribution is an exact identity; only the parameter contribution requires an inequality. Apply the single-pair proximal energy result to every summand. Using \(\sum_i\|J_i(z-a)\|^2=N\|z-a\|^2\) and \(G_2=N^{-1}\sum_i g_2\circ J_i\) gives

\[ \|\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda}(z)-a\|^2 \le\|z-a\|^2-2\lambda\bigl(G_2(z)-G_2(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2C. \]

This lifted energy inequality is fully proved for actual minimizers. It repairs the deterministic proof bridge needed in Corollary A.13 while preserving the paper's particle algorithm and its original nonsmooth energy. It is still only one part of the full stochastic convergence proof.

The failure of the lifted-proximal identity has a concrete Lipschitz witness. Take \(N=2\), \(g_2(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\), smoothing one, common input parameter \(1\) and physical particles \((0,4)\). The genuine pairwise proximal points are \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((2,3)\). Averaging only their parameter components gives \((5/4,1/2,3)\). In the lifted proximal objective with its scaled particle norm, the feasible point \((1,1,3)\) has value \(3/2\), while this pairwise output has value \(51/32\). The strict inequality is kernel checked below. The averaged energy proof above repairs the necessary estimate without this false identity.

Apply the preceding true proximal energy inequality separately at \(A_i z\), comparing to \(A_i y\). Sum all \(N\) inequalities, and use \(\sum_i\|A_i(z-y)\|^2=N\|z-y\|^2\). Jensen's inequality bounds the squared norm of the averaged parameter output, while the scaled latent output gives exact squared terms. After division by positive \(N\), the energy difference is \(N^{-1}\sum_i[f(A_i z)-f(A_i y)]\), and the remainder is the average of the actual squared subgradient bounds. This establishes the inequality for the implemented pairwise map without identifying it with a single proximal map on the shared state.

Formal correspondence: pairwise_prox_energy_le : The actual averaged pairwise proximal update satisfies the lifted energy estimate for the original nonsmooth potential. This proves the bridge needed in v3 Corollary A.13 directly, without a false prox -of-a-sum identity. The bound only needs one bounded subgradient at each pair input. In particular the paper's bound on the least-norm subgradient supplies this hypothesis whenever that minimal section is available.

After applying the single-pair inequality, the initial squared distances sum to \(N\|z-a\|^2\). The potential differences sum to \(N[G_2(z)-G_2(a)]\), and the squared subgradient bounds average to the stated forcing constant. Dividing by \(N>0\) therefore gives the required state estimate. The argument uses only a comparison inequality for the actual averaged output; it does not claim that this output solves a shared-parameter minimization problem.

ProximalLangevin/Algorithms.lean.title: Exact maps for MYIPLA, PIPULA and PIPGLA
ProximalLangevin/Algorithms.lean.summary:
The three proximal particle schemes use the same scaled state geometry but place deterministic drift, proximity and Gaussian noise in different orders. These pointwise definitions are valid before choosing a probability law. Residual calculus then identifies which updates are exactly Euler steps for a Moreau-smoothed potential and which require a separate splitting analysis.

Write \(F_g(z)=\sum_i g(J_i z)\), \(h=\gamma/N\), and \(a=\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\). This module first defines pointwise algorithms for an arbitrary joint map \(P\); probabilistic assumptions enter later modules.

steps.title: The pair map and coordinate outputs
steps.body:
Define \(\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)_\theta=N^{-1}\sum_i(P(J_i z))_\theta\) and \(\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)_{x_i}=N^{-1/2}(P(J_i z))_x\). These coordinate formulas specify the map separately on its parameter and latent blocks. This averaging is part of the algorithm, and does not assert that the map minimizes a lifted objective.

Formal correspondence: pairwiseMap : Apply a joint map to each common-parameter/particle pair, then average its parameter outputs and rescale its particle outputs.

The map acts on every physical pair using the same old parameter, then returns one parameter by averaging all proposed parameter outputs. Each proposed latent output returns only to its own particle block. The factors \(1/N\) and \(1/\sqrt N\) thus have different roles. They encode a common parameter and the scaled latent geometry, rather than independent parameter copies evolving alongside the particles.

steps.title: Where each algorithm places its noise
steps.body:
PIPGLA, v3 equations (11)–(14), first takes the noisy smooth \(g_1\) step and then applies the averaged pairwise proximal map. In scaled coordinates it is

\[ y_n=z_n-\frac\gamma N\nabla\!\left(\sum_i g_1(J_i z_n)\right) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\xi_n, \qquad z_{n+1}=\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda}(y_n). \]

PIPULA is the special MYIPLA update with \(g_1=0\) and \(\lambda=\gamma\), followed by Gaussian noise. Both distinctions are encoded in separate definitions and proved reduction identities. The PIPGLA proximity step occurs after the noise; its target in the v3 convergence analysis is the original nonsmooth Gibbs model. The MYIPLA theorem cannot be reused merely by renaming this composition.

For clarity, the expanded MYIPLA definition itself is

\[T_{\mathrm{MY}}(z,\xi)=(1-\gamma/\eta)z-\frac\gamma N\nabla F_{g_1}(z)+\frac\gamma\eta\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\xi.\]

These are exact definitions of pointwise maps. The residual-gradient theorem below proves when this expanded map equals a smoothed Euler step.

Formal correspondence: pipulaUpdate : PIPULA: pairwise proximity, followed by noise. myiplaUpdate : MYIPLA, with independent smoothing and time steps. pipglaUpdate : PIPGLA: the noisy smooth forward step is followed by the pairwise proximal map. The common parameter is averaged only at the end.

In MYIPLA, proximity is evaluated at the old state and appears through its residual in an explicit drift. In PIPGLA, proximity is evaluated after the smooth drift and Gaussian perturbation. These compositions give different random variables even with the same innovation. Therefore their deterministic identities must be checked separately before any convergence theorem is transferred from a smooth Euler chain.

steps.title: A recursion with supplied innovations
steps.body:
For an update \(T\), define \(Z_0=z_0\) and \(Z_{n+1}=T(Z_n,\xi_n)\). The zero and successor lemmas unfold these equations. Supplying the three explicit updates defines their full chains for any initial state and innovation sequence; Gaussianity, measurability and convergence are not premises of these pointwise definitions.

Formal correspondence: algorithmChain : Iterate the displayed state update against a specified innovation sequence. myiplaChain : The full MYIPLA recursion, without any convergence assumption.

A finite recursion requires only an update function, an initial state and a sequence of innovation vectors. Induction determines every iterate uniquely. When measurability and independence are later imposed, this same deterministic map of the inputs defines the probability law. Separating the pointwise construction from these probabilistic requirements allows the exact algorithm identities to be reused on different coupling spaces.

steps.title: The PIPULA specialization is an identity
steps.body:
PIPULA has parameter update \(N^{-1}\sum_i(P(J_i z))_\theta+a\xi_\theta\). In MYIPLA set \(g_1=0\) and \(\eta=\gamma\ne0\). The lifted gradient of the constant potential vanishes, \(1-\gamma/\gamma=0\), and \(\gamma/\gamma=1\), so the updates agree. Replacing the update in the common recursion proves equality at every iteration.

Formal correspondence: pipulaUpdate_parameter : PIPULA's parameter component is precisely the averaged joint proximal parameter output, followed by the parameter Gaussian noise. pipulaUpdate_eq_myiplaUpdate : Removing the smooth part and equating the two time scales recovers PIPULA exactly, including its noise placement. pipulaChain_eq_myiplaChain : The exact PIPULA/MYIPLA specialization holds for every iteration.

When the two positive scales are equal, the coefficient multiplying the old state in the expanded residual update is zero and the coefficient multiplying its pairwise proximal image is one. With no smooth potential, nothing remains before the added noise except that image. The equality holds for each input and innovation, so induction gives equality of all finite-time chains and subsequently of their laws.

steps.title: Recover physical parameter and particle formulas
steps.body:
Differentiate the lifted sum: its parameter block is \(\sum_i\nabla_\theta g_1(J_i z)\), while its scaled latent block is \(\sqrt N\nabla_x g_1(J_i z)\). Substitution gives the displayed MYIPLA coordinate equations. Multiplying a latent coordinate by \(\sqrt N\) changes its noise coefficient to \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) and its smooth force coefficient to \(\gamma\), using \(\sqrt N\sqrt{2\gamma/N}=\sqrt{2\gamma}\).

Formal correspondence: myiplaUpdate_parameter : The MYIPLA parameter coordinate is the displayed averaged pairwise formula. myiplaUpdate_particle : The MYIPLA physical-particle coordinate is exactly the displayed physical-particle formula.

The physical parameter equation retains the average smooth force and the average proposed proximal parameter. The physical latent equation retains its individual force and proximal latent output. Multiplying by \(\sqrt N\) removes the scaling only from the latent block, including its Gaussian coefficient. This conversion shows directly that the state-space definitions implement the intended particle equations with parameter variance reduced by particle count.

steps.title: Residual proximity is exactly an Euler step
steps.body:
Given any map \(P\) on one joint parameter-particle pair, define its particle action by applying \(P\) separately to each \(J_i z\), averaging the resulting parameter coordinates, and dividing each resulting physical particle coordinate by \(\sqrt N\). The common parameter is not optimized independently for each particle and then kept as \(N\) separate state variables; the averaging is part of the algorithm.

With \(P=P_\lambda\), MYIPLA in v3 equations (9)–(10) is exactly the noisy Euler step for \(V_\lambda=g_1+g_2^\lambda\). Indeed, the pairwise residual-gradient identity gives

\[ \operatorname{Pair}_P(z)=z-\frac\lambda N\nabla\!\left(\sum_i g_2^\lambda(J_i z)\right). \]

Substituting this into the expanded MYIPLA formula cancels the extra multiples of \(z\), leaving

\[ z_{n+1}=z_n-\frac\gamma N\nabla\mathcal V_\lambda(z_n) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi_n. \]

The coordinate proofs also recover parameter noise \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) and physical-particle noise \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). The full recursion identity follows by induction on the iteration count.

The recursion declarations include the initial and successor identities for each supplied innovation sequence. All pointwise identities concern the explicit state update, before any stochastic convergence theorem is applied.

For \(P(x)=x-\lambda r(x)\), the parameter coordinate of the pairwise map is its original parameter minus \(\lambda\) times the average parameter residual. Each latent coordinate similarly loses \(\lambda/\sqrt N\) times its pair residual. These are exactly the blocks of \((\lambda/N)\nabla V_N(r)\), using the previously proved lifted-gradient identities. Add \(\nabla g_1+\nabla e=\nabla(g_1+e)\) under differentiability and set the proximal scale to the Euler scale to identify the MYIPLA update with scaledUpdate. Induction then identifies the entire pointwise chain, not merely its first step.

Formal correspondence: pairwiseMap_eq_gradient_step : A pairwise residual gradient becomes the corresponding lifted Euler step. This is an equality of actual coordinate maps, not an assumed law identity. gradient_add_of_differentiable : The gradient of a sum, with the differentiability hypotheses explicit. myiplaUpdate_eq_scaledUpdate : The expanded MYIPLA step is exactly IPLA for g₁ + e whenever e has the genuine proximal residual gradient. myiplaChain_eq_scaledChain : The entire expanded recursion agrees pointwise with the existing IPLA recursion for the smoothed potential.

Substitute \(P_\eta(v)=v-\eta\nabla g_2^\eta(v)\) in every pair. Averaging the parameter residual and rescaling each latent residual reproduces exactly \((\eta/N)\nabla F_{g_2^\eta}\). Inserting this identity into MYIPLA cancels the extraneous old-state coefficients. Adding the smooth gradient leaves the Euler force of \(g_1+g_2^\eta\), with the original Gaussian perturbation unchanged. Equality of full chains follows from equality of these updates.

ProximalLangevin/MYIPLA.lean.title: Smoothed-model MYIPLA laws and finite-time convergence
ProximalLangevin/MYIPLA.lean.summary:
MYIPLA is exactly Gaussian interacting Langevin for the split-smoothed joint potential \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\). The unsmoothed strongly convex part preserves curvature, while the Moreau residual adds gradient Lipschitz constant \(1/\eta\). The resulting theorem concerns actual finite-moment algorithm laws and their error about the smoothed marginal maximizer.

Let \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\), where \(g_1\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex and \(g_2\) is convex and bounded below. The actual expanded proximal recursion is identified with Gaussian IPLA for \(V_\eta\).

steps.title: Construct the right convexity and smoothness constants
steps.body:
The scalar potential is \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\). Its envelope is convex, so adding the two convex-combination inequalities preserves strong convexity \(m\). Differentiability of both terms proves \( abla V_\eta= abla g_1+ abla g_2^\eta\); the triangle inequality then adds gradient constants. The nonnegative-real constant used by Lean equals \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\) when \(\eta>0\).

Formal correspondence: smoothedPotential : The pair potential of MYIPLA, with only its nonsmooth part regularized. smoothingLipschitz : Smoothing adds the inverse smoothing scale to the smooth gradient bound. smoothed_strongConvex : Adding a convex envelope preserves the strong convexity of the smooth part. smoothed_gradient_lipschitz : The gradient Lipschitz constants of the smooth part and envelope add.

For convex-combination weights, the envelope contributes a nonpositive convexity deficit and the smooth part contributes the quadratic deficit with modulus \(m\). Their sum therefore has the same strong-convexity modulus. For gradients, subtract at two points and use the triangle inequality on the two component differences, giving \(L_\eta=L_1+1/\eta\). These are joint-space constants; lifting multiplies both by particle count.

steps.title: Identify actual laws before using convergence
steps.body:
Define \(\rho_n=Q\circ Z_n^{-1}\) from the explicitly expanded chain. The pointwise chain identity gives equality of pushforward laws with IPLA for any differentiable envelope having the stated residual gradient. The IPLA recursion is an actual \(L^2\) random variable. Projection by the bounded parameter map and subtraction of a constant preserve \(L^2\), proving finite parameter error about every fixed center without any convergence assumption.

The random variables are first identified by the exact residual-envelope update equality. Their almost-everywhere representative equalities then imply equality of pushforward measures, so the later convergence theorem concerns the actual MYIPLA law. Finite second moments follow from a Lipschitz score acting on \(L^2\) initial data and \(L^2\) innovations; the parameter error about a fixed center remains in \(L^2\) after applying the continuous parameter projection and subtracting a constant. These moment facts justify the ordinary RMS integral in the public bound.

Formal correspondence: myiplaLaws : The law of the expanded MYIPLA recursion, for arbitrary supplied maps. myiplaLaws_eq_iplaLaws : Pointwise equivalence identifies the actual MYIPLA law with the IPLA law. myiplaLaws_parameter_memLp : Every projected MYIPLA error has a finite second moment whenever the initialization and innovations are in L2 . This is derived from the actual chain, without Gaussianity, equilibrium, or an error bound assumption.

The exact pointwise recursion equality is stronger than a comparison estimate: both descriptions produce the same state for the same inputs. Their distributions therefore agree under any admissible initialization and innovation law. Lipschitz drift growth propagates finite second moments, and parameter projection is bounded. Subtraction of a deterministic center preserves square integrability, ensuring the final parameter RMS is an ordinary finite expectation.

steps.title: Apply sharp IPLA to a general residual envelope
steps.body:
The Moreau envelope is convex. Therefore adding it to the \(m\)-strongly convex function \(g_1\) preserves the constant \(m\). Adding their gradient-Lipschitz estimates gives \(L_\lambda=L_1+1/\lambda\). The replicated-pair identity \(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2\) then yields lifted strong convexity \(Nm\), lifted smoothness \(NL_\lambda\), and lifted dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\).

Applying the existing Gaussian ULA result at step \(\gamma/N\) produces the contraction \((1-m\gamma)^n\) and the discretization term

\[ \frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\lambda}{m} \sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma. \]

The step condition \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_\lambda)\) is the corresponding scaled ULA condition. Initial finite second moments and Gaussian-law independence are explicit. The continuous reference and finite transport quantities are constructed by the shared theorem, so no convergence estimate or invariant measure is an additional MYIPLA hypothesis.

The law-identification helpers also prove that the actual expanded recursion is probability-valued and that its parameter error about every fixed center belongs to \(L^2\). These guards are used before passing from extended norms to ordinary real square-root integrals in the original-center theorem.

With \(\theta_\eta\) a maximizer of the smoothed marginal and \(\Pi_{N,\eta}\) its actual Gibbs reference, the complete statement is

\[\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\eta})+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The generic theorem allows any convex differentiable envelope with the stated residual gradient and \(\eta^{-1}\) gradient constant; the next step derives those properties for the true Moreau envelope.

Formal correspondence: myipla_parameter_rms_smoothed : An explicit finite-time RMS parameter bound for MYIPLA around the maximizer of its smoothed marginal likelihood. All Gaussian-law hypotheses describe the algorithm's actual innovations. The dependence on the smoothing scale is explicit through L₁ + eta-¹ .

The sharper equilibrium radius is \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\), while the Euler bias depends on \(L_\eta/m\). The physical step restriction is precisely the lifted restriction after canceling \(N\). Thus increasing particle count reduces equilibrium parameter spread but does not compensate for arbitrarily small smoothing scale in the gradient constant. All terms refer to the continuous smoothed Gibbs reference and the actual discrete MYIPLA law.

steps.title: Discharge the envelope and moment hypotheses
steps.body:
For the actual Moreau envelope, the proximal calculus proves all inputs: convexity, differentiability, \(\nabla g_2^\eta=\eta^{-1}(I-P_\eta)\), and gradient Lipschitz constant \(\eta^{-1}\). Substitute these into the generic smoothed theorem and the finite-moment lemma. The output is the pushforward by an almost everywhere measurable \(L^2\) representative; mapping the whole probability space to the whole state space proves total mass one.

For the genuine envelope, the proximal module supplies the residual identity \(\nabla g_2^\eta=(I-P_\eta)/\eta\), its differentiability and convexity, and the score Lipschitz constant \(\eta^{-1}\). Adding the smooth part gives \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), modulus \(m\) and score constant \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\). The theorem therefore discharges each abstract envelope assumption before applying the sharp IPLA estimate. The associated probability and moment declarations establish that the final law has total mass one and a finite projected RMS, independently of merely writing its integral.

Formal correspondence: moreau_myipla_parameter_rms : MYIPLA with the actual proximity minimizer and its actual Moreau envelope. Every analytic envelope property used by the stochastic theorem is derived from convexity and a lower bound on g₂ . In particular, no residual-gradient identity, stationarity result, concentration bound, or convergence estimate is an additional hypothesis of this theorem. moreau_myipla_parameter_memLp : Finite moments for MYIPLA with its genuine Moreau/proximal construction. moreau_myipla_isProbability : The actual MYIPLA output is a probability law. Measurability follows from the identified L2 recursion, rather than being assumed for the map.

Actual proximal minimization supplies the envelope's convexity, differentiability and residual gradient. Its complement contraction supplies the \(1/\eta\) score constant. Substituting these established facts removes the abstract envelope premises from the general result. Probability mass follows from the measurable pushforward of a probability source, and finite moments follow independently from the recursion, so the numerical convergence bound does not conceal either requirement.

ProximalLangevin/Theorem.lean.title: MYIPLA about the original nonsmooth marginal maximizer
ProximalLangevin/Theorem.lean.summary:
The original-center MYIPLA bound combines smoothed-model convergence with a finite uniform potential gap. Integrating that gap gives a gap between marginal potentials, which controls displacement of their actual maximizers by strong convexity. The result keeps the smoothing, equilibrium, transient and discretization terms separate, with no asymptotic Taylor remainder assumed.

Assume \(g_1\) is differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(g_2\) is convex, bounded below and \(K\)-Lipschitz. Let \(m,\eta,\gamma>0\), \(N>0\), and \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_1+\eta^{-1})\). Initialization is in \(L^2\), and the actual Gaussian innovations are independent across times and coordinates and independent of initialization.

steps.title: A finite approximation creates an actual original center
steps.body:
The envelope gap gives \(V_\eta\le U\le V_\eta+\eta K^2/2\), where \(U=g_1+g_2\). The smooth strongly convex comparison supplies Gaussian domination and decay of the original marginal \(k_U(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\). Its continuity and vanishing at infinity imply that it attains a positive maximum. Existence of this original center is derived, rather than added as an independent model premise.

Formal correspondence: smoothedPotential_gap : The true smoothed pair potential is a one-sided uniform approximation of the original pair potential, with the sharp Lipschitz Moreau value gap. moreau_original_maximizer_exists : The original nonsmooth model has an actual marginal maximizer under the primitive MYIPLA assumptions; no maximizer existence assumption is hidden.

The inequalities \(e^{-\eta K^2/2}e^{-V_\eta}\le e^{-U}\le e^{-V_\eta}\) hold on every latent fiber. The smooth comparison has Gaussian tails, so the original marginal is finite, positive and dominated by a decaying Gaussian. Continuity follows by dominated convergence. A positive continuous function decaying at infinity attains a maximum, proving that the original statistical center exists under the primitive assumptions.

steps.title: Compare the actual marginal centers
steps.body:
For the actual split Moreau approximation, \(\delta=\lambda K^2/2\), so

\[ \|\theta_\star-\theta_{\lambda,\star}\| \le\sqrt{\frac{\lambda K^2}{m}}. \]

The original and smoothed marginal maximizers exist under the primitive assumptions. The square-integrable triangle inequality then gives

\[ \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_{\lambda,\star}\|^2\right)^{1/2} +\|\theta_{\lambda,\star}-\theta_\star\|. \]

The finite-moment guards are proved before identifying extended norms with real square-root integrals. Substituting the smoothed-model convergence estimate proves the original-center result stated above.

This is deliberately weaker in smoothing order than Proposition A.1's claimed linear expansion. The result requires no Hessian along a parameter fiber and no uniform Taylor domination. The weaker order is a change in the established result, not a silently omitted term.

The finite envelope gap is \(0\le U-V_\eta\le\delta=\eta K^2/2\). Integrating the corresponding exponential inequalities in the latent variable and taking logarithms gives a parameter-marginal potential gap of the same size. If \(\theta_\eta\) minimizes the smoothed marginal potential, strong convexity yields \[\frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|^2\le\delta,\qquad\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|\le\sqrt{\eta K^2/m}.\] The hypotheses hmaxU and hmaxη identify the actual two marginal maximizers, so this is a bound on their displacement rather than the choice of an arbitrary comparison center.

Formal correspondence: moreau_marginal_center_distance : A genuine finite smoothing-bias bound for marginal maximizers. It holds without twice differentiability, a fibrewise Hessian premise, or Taylor remainders: squared displacement is at most eta*K²/m .

At their respective minimizing parameters, compare \(F_{V_\eta}(\theta_U)\) with \(F_{V_\eta}(\theta_\eta)\) using the marginal sandwich and minimality of \(\theta_U\). The increase is at most \(\eta K^2/2\). Quadratic growth gives at least \((m/2)\|\theta_U-\theta_\eta\|^2\). Comparing and taking square roots yields the finite \(O(\sqrt\eta)\) center displacement; a linear-order claim would need additional arguments.

steps.title: Move the finite error and substitute the proved bound
steps.body:
Let \(U=g_1+g_2\) on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\). Assume \(g_1\) is differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), and has \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient. Assume \(g_2\) is finite-valued, convex, bounded below, and \(K\)-Lipschitz. For \(\lambda>0\), set

\[ V_\lambda=g_1+g_2^\lambda,\qquad L_\lambda=L_1+\lambda^{-1}. \]

Take \(N>0\), an initial state with finite second moment, independent standard Gaussian innovations at every coordinate and time, independent of initialization, and

\[ 0<\gamma\le\frac{2}{m+L_\lambda}. \]

Write \(\mu_n\) for the law of the actual scaled MYIPLA state and \(\Pi_{\lambda,N}\) for its continuous Gibbs target. Let \(\theta_\star\) maximize the original latent marginal \(\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\). The formal estimate is

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\sqrt{\frac{\lambda K^2}{m}} +\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+(1-m\gamma)^n W_2(\mu_0,\Pi_{\lambda,N})\\ &+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\lambda}{m} \sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma. \end{aligned} \]

The target normalization, finite transport moments, stationary reference, and equilibrium concentration are derived through the existing IPLA/ULA development. Neither the displayed convergence bound nor the smoothing bias is an extra assumption. The last term retains its explicit dependence on \(\lambda\); no uniformity in the smoothing scale is asserted. The paper's \(O(\lambda)+O(\lambda^2)\) smoothing expression is replaced by a finite \(O(\sqrt\lambda)\) guarantee, so this is a related proved theorem, not a verbatim reproduction of Theorem 4.1.

In Lean the proof first establishes that the actual MYIPLA law is probability-valued and its error about the smoothed center is square integrable. The center-change inequality then has valid finite real square-root integrals. Add the proved center displacement to the smoothed theorem, giving exactly the displayed four terms.

First apply the proved MYIPLA bound about \(\theta_\eta\). Its finite second moment makes the center-change inequality valid in real RMS form. Then \[\bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_U\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\le\bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}+\|\theta_\eta-\theta_U\|.\] Substitute the preceding center displacement estimate. Thus smoothing bias, equilibrium concentration and finite-step algorithmic error enter for three different proved reasons; the original nonsmooth target is never assumed to have a Lipschitz score.

Formal correspondence: moreau_myipla_parameter_rms_original : A fully proved finite-time theorem for the actual MYIPLA iterates and the original nonsmooth model's marginal maximizer. This is a finite replacement for the Taylor-based statement in v3 Theorem 4.1: the smoothing bias is sqrt (eta*K²/m) , and the discretization constant explicitly depends on eta . There are no interpolation, entropy-production, or convergence hypotheses.

Apply Minkowski to \(\theta_n-\theta_U=(\theta_n-\theta_\eta)+(\theta_\eta-\theta_U)\). The first term is controlled by the smoothed algorithm theorem and the second is a deterministic constant with the proved displacement bound. This produces exactly the four displayed contributions. The discretization coefficient still contains \(L_1+1/\eta\), so the statement records the actual tradeoff between smoothing scale and admissible time step.

ProximalLangevin/ProjectionCenter.lean.title: Move the center of a finite projected RMS error
ProximalLangevin/ProjectionCenter.lean.summary:
Changing a deterministic comparison center costs at most the distance between the two centers in RMS. The proof first works with extended norms, establishes finiteness at the new center, and only then writes ordinary square-root expectations. Probability normalization makes the norm of a constant equal to its Euclidean norm.

For a probability measure \(\mu\) and bounded linear map \(T\), write \(R_\mu(a)=\|T(\cdot)-a\|_{L^2(\mu)}\), initially as an extended nonnegative number. Finiteness is checked before converting this norm to a real number.

steps.title: Minkowski and finiteness
steps.body:
The identity \(Tx-a=(Tx-b)+(b-a)\) and Minkowski yield \(R_\mu(a)\le R_\mu(b)+\|b-a\|\). A constant has that \(L^2\) norm because \(\mu\) has mass one. If \(R_\mu(b)<\infty\), the right side is finite, hence the error about \(a\) is finite too.

Write \(R_a=\|Tx-a\|_{L^2(\mu)}\). The code's heq is the pointwise identity \(Tx-a=(Tx-b)+(b-a)\). Since \(\mu\) has mass one, the constant function \(b-a\) has \(L^2\) norm exactly \(\|b-a\|\). Thus eLpNorm_add_le gives \(R_a\le R_b+\|b-a\|\) even if \(R_b=\infty\). The second declaration uses the finite right-hand side to prove \(R_a<\infty\); it does not assume a second moment about the new center.

Formal correspondence: projectedRMS_center_le : Minkowski controls the change of a parameter center, with infinite moments still represented by the extended norm. projectedRMS_center_finite : A finite error about one center implies finiteness about every center.

For a finite measure of mass \(M\), a constant vector would instead have \(L^2\) norm \(\sqrt M\|b-a\|\). Here \(M=1\), which explains the exact center-distance term. Minkowski is valid before finiteness, and a finite old-center RMS makes its right side finite. Thus existence of the new-center second moment is a consequence of the comparison, rather than an additional assumption.

steps.title: Pass to ordinary square-root integrals
steps.body:
Monotonicity of the extended-to-real conversion is valid once the upper bound is finite. This proves the real RMS inequality. Use the proved finite moments at both centers to identify the norms with \(\sqrt{\int\|Tx-a\|^2d\mu}\) and \(\sqrt{\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu}\). The resulting formula cannot hide an infinite moment through the totalized real integral.

The order of operations matters: first prove finiteness at \(b\), then at \(a\), then apply ENNReal.toReal_mono. Only after these guards does projectedRMSReal_eq_sqrt_integral identify both real norms with \((\int\|Tx-a\|^2d\mu)^{1/2}\) and \((\int\|Tx-b\|^2d\mu)^{1/2}\). This prevents an infinite moment from being silently converted to the real number zero.

Formal correspondence: projectedRMSReal_center_le : The usual real-valued center-change inequality, guarded by a proved finite moment at the comparison center. sqrt_integral_center_le : The integral form follows after both finite quadratic moments have been established.

Once the two moments are finite, the extended norms agree with the nonnegative square roots of their squared-distance integrals. The same inequality then becomes \(R_\mu(a)\le R_\mu(b)+\|a-b\|\) in real numbers. This order is important because totalized real integration or extended-to-real conversion alone would not distinguish an infinite moment from a valid finite quantity.

ProximalLangevin/Perturbation.lean.title: Uniform potential gaps and marginal-center displacement
ProximalLangevin/Perturbation.lean.summary:
A one-sided uniform gap between potentials survives latent integration with the same gap size after taking negative logarithms. A smooth strongly convex comparison also supplies analytic control of the original marginal. Combining the marginal sandwich with strong quadratic growth proves an explicit displacement bound for the two actual centers.

Let \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), with \(V\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, \(m>0\), and \(U\) continuous. Write \(k_W(\theta)=\int e^{-W(\theta,x)}dx\) and \(F_W=-\log k_W\). This module derives positive finite marginals and actual maximizers before comparing centers.

steps.title: Quadratic growth needs only strong convexity
steps.body:
Let \(F\) be \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m\ge0\), and let \(z\) be a global minimizer. Fix any comparator \(x\), and set

\[ A=\frac m2\|x-z\|^2,\qquad G=F(x)-F(z). \]

Both numbers are nonnegative. For \(0<t<1\), apply strong convexity along the segment from \(z\) to \(x\), and use global minimality at the intermediate point:

\[ F(z)\le F((1-t)z+tx) \le (1-t)F(z)+tF(x)-t(1-t)A. \]

Subtract \(F(z)\) and divide by the positive number \(t\). This gives \((1-t)A\le G\) for every such \(t\). To conclude using only a finite comparison, suppose \(G<A\). Then \(A>0\), and the choice

\[ t=\frac{A-G}{2A}\in(0,1/2] \]

is admissible. But it makes \((1-t)A=(A+G)/2>G\), contradicting the preceding inequality. Therefore \(A\le G\), which is the sharp growth bound

\[ F(x)\ge F(z)+\frac m2\|x-z\|^2. \]

No derivative of \(F\) is used: the argument needs only the convex-combination inequality and actual global minimality. In the marginal-center comparison, this lower bound turns a finite increase in marginal potential into an upper bound on the squared distance between centers.

Formal correspondence: strongConvex_minimum_growth : A global minimizer of a strongly convex function has the sharp quadratic growth bound, even when the function is not differentiable.

steps.title: Integrate the gap before taking logarithms
steps.body:
For any potentials \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), exponentiation and integration in the latent variable give

\[ e^{-\delta}k_V(\theta)\le k_U(\theta)\le k_V(\theta), \qquad k_W(\theta)=\int e^{-W(\theta,x)}dx. \]

The smooth strongly convex comparison potential \(V\) supplies positive finite integrals and an integrable Gaussian bound. The original marginal is continuous and decays at infinity; hence it has an actual maximizer. Taking negative logarithms, which is justified by positivity, gives

\[ F_V(\theta)\le F_U(\theta)\le F_V(\theta)+\delta, \qquad F_W=-\log k_W. \]

Let \(\theta_U\) minimize \(F_U\) and \(\theta_V\) minimize the \(m\)-strongly convex \(F_V\). Minimality and the sandwich imply \(F_V(\theta_U)-F_V(\theta_V)\le\delta\). Strong-convexity growth about its minimizer therefore yields

\[ \frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le\delta. \]

This argument never differentiates the original marginal and never integrates an asymptotic remainder.

The sharp quadratic-growth lemma uses strong convexity and global minimality, without differentiability of the marginal potential. The comparison model supplies an integrable Gaussian bound for the original weights, giving continuity and existence of an original marginal maximizer by dominated convergence and decay at infinity. Finite positive marginal integrals are established before logarithms and real conversions.

For \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), exponentiation reverses the potential order: \(e^{-\delta}e^{-V}\le e^{-U}\le e^{-V}\). Integrating each latent fiber gives \(e^{-\delta}M_V(\theta)\le M_U(\theta)\le M_V(\theta)\). Positivity and finiteness of the reference marginal then imply the same for \(M_U\); only after that can one use monotonicity of the logarithm to obtain \(F_V\le F_U\le F_V+\delta\), where \(F=-\log M\). These guards exclude taking logarithms of zero or infinite marginal integrals.

Formal correspondence: marginalDensity_sandwich : A one-sided uniform perturbation transfers directly to the actual extended-valued latent integrals. No real conversion or normalization is used. marginalPotential_sandwich : The two negative log marginal likelihoods differ by at most the same uniform potential gap. Integrability of the nonsmooth original weight is derived by domination by the smooth strongly convex comparison potential.

Exponentiation reverses the potential order, while integration preserves the order of nonnegative functions. Because the reference marginal is positive and finite, the original marginal inherits both properties. Taking logarithms is now legitimate and gives the same finite additive gap \(\delta\). Performing integration before logarithms avoids any unsupported replacement of a logarithm of an integral by an integral of a logarithm.

steps.title: Establish original-marginal existence
steps.body:
The inequality \(e^{-U}\le e^{-V}\) and strong-convexity Gaussian bounds prove integrability. Continuity follows by dominated convergence on parameter neighborhoods, using the comparison potential to provide an integrable latent majorant. The same Gaussian estimate proves decay at parameter infinity. A positive continuous function that vanishes at infinity attains its maximum on a sufficiently large compact ball.

The uniform gap dominates the original latent weight by an integrable reference weight, giving finite latent integrals. Locally uniform domination also permits passage to the limit in the parameter and proves continuity of the original marginal integral. The reference's Gaussian decay in the parameter then transfers through the sandwich, so the original marginal vanishes at infinity. A continuous positive marginal attaining a positive value must achieve its maximum on a sufficiently large compact ball. This is how existence of the original center follows from finite smoothing, rather than an added optimizer-existence assumption.

Formal correspondence: integrable_original_marginal : A continuous nonsmooth original potential has finite latent integrals when it dominates the smooth strongly convex comparison potential. continuous_original_marginal : The original marginal is continuous by a Gaussian dominated convergence argument, even though its joint potential may be nonsmooth. exists_original_marginalMaximizer : A maximizer of the actual nonsmooth marginal exists; existence is not an extra statistical premise added to the Moreau comparison argument.

For a convergent parameter sequence, continuity of the original potential gives pointwise convergence of the latent weights. The comparison Gaussian gives an integrable dominating function uniform on that sequence. Dominated convergence proves marginal continuity. Retaining the Gaussian's parameter factor proves decay at infinity, so compact attainment supplies an actual original maximizer. These facts justify using real marginal potentials at every parameter value.

steps.title: Strong growth controls the center shift
steps.body:
Positive finite marginal densities make \(-\log\) order-reversing, so an original marginal maximizer minimizes \(F_U\). At minimizers \(\theta_U,\theta_V\), the sandwich and minimality give \(F_V(\theta_U)\le F_U(\theta_U)\le F_U(\theta_V)\le F_V(\theta_V)+\delta\). The preserved marginal strong convexity yields \(\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le2\delta/m\); taking the nonnegative square root gives the distance estimate.

Formal correspondence: original_maximizer_minimizes : Marginal maximization for the actual nonsmooth model is equivalent to minimization of its finite negative log marginal likelihood. marginal_center_distance_sq : A fully nonasymptotic marginal-center perturbation bound. Only the comparison model is assumed smooth. The centers maximize the actual marginal integrals; they are not joint modes. marginal_center_distance : The square-root form of the uniform-gap marginal-center estimate.

The chain of comparisons uses minimality only once, at \(\theta_U\): \(F_U(\theta_U)\le F_U(\theta_V)\). The uniform gap handles the two other links. Thus the comparison-potential increase at \(\theta_U\) is at most \(\delta\), and strong growth gives distance at most \(\sqrt{2\delta/m}\). The original potential need not itself be differentiable or have a Lipschitz gradient.

ProximalLangevin/PIPULA.lean.title: Full-potential PIPULA and its smoothed-center theorem
ProximalLangevin/PIPULA.lean.summary:
PIPULA is a genuine proximal step for the whole potential followed by Gaussian noise. It equals Euler Langevin for the full Moreau envelope at the same scale. Full smoothing reduces curvature, so the theorem must use \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\) and targets the smoothed marginal center. The resulting generic Euler bias is retained with its actual scale dependence.

Assume the full nonsmooth potential \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex and bounded below, with \(m,\gamma>0\). Global Lipschitzness of \(U\) is not required. The theorem concerns the maximizer of the marginal of \(U^\gamma\).

steps.title: The actual full-envelope modulus makes the step admissible
steps.body:
Set \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)>0\). Since \(\gamma m_\gamma=m\gamma/(1+m\gamma)\le1\), we have \(\gamma(m_\gamma+\gamma^{-1})\le2\), equivalently \(\gamma\le2/(m_\gamma+\gamma^{-1})\). All multiplications and divisions have positive denominators.

Formal correspondence: fullSmoothingModulus : Strong convexity after smoothing the entire potential. pipula_admissible_step : With smoothing equal to the time step, the envelope always meets the proved Gaussian ULA step restriction.

Since \(m\gamma/(1+m\gamma)<1\), multiplication by the positive step gives \(\gamma m_\gamma+1\le2\). Rearranging yields the required Euler restriction for gradient constant \(1/\gamma\). The same formula shows \(1-m_\gamma\gamma=1/(1+m\gamma)>0\), the exact contraction factor arising from the full envelope. No global Lipschitz bound on the strongly convex original potential is needed.

steps.title: The proximal/noise law is the actual IPLA law
steps.body:
The law is the pushforward of the exact PIPULA recursion. Set \(g_1=0\) and \(\eta=\gamma\) in the pointwise MYIPLA identity. Actual proximal optimality gives \(P_\gamma=I-\gamma\nabla U^\gamma\), so the full chain equals IPLA for \(U^\gamma\), and hence their pushforwards agree.

Formal correspondence: pipulaLaws : The probability law defined by the paper's pairwise PIPULA recursion. pipulaLaws_eq_iplaLaws : Exact equality between the displayed PIPULA law and IPLA for the genuine full Moreau envelope.

Proximal optimality identifies \(P_\gamma(v)=v-\gamma\nabla U^\gamma(v)\) for the full joint envelope. The pairwise residual identity lifts this to a state-space Euler drift. Adding the Gaussian vector after proximity gives the actual PIPULA update. Pointwise equality propagates through the recursion, and its measurable pushforward then equals the corresponding Gaussian IPLA law at every finite iteration.

steps.title: Sharp concentration and Gaussian discretization
steps.body:
The algebraic reduction \(g_1=0\), \(\lambda=\gamma\) is proved for the actual update and its full recursion. Together with the envelope theory, it supplies genuine proximity, smoothness, and strong-convexity facts for a full-potential scheme.

It does not reproduce v3 Corollary A.6's original-center finite-time bound. In assumption B1, the displayed proximal inner-product deficit \(\mu\) gives the envelope-gradient strong-monotonicity constant \(\mu/\gamma\), since the residual is divided by \(\gamma\). A scale-uniform PIPULA discretization theorem and an original-center estimate with the paper's rate remain unproved here; substituting a \(1/\gamma\) smoothness bound into a generic ULA estimate alone would not establish the claimed vanishing error.

A separate proved finite-time result is supplied for the actual PIPULA chain around the maximizer of its smoothed marginal. Assume the original finite-valued potential is \(m\)-strongly convex and bounded below; global Lipschitzness of the strongly convex potential is not imposed. For \(\gamma>0\), its full envelope has modulus \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\) and gradient Lipschitz constant \(1/\gamma\). The actual proximal/noise recursion equals IPLA for that envelope, and the admissible-step inequality holds automatically. The resulting sharp concentration and Gaussian-chain bound are fully proved. Its conservative discretization term is \((33/20)(1/(\gamma m_\gamma))\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma\), whose coefficient diverges as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). This is not a reproduction of the paper's original-center \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\) convergence rate.

Writing \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\), \(\Pi_{N,\gamma}\) for the full-envelope target and \(\theta_\gamma\) for its marginal maximizer, the exact bound is

\[\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\gamma\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm_\gamma}}+(1-m_\gamma\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\gamma})+\frac{33}{20}\frac{\gamma^{-1}}{m_\gamma}\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

Prove full-envelope convexity and differentiability, identify the exact algorithm law, apply the sharp IPLA theorem with gradient constant \(\gamma^{-1}\), and use the already proved admissible-step inequality. This gives every displayed term from the actual chain.

Here the whole joint potential is smoothed, so the relevant modulus is \(m_\eta=m/(1+m\eta)\), rather than \(m\). The score constant of the full envelope is \(1/\eta\). The exact proximal/noise update identity reduces PIPULA to IPLA for that envelope, after which the theorem applies the sharp concentration and Gaussian discretization estimates with these constants. The admissible-step proof checks the actual inequality \(\gamma\le2/(m_\eta+1/\eta)\); substituting the unsmoothed modulus would give a different and unjustified step restriction.

Formal correspondence: pipula_parameter_rms_smoothed : A complete finite-time bound for PIPULA around the maximizer of the smoothed marginal. The original potential may be nonsmooth and need not be globally Lipschitz. All envelope properties, the time-step restriction, normalization, finite transport moments, and equilibrium concentration are proved from the displayed assumptions and the actual Gaussian innovations.

The equilibrium radius uses the reduced modulus, and the discretization term uses \((1/\gamma)/m_\gamma\). Thus this application of the generic theorem does not prove a vanishing discretization error as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). Its valid conclusion is the displayed finite-step bound about the smoothed center. An original-center theorem with a uniform small-step rate would require a sharper full-envelope analysis beyond this substitution.

ProximalLangevin/PIPULAConsistency.lean.title: A conditional consistency test for global assumptions
ProximalLangevin/PIPULAConsistency.lean.summary:
Positive strong monotonicity forces an unbounded field on a nontrivial Euclidean space. A globally Lipschitz potential has a bounded Moreau gradient, so combining that property with a positive global residual deficit can be inconsistent. The conclusion applies to the literal conjunction of those global assumptions and does not invalidate different full-potential hypotheses.

On a nontrivial real Hilbert space, a globally bounded field cannot be strongly monotone with a positive constant. This is used only for the literal specialization that also makes the full potential globally Lipschitz.

steps.title: Boundedness contradicts positive global monotonicity
steps.body:
Assume \(\|R(x)\|\le K\) and \(c\|x-y\|^2\le\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle\) with \(c>0\). Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality give \(c\|x-y\|^2\le2K\|x-y\|\). Choose a nonzero vector and scale its norm beyond \(2K/c\). The two inequalities are incompatible.

If \(\|b(x)\|\le K\) globally but \(\langle b(x)-b(y),x-y\rangle\ge q\|x-y\|^2\) with \(q>0\), Cauchy–Schwarz implies \(q\|x-y\|\le2K\) for every distinct pair. Along a nonzero direction one can choose arbitrarily distant points, contradicting this uniform upper bound. The second theorem applies the obstruction to a true proximal residual: a globally Lipschitz potential gives a bounded residual. Thus the stated positive global deficit condition cannot be combined with those hypotheses in positive dimension.

Formal correspondence: bounded_field_not_stronglyMonotone : A globally bounded field cannot have a positive strong-monotonicity constant on a nontrivial real Hilbert space.

Choose points separated by a distance \(r>2K/c\). Strong monotonicity gives a lower bound \(cr^2\) for the pairing, whereas boundedness gives an upper bound \(2Kr\). Division by positive \(r\) yields \(cr\le2K\), contradicting the choice. A nonzero direction supplies arbitrarily large \(r\), so positive dimension is essential to the obstruction.

steps.title: Apply the obstruction to the true proximal residual
steps.body:
This check is conditional on how the appendix’s reduction is read. If setting \(g_1=0\) also carries A3 onto \(U=g_2\), then \(U\) is globally \(K\)-Lipschitz. Its actual Moreau gradient \(R_\gamma=\gamma^{-1}(I-P_\gamma)\) satisfies \(\|R_\gamma(x)\|\le K\). But B1 with positive deficit gives

\[ \frac{\mu}{\gamma}\|x-y\|^2 \le\langle x-y,R_\gamma(x)-R_\gamma(y)\rangle \le2K\|x-y\|. \]

A nontrivial real Hilbert space contains points at arbitrarily large distance, so these global premises are incompatible. This is kernel-checked for the actual proximal minimizer. If A3 is instead retained for an independent original decomposition \(U=g_1+g_2\), it does not make the full \(U\) Lipschitz; that reading requires its own full-envelope analysis. The result here is therefore a conditional consistency check, not a blanket assertion that Corollary A.6 is false. The separate PIPULA endpoint assumes strong convexity of the full potential and does not impose global Lipschitzness on it.

Formal correspondence: lipschitz_full_potential_not_proximal_deficit : Under a literal full-potential globally Lipschitz reading, B1 cannot hold with positive deficit in positive dimension. The separate PIPULA theorem therefore does not assume global Lipschitzness of the full strongly convex U.

The actual residual \(R_\gamma=(I-P_\gamma)/\gamma\) is bounded by the potential's global value Lipschitz constant. The proximal deficit gives strong monotonicity with coefficient \(\mu/\gamma\), including its inverse-step factor. Substitution in the general obstruction proves incompatibility when \(\mu>0\) and the space is nontrivial. A decomposition whose nonsmooth component is Lipschitz need not make the entire potential Lipschitz, so its analysis is a different case.

ProximalLangevin/SharpConcentration.lean.title: Sharp Gibbs concentration by dilation
ProximalLangevin/SharpConcentration.lean.summary:
A radial contraction of space compares an unnormalized Gibbs partition with its second moment. A one-sided scalar derivative at the identity dilation yields the sharp dimension-over-curvature constant. The argument differentiates an explicit polynomial in the dilation factor and requires only continuity and strong convexity of the potential itself.

Let \(F\) be continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space of dimension \(d\), with \(q>0\) and global minimizer \(z\). Gaussian domination supplies the integrals used below.

steps.title: A radial contraction compares partition integrals
steps.body:
Strong convexity and minimality imply \(F(z+r(x-z))\le F(x)-\frac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2\) for \(0\[Z+\frac q2(1-r^2)M\le r^{-d}Z,\qquad Z=\int e^{-F},\quad M=\int\|x-z\|^2e^{-F}.\]

Let \(w(x)=e^{-F(x)}\), \(Z=\int w\), \(M=\int\|x-z\|^2w(x)\,dx\), and \(d=\dim H\). Continuity and positive strong convexity first give integrability of both \(w\) and \(\|x-z\|^2w\). Strong convexity and the minimizer growth bound combine to give \[F(z+r(x-z))\le F(x)-\tfrac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2.\] Exponentiation and \(e^u\ge1+u\) imply \[w(z+r(x-z))\ge w(x)+\tfrac q2(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2w(x).\]

The local fact hpoint is exactly this last inequality. hip separately proves that the dilated weight is integrable, using translation invariance and nonzero scalar dilation. htrans computes its integral as \(r^{-d}Z\). Integrating hpoint now proves \(Z+\frac q2(1-r^2)M\le r^{-d}Z\), with every integral finite before the comparison.

Formal correspondence: sharp_gibbs_mode_dilation_inequality : The dilation inequality before taking the tangent limit.

Strong convexity along the segment from the mode to \(x\), together with quadratic growth from that mode, gives the radial deficit \(q(1-r^2)\|x-z\|^2/2\). Exponentiating and using \(e^u\ge1+u\) converts this into a density-plus-moment lower bound. Dilation changes volume by \(r^d\), so integrating the dilated density contributes \(r^{-d}Z\). Gaussian domination makes both sides finite.

steps.title: Take the sharp limit and normalize
steps.body:
