Multiply the dilation inequality by \(r^d\) and define \(\Phi(r)=r^d[Z+(q/2)(1-r^2)M]\). Then \(\Phi(r)\le Z=\Phi(1)\) for \(0\[\int\|x-z\|^2\pi(dx)=M/Z\le d/q,\qquad\pi(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-F(x)}dx.\]

The proof differentiates no potential and remains valid for continuous nonsmooth strongly convex \(F\).

Here hZ proves \(Z>0\), and hpart identifies the extended partition function with \(\iota Z\). The density change in heq therefore gives \[\int\|x-z\|^2\,d\pi(x)=Z^{-1}M.\] Multiplication of the unnormalized inequality by the nonnegative \(Z^{-1}\), followed by \(Z^{-1}Z=1\), yields \(\int\|x-z\|^2d\pi\le d/q\). Positive normalization is proved from the potential assumptions, rather than supplied as a moment or probability premise.

Formal correspondence: sharp_integral_sq_dist_gibbs_le : A continuous q -strongly convex Gibbs potential concentrates around its minimizer with sharp second moment at most dim / q . Every normalization and integrability fact used in the conclusion is proved from the stated inputs.

After obtaining \(qM\le dZ\), strict positivity of \(Z\) permits division. The normalized Gibbs moment is exactly \(M/Z\), by its density definition and the finite integrability of the moment weight. Therefore the estimate is \(d/q\). Neither a derivative of the potential nor a boundary integration identity is needed, making the estimate directly applicable to continuous nonsmooth strongly convex energies.

steps.title: The one-sided tangent calculation gives d/q
steps.body:
Retain \(Z,M,d\) from the dilation inequality and define \[\Phi(r)=r^d\bigl[Z+\tfrac q2(1-r^2)M\bigr].\] For \(0<r<1\), dilation proves \(\Phi(r)\le Z=\Phi(1)\). Thus for \(-1<u<0\), the quotient \((\Phi(1+u)-\Phi(1))/u\) is nonnegative: both numerator and denominator are nonpositive.

Differentiate this explicit scalar polynomial, rather than differentiating \(F\): \[\Phi'(1)=dZ-qM.\] In Lean, hinner differentiates the bracket, hder applies the product rule, and hnonneg records the sign of the left difference quotient. Its limit is \(\Phi'(1)\), so hbound gives \(dZ-qM\ge0\). Since \(q>0\), divide to obtain \(M\le(d/q)Z\).

Formal correspondence: sharp_integral_sq_dist_mul_exp_neg_le : Taking the tangent limit of the dilation inequality gives the exact dimension dependence, without differentiating the potential.

For negative increments \(u\) approaching zero, both \(\Phi(1+u)-\Phi(1)\) and \(u\) are nonpositive, so their quotient is nonnegative. Its limit equals \(dZ-qM\), computed by the product rule on the explicit scalar expression. The limit is therefore nonnegative. This sign argument explains why a bound valid only for contractions \(r<1\) still determines the derivative inequality at \(r=1\).

ProximalLangevin/SharpIPLA.lean.title: Sharp parameter concentration and the IPLA RMS bound
ProximalLangevin/SharpIPLA.lean.summary:
The sharp continuous-potential concentration estimate improves the equilibrium contribution in the particle theorem from twice dimension over curvature to dimension over curvature. The transport and Gaussian discretization arguments are unchanged. Exact marginal identification ensures that the improved estimate uses parameter dimension and the \(N\)-amplified marginal curvature.

A differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex pair potential \(U\), \(m>0\), has a marginal potential whose \(N\)-replicate target is \(Nm\)-strongly convex. The sharp dilation theorem improves its parameter second moment to \(d_\theta/(Nm)\).

steps.title: Concentration of the actual marginal target
steps.body:
For a continuous \(a\)-strongly convex potential \(f\) with minimizer \(x_\star\), the new dilation argument proves

\[ \int\|x-x_\star\|^2\,\pi(dx)\le\frac d a, \qquad\pi(dx)\propto e^{-f(x)}dx. \]

The proof uses a sharp radial growth inequality and a change of variables under dilation, rather than assuming an integration-by-parts identity for a nonsmooth density. It therefore applies directly to the continuous strongly convex Gibbs potentials needed here.

The existing Prékopa argument preserves strong convexity when latent variables are integrated out. Raising the marginal density to the \(N\)th power multiplies that modulus by \(N\). Applying the sharp estimate to its actual marginal potential gives

\[ W_2(\Pi_{\lambda,N}^{\theta},\delta_{\theta_{\lambda,\star}}) \le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}. \]

This matches the constant in v3 equation (17) and Lemma A.14. The previous IPLA theorem's \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\) estimate would have been weaker; the new result proves the sharper constant rather than labeling that factor as an error in the paper.

The exact parameter marginal of the lifted Gibbs measure is \(M(\theta)^N\) after normalization. Its negative log potential is \(NF(\theta)\), and the earlier Prékopa argument proves that it is \(Nm\)-strongly convex with minimizer \(\theta_*\). Sharp Gibbs concentration in dimension \(d_\theta\) gives \(\int\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2d\Pi_N\le d_\theta/(Nm)\). The pushforward identity transfers this same moment to the lifted state law before a square root is taken.

Formal correspondence: sharp_marginalTarget_secondMoment_le : Sharp equilibrium second moment of the actual powered marginal density. sharp_gibbsTarget_parameter_secondMoment_le : The exact parameter-marginal identity transfers sharp concentration to the full lifted Gibbs measure. sharp_gibbsTarget_parameter_concentration : The parameter RMS radius with the sharp dimension constant.

The parameter marginal density is proportional to \(e^{-N\Phi}\), so its mode is the actual statistical maximizer and its curvature is \(Nm\). Apply the sharp theorem in dimension \(d_\theta\), obtaining the second moment \(d_\theta/(Nm)\). The exact pushforward identity transfers this same moment to the enlarged target. Taking a nonnegative square root yields the improved equilibrium RMS radius.

steps.title: Combine sharp concentration with the actual Gaussian-chain law
steps.body:
For \(N>0\), \(\gamma>0\), \(\gamma\le2/(m+L)\), Gaussian independent innovations and \(L^2\) initialization, use the scaled ULA transport theorem and the nonexpansive parameter projection. The projected triangle inequality gives

\[\operatorname{RMS}_n\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_N)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The private lemma handles nonempty coordinate sets. The public theorem splits off the empty-coordinate case, where the parameter norm and its error vanish, so no artificial positive-dimension assumption remains.

For \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), the lifted state has score constant \(NL\), convexity \(Nm\) and step \(\gamma/N\). The shared Gaussian ULA theorem controls its \(W_2\) error, while the parameter projection has norm at most one. The projected RMS therefore is at most the sharp equilibrium scale \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\) plus that transport error. The nonempty-dimensional case proves this combination directly; the final declaration splits off zero-dimensional cases so that no unspoken positive-dimension premise remains.

Formal correspondence: sharp_ipla_parameter_rms : A complete actual Gaussian IPLA parameter bound with sharp concentration. This theorem includes zero parameter/latent dimensions.

For any coupling of the current state and Gibbs reference, project the difference with the norm-one parameter map and add the equilibrium parameter error. Minkowski then bounds current RMS by transport plus the sharp radius. Insert the established state-space Gaussian Euler bound. The zero-dimensional parameter case has zero error, and the singleton-state case has zero transport, so the same public inequality covers all independent natural dimensions.

ProximalLangevin/MYPGDNoise.lean.title: Orthogonal masks and the exact removed-noise cost
ProximalLangevin/MYPGDNoise.lean.summary:
Removing parameter noise can be compared exactly with retaining full Gaussian noise by using orthogonal coordinate masks. Independence of a fresh centered Gaussian makes the mixed squared-error term vanish. The additional mean-square cost is exactly the removed noise variance, involving parameter dimension and no latent dimension.

Let \(P_\theta\) retain the common parameter block of the scaled particle state, and \(P_x=I-P_\theta\) retain the latent blocks. For a standard Gaussian vector \(\xi\), the removed parameter noise has mean zero and second moment \(d_\theta\).

steps.title: Define the actual complementary coordinate projections
steps.body:
Set \(P_\theta(\theta,x)=(\theta,0)\) and \(P_x(\theta,x)=(0,x)\). Coordinate evaluation proves the four block identities by unfolding the definitions. These are bounded linear maps, so masking an \(L^2\) innovation remains an actual \(L^2\) random variable.

Denote the two maps by \(P_\theta\) and \(P_x=I-P_\theta\). On a scaled particle state, \(P_\theta(\theta,z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(\theta,0,\ldots,0)\), while \(P_x(\theta,z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(0,z_1,\ldots,z_N)\). The four coordinate lemmas establish these formulas directly; the subtraction defining latentNoiseCLM is an equality of continuous linear maps, so all later compositions are measurable.

Formal correspondence: parameterNoiseCLM : Retain the parameter coordinates and erase the latent coordinates. latentNoiseCLM : Retain precisely the latent noise of the original particle scheme.

The masks satisfy \(P_\theta+P_x=I\), \(P_\theta P_x=0\), and \(P_\theta^2=P_\theta\), \(P_x^2=P_x\). Thus their ranges are the orthogonal parameter and latent subspaces. Applying \(P_x\) changes only the innovation block; it leaves the deterministic drift map untouched. This is the geometry needed to compare MYPGD with its full-noise counterpart.

steps.title: Compute the projection geometry and Gaussian moments
steps.body:
The Euclidean square is \(\|P_\theta z\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}z_j^2\), hence \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\). A bounded linear map commutes with the Gaussian expectation, giving \(\mathbb E P_\theta\xi=0\). Each retained standard coordinate has second moment one; finite summation gives \(\mathbb E\|P_\theta\xi\|^2=d_\theta\).

The squared norm expands to \(\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}z_j^2\), with no latent terms. Every coordinate square is integrable because the standard Gaussian identity map belongs to \(L^2\). The coordinate variance identity gives \(\mathbb E z_j^2=1\) and the continuous-linear-map integration identity gives \(\mathbb E P_\theta Z=P_\theta\mathbb EZ=0\). Interchanging only a finite sum and the integral yields \(\mathbb E\|P_\theta Z\|^2=d_\theta\). No factor \(N\) belongs in this dimension count.

The projection keeps exactly \(d_\theta\) independent standard scalar coordinates. Their squares each have expectation one, so summing gives \(d_\theta\). The expectation is zero by linearity of the projection and centering of the full Gaussian. The moment calculation does not require assigning a particle noise variance to these coordinates: the particle factor enters later through the amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\).

steps.title: The product law cancels the mixed term exactly
steps.body:
For any square-integrable \(g\) on a probability space independent of \(\xi\), expand \(\|g+bP_\theta\xi\|^2\). Fubini and bilinearity factor its mixed expectation as \(\langle\mathbb E g,\mathbb E P_\theta\xi\rangle=0\). Thus

\[\mathbb E\|g+bP_\theta\xi\|^2=\mathbb E\|g\|^2+b^2d_\theta.\]

The proof establishes integrability of every term before distributing the integral.

For a general \(g\in L^2(\mu)\), use the actual product law \(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\), and expand \[\|g(x)+bP_\theta z\|^2=\|g(x)\|^2+2b\langle g(x),P_\theta z\rangle+b^2\|P_\theta z\|^2.\] The facts hgsq and hzsq prove integrability of the two squares on the product; hcross proves integrability of the bilinear term, so splitting the integral is justified. Independence here is the product-measure construction itself: integral_prod_bilin factors the mixed integral as \(\langle\mathbb Eg,\mathbb E P_\theta Z\rangle=0\). Hence \(\mathbb E\|g+bP_\theta Z\|^2=\mathbb E\|g\|^2+b^2d_\theta\), with no assumption that \(g\) is centered.

Formal correspondence: integral_add_parameterNoise_sq : Exact independent-noise identity, for an arbitrary square-integrable source. The mixed term vanishes by the actual product Gaussian law.

Independence concerns the fresh Gaussian and the preexisting discrepancy \(g\). It does not require \(g\) itself to be centered. In the squared expansion, Fubini factors \(\mathbb E\langle g,P_\theta\xi\rangle\) as the pairing of the two expectations; the second is zero. Consequently adding or subtracting the removed block has exactly the same variance cost \(b^2d_\theta\), without a triangle-inequality loss.

The proof uses the actual independence and common-law hypotheses, without assuming a stochastic error estimate.

For a measurable update, the time-\(n\) state is a measurable function of initialization and the innovation path. Independence of initialization from that path makes their joint law a product; iid innovations make the path law \(\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). ProximalLangevin/SplittingGaussianLaw.le.title: Canonical Gaussian law of the actual splitting algorithm
ProximalLangevin/SplittingGaussianLaw.le.summary:

The measurable splitting recursion depends only on this path law and its independent initial law. Hence the canonical scalar-product and vector-product descriptions yield the same actual PIPGLA distributions.

The scalar-coordinate Gaussian hypotheses determine the complete vector innovation law and its infinite iid path. Hence every realization with a fixed initial law gives the same actual PIPGLA output law.

steps.title: Assemble scalar coordinates into iid standard Gaussian vectors
steps.body:
The coordinate laws and their joint independence imply \(\xi_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\) as a full state vector, and independence of these vectors across \(k\). Together with initialization/path independence, the generic iid transfer theorem gives the chain law driven by \(\mathcal N(0,I)^{\otimes\mathbb N}\).

The hypothesis GaussianInnovations specifies laws and independence of all scalar coordinates over all times, as well as independence of initialization from the whole path. gaussianInnovations_vectorLaw groups a finite set of independent standard scalar Gaussians into a standard state-space Gaussian; gaussianInnovations_vectorIndependent groups the time slices into an independent vector family. The measurable recursion can then be pushed forward from the product of the initial law and this iid path law. Equality follows for the actual PIPGLA iterate at every finite time; it requires no invariant target.

Formal correspondence: pipglaLaws_eq_canonicalGaussian : The full iid vector Gaussian algorithm law follows from the original scalar-coordinate Gaussian hypotheses.

Each finite vector has the product of its coordinate standard Gaussian laws. Independence of disjoint time-coordinate index sets then gives independence of the full vectors at distinct times. These two facts determine the vector path product law. Together with initialization independence they supply exactly the inputs of the general iid recursion theorem, without requiring any stationary law of the chain.

steps.title: Use either canonical noise-path representation
steps.body:
The countable product of scalar Gaussian coordinates, grouped by iteration, has the same noise-path pushforward law as the vector product. Apply the measurable chain to this identity. Two probability-space realizations with the same initialization law therefore both equal the same canonical Gaussian chain law at time \(n\), proving equality of their actual output laws.

There are two descriptions of the same noise source: a countable product of scalar coordinates, packed into vectors, or a countable product of standard vector Gaussians. The first law identity uses noisePath_law directly; the second uses vector iid laws. To compare two probability spaces, rewrite both output laws in the vector representation and substitute the equal initial laws. The ambient probability spaces and their concrete random-variable representatives therefore disappear from the conclusion.

Grouping scalar coordinates into vectors is a measurable coordinate rearrangement. Its pushforward carries the scalar product Gaussian measure to the vector product Gaussian measure. Applying the same finite recursion to either source therefore gives identical laws. For two different probability spaces, only the common initial law remains to be matched; the concrete representatives and noise-source constructions disappear from the distributional conclusion.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingMoments.lean.title: Reference drift moments uniform over smoothing scales
ProximalLangevin/SplittingMoments.lean.summary:
The splitting reference requires a bound on its total drift magnitude that remains finite as the envelope scale decreases. Value Lipschitzness bounds the envelope gradient uniformly, while strong convexity and sharp Gibbs concentration control the smooth score relative to a true mode. This avoids using the envelope's diverging gradient Lipschitz constant in the numerical moment bound.

For \(F=f+e\), assume \(F\) is \(m\)-strongly convex, \(f,e\) differentiable, \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(\|\nabla e\|\le K\). The goal is a Gibbs drift bound using \(L,m,K\), without an inverse smoothing scale.

steps.title: The envelope preserves a global value Lipschitz constant
steps.body:
Let \(p=P_\lambda(y)\). As a competitor at \(x\), use \(p+x-y\), so its quadratic penalty equals that of \(p\) at \(y\). The \(K\)-Lipschitz inequality for \(f\) changes the function value by at most \(K\|x-y\|\). Thus \(f^\lambda(x)\le f^\lambda(y)+K\|x-y\|\), and reversing \(x,y\) proves the same global Lipschitz constant.

Choose the actual minimizer \(p=P_\lambda(y)\), and test the objective at \(x\) with \(p+(x-y)\). The two quadratic penalties agree because \(p+(x-y)-x=p-y\); only the potential value changes, by at most \(K\|x-y\|\). Therefore \(f^\lambda(x)\le f^\lambda(y)+K\|x-y\|\). Reversing the inputs gives the absolute-value bound. This competitor argument proves a value Lipschitz bound uniform in \(\lambda\), rather than using the score's larger constant \(1/\lambda\).

Formal correspondence: moreau_lipschitz_of_lipschitz : A Lipschitz potential has a Moreau envelope with the same Lipschitz constant.

The translated competitor makes the quadratic penalties identical, so the only difference comes from the original potential values. The original value Lipschitz constant therefore passes to the envelope unchanged. This argument is independent of the proximal scale and does not require a bound on how rapidly the envelope gradient varies. It is the magnitude of that gradient, rather than its Lipschitz constant, that is needed later.

steps.title: Find a true minimum and bound the smooth force there
steps.body:
Strong convexity gives quadratic coercivity. Minimize \(F\) on a sufficiently large closed ball, with radius \(2\| abla F(0)\|/m+1\); the quadratic lower bound proves the resulting point minimizes globally. At a global minimum \(z\), the local-extremum derivative vanishes. Hence \( abla f(z)=- abla e(z)\) and \(\| abla f(z)\|\le K\).

The strong-convexity lower bound forces the total potential above its value at zero outside a finite ball. A minimizer on the compact ball is therefore global; this is the radius construction in exists_strongConvex_minimum. At a global minimizer of \(F=f+e\), the derivative vanishes, giving \( abla f(z)=- abla e(z)\). Thus a pointwise bound \(\| abla e\|\le K\) yields \(\| abla f(z)\|\le K\). This is the only value of the smooth score at a specific point needed in the moment estimate.

Formal correspondence: gradient_eq_zero_at_minimum : A differentiable function has zero gradient at an actual global minimizer. exists_strongConvex_minimum : A smooth strongly convex real-valued function attains its minimum. gradient_smoothPart_at_minimum : At a minimum of the sum, a bounded second gradient bounds the first gradient.

A quadratic lower bound on the total strongly convex potential makes it exceed a known competitor outside a finite ball. Compact minimization supplies an actual global mode. At this differentiable mode, \( abla(f+e)=0\), so the smooth score equals the negative envelope score. The uniform envelope-gradient magnitude therefore gives a finite anchor value \(\| abla f(z)\|\le K\) for the smooth-score growth estimate.

steps.title: A bounded gradient remains bounded in L²
steps.body:
The norm of the derivative of a \(K\)-Lipschitz scalar function is at most \(K\); the gradient is its Riesz representative and has the same norm. For a pointwise bounded drift \(\|b(x)\|\le K\), almost everywhere representative equality gives \(\|b(Y)\|_{L^2}\le K\) on a probability space.

The derivative of a globally \(K\)-Lipschitz scalar function has operator norm at most \(K\), and the Riesz identification preserves this norm, giving \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le K\). Separately, if \(\|b(x)\|\le K\) for every input, then the representative equality for lpDrift gives \(\|b(Y(\omega))\|\le K\) almost everywhere. Since \(P\) has mass one, its \(L^2\) norm is at most \(K\). This explains why a state-space uniform bound transfers without a dimension or measure-mass factor.

Formal correspondence: gradient_norm_le_of_lipschitz : Global Lipschitzness bounds the actual gradient norm. lpDrift_norm_le_of_bounded : A pointwise bounded Lipschitz drift is bounded by the same constant in L2 .

For a differentiable \(K\)-Lipschitz function, difference quotients in every unit direction are bounded in absolute value by \(K\). Passing to the derivative and taking the supremum over directions gives the gradient norm bound. If that bound holds pointwise, integration over a probability space gives \(\mathbb E\|b(Y)\|^2\le K^2\). No particle dimension or inverse envelope scale is introduced.

steps.title: Integrate a sharp quadratic bound about the mode
steps.body:
Lipschitz continuity and the mode bound give \(\| abla f(x)\|\le L\|x-z\|+K\), so \(\| abla f(x)\|^2\le2L^2\|x-z\|^2+2K^2\). Sharp Gibbs concentration supplies \(\mathbb E_\pi\|x-z\|^2\le d/m\), yielding

\[\mathbb E_\pi\| abla f\|^2\le2L^2d/m+2K^2.\]

For any \(Y\) with actual Gibbs law \(\pi\), the pushforward integral formula transfers this estimate and taking square roots gives \(\| abla f(Y)\|_2\le\sqrt{2L^2d/m+2K^2}\).

Let \(z\) minimize \(F=f+e\), with \(F\) \(m\)-strongly convex. From the previous stage, \(\| abla f(z)\|\le K\), and score Lipschitzness gives \(\| abla f(x)\|\le L\|x-z\|+K\). Consequently \[\| abla f(x)\|^2\le2L^2\|x-z\|^2+2K^2.\] The Gibbs second moment is integrable by strong convexity; the right side therefore supplies an integrable majorant for the score square. The facts hbound and hgrad discharge that prerequisite before integral_mono is applied.

Sharp concentration yields \(\mathbb E_\pi\|X-z\|^2\le d/m\), so \(\mathbb E_\pi\| abla f(X)\|^2\le2L^2d/m+2K^2\). The next declaration transfers this actual Gibbs-law integral to any random variable with that law and takes its square root, obtaining the \(L^2\) drift bound used in the splitting reference.

Formal correspondence: integral_sq_smooth_gradient_le : A smoothing-uniform second moment for the smooth part of a Gibbs drift. Only the smooth part's own Lipschitz constant enters the bound. lpDrift_smooth_gradient_norm_le : The corresponding actual L2 smooth-drift bound for a random variable with the proved reference Gibbs law.

Center the smooth score at a mode of the total potential, not necessarily a mode of the smooth part alone. Lipschitzness gives \(\| abla f(x)\|\le L\|x-z\|+K\). Squaring and using \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) produces an integrable quadratic majorant. Sharp Gibbs concentration then gives the moment \(2L^2d/m+2K^2\), valid uniformly over any smoothing scales satisfying the same magnitude bound.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingCoupling.lean.title: Lipschitz energy and the averaged lifted potential
ProximalLangevin/SplittingCoupling.lean.summary:
The stochastic splitting proof needs an energy estimate for the actual averaged proximity map and a value Lipschitz estimate for the averaged particle potential. Both follow from genuine single-pair proximity, Jensen's inequality and the scaled replication identity. The resulting constants do not require a false identification with a shared-state proximal minimizer.

Let \(g\) be convex, bounded below and \(K\)-Lipschitz, \(\lambda>0\), and \(N>0\). The following arguments prove energy estimates for the true pairwise proximal map and a value-Lipschitz bound for \(G=N^{-1}\sum_i g(J_i z)\).

steps.title: Obtain energy from value Lipschitzness
steps.body:
At \(p=P_\lambda(x)\), the residual support at a comparator \(a\) controls \(f(p)-f(a)\). Bound \(f(x)-f(p)\le K\|x-p\|\), expand \(\|x-a\|^2\), and use \((\|x-p\|-\lambda K)^2\ge0\). Thus \(\|p-a\|^2\le\|x-a\|^2-2\lambda(f(x)-f(a))+\lambda^2K^2\). Sum over pairs, use Jensen for the shared parameter, and divide by \(N\) to get the exact averaged energy inequality with remainder \(\lambda^2K^2\).

The pointwise input is a genuine proximal minimizer \(p\). Its residual \(r=(x-p)/\lambda\) is a subgradient at \(p\) and has norm at most \(K\) when the potential is \(K\)-Lipschitz. Combining the support at \(p\), \(f(x)-f(p)\le K\|x-p\|\), and the quadratic expansion yields \[\|p-y\|^2\le\|x-y\|^2-2\lambda(f(x)-f(y))+\lambda^2K^2.\] Sum this for the original pairs and use parameter averaging to pass to the scaled state. The input is value Lipschitzness; no bounded subgradient selection or unproved lifted-proximal identity is hidden in the estimate.

Formal correspondence: isProxPoint_energy_le_of_lipschitz : The proximal energy inequality follows directly from a Lipschitz potential. pairwise_prox_energy_le_lipschitz : The nonsmooth energy bound for the actual averaged pairwise proximal map, with a global Lipschitz hypothesis instead of an assumed subgradient selection.

The residual support at the proximal output controls the comparator energy. To replace the output energy by the input energy, use the global value bound \(f(x)-f(p)\le K\|x-p\|\). The remaining displacement expression is bounded by \(\lambda^2K^2\) through completion of a square. Summing these valid single-pair inequalities gives the state energy estimate with exactly the averaged potential difference.

steps.title: Averaged pair distances control the physical-time potential
steps.body:
Define \(G(z)=F_g(z)/N\). Jensen and \(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2\) imply \(N^{-1}\sum_i\|J_i v\|\le\|v\|\). Therefore

\[|G(z)-G(w)|\le\frac KN\sum_i\|J_i(z-w)\|\le K\|z-w\|.\]

The same constant survives the averaging because the latent coordinates were scaled by \(N^{-1/2}\).

Let \(\bar f_N(z)=N^{-1}\sum_i f(A_i z)\). Cauchy–Schwarz and the replication identity give \[\frac1N\sum_i\|A_i v\|\le\left(\frac1N\sum_i\|A_i v\|^2\right)^{1/2}=\|v\|.\] Applying \(|f(a)-f(b)|\le K\|a-b\|\) to each pair and summing proves \(|\bar f_N(z)-\bar f_N(w)|\le K\|z-w\|\). The declarations separate the average norm estimate from the value estimate so that the particle scaling can be checked independently.

Formal correspondence: averagedPotential : The averaged lifted potential in the physical-time Langevin equation. average_joint_norm_le : Average pair distances are controlled by the scaled state norm. averagedPotential_lipschitz : Averaging in the scaled coordinates preserves the pair potential's Lipschitz constant.

Cauchy–Schwarz for the finite particle average bounds the mean pair distance by the square root of the mean pair squared distance. The latter is exactly the scaled state distance by replication. Therefore averaging cancels the apparent particle factor in the sum of value differences. The physical-time potential \(G=F_g/N\) retains Lipschitz constant \(K\), which is used in the finite expected-energy estimates.

ProximalLangevin/ParticleSmoothing.lean.title: Uniform Moreau gaps in scaled particle coordinates
ProximalLangevin/ParticleSmoothing.lean.summary:
Single-pair Moreau estimates lift to the particle potential by exact finite sums. The full lifted envelope score has magnitude at most \(NK\), while its finite value gap is at most \(N\eta K^2/2\). These estimates use value Lipschitzness and remain distinct from the larger gradient Lipschitz constant involving \(1/\eta\).

Write \(F_g(z)=\sum_i g(J_i z)\), with \(N>0\). If \(g\) is convex, bounded below and \(K\)-Lipschitz, its lifted envelope term has a bounded gradient independent of the positive Moreau scale.

steps.title: Lift value Lipschitzness and a bounded envelope score
steps.body:
The averaged potential is \(K\)-Lipschitz, so multiplying it by \(N\) proves \(\operatorname{Lip}(F_g)\le NK\). The envelope has the same value Lipschitz constant \(K\), hence \(F_{g^\eta}\) has constant \(NK\) too. Its actual gradient norm is therefore at most \(NK\), uniformly over \(\eta>0\).

Multiplying the preceding averaged-potential inequality by \(N\) proves that the lifted sum has value Lipschitz constant \(NK\). The true Moreau envelope has the same value Lipschitz constant \(K\), so its lifted score satisfies \(\|\nabla V_{N,\eta}^{(2)}\|\le NK\). This follows from the norm of the derivative of a globally Lipschitz function, not from its score Lipschitz constant \(N/\eta\). Consequently this magnitude bound remains uniform as \(\eta\downarrow0\).

Formal correspondence: potential_lipschitz : Lifting a globally Lipschitz pair potential to the scaled state multiplies its Lipschitz constant by the number of particles. potential_moreau_lipschitz : The lifted true Moreau approximation preserves the particle Lipschitz constant, uniformly over positive smoothing scales. potential_moreau_gradient_norm_le : The actual gradient of the lifted Moreau term is bounded by N*K , independently of the smoothing scale.

The averaged lifted potential has value Lipschitz constant \(K\), so the full sum has constant \(NK\). The envelope preserves the single-pair value constant, and differentiability converts that value bound into a gradient magnitude bound. This supplies \(\|\nabla F_{g_2^\eta}\|\le NK\) uniformly in \(\eta\). The force can vary rapidly at small scale, yet its magnitude stays bounded.

steps.title: Sum the finite gap and preserve the split decomposition
steps.body:
Apply \(0\le g-g^\eta\le\eta K^2/2\) at every joint pair and add:

\[0\le F_g(z)-F_{g^\eta}(z)\le N\eta K^2/2.\]

Finite sum distributivity also proves \(F_{g_1+g_2^\eta}=F_{g_1}+F_{g_2^\eta}\) as an equality of functions. These exact identities supply the deterministic inputs to the stochastic splitting estimate.

At every pair, \(0\le g_2-g_2^\eta\le\eta K^2/2\). The finite sum has exactly \(N\) terms, giving \[0\le V_N^{(2)}-V_{N,\eta}^{(2)}\le N\eta K^2/2.\] The decomposition lemma is equality of functions: expand \(V_N(g_1+g_2^\eta)\) and distribute the finite sum to obtain \(V_N(g_1)+V_N(g_2^\eta)\). This identifies the two gradient pieces used by the reference process with the actual smoothed potential.

Formal correspondence: potential_moreau_gap : The finite one-sided Moreau gap for the actual sum over particles. potential_smoothed_decomposition : Lifting commutes with the smooth-plus-Moreau decomposition.

Every summand has a nonnegative gap bounded by the same \(\eta K^2/2\). Adding exactly \(N\) terms gives the lifted gap without any norm inequality. Distributing the lifted sum over the two potential components gives a function identity, so differentiation splits their scores under the already proved differentiability. These identities align the reference drift with the actual smoothed Gibbs potential.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingL2Energy.lean.title: Quadratic Hilbert identities and integrated convex energy
ProximalLangevin/SplittingL2Energy.lean.summary:
The deterministic energy estimate must be integrated with every term justified as a finite expectation. Lipschitz value growth and square-integrable states supply that integrability. Weighted quadratic inequalities preserve a useful contraction in squared error, while integrated convex supports put the nonsmooth reference force in the form needed for energy cancellation.

The pointwise proximal estimate is lifted to actual \(L^2\) random variables. All scalar energy expectations are proved integrable before distributing integrals or comparing them.

steps.title: Weighted Young inequality preserves a linear squared contraction
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), expansion and \((t\|v\|-\|r\|)^2\ge0\) prove

\[\|v+r\|^2\le(1+t)\|v\|^2+(1+t^{-1})\|r\|^2.\]

If \(0

Expanding \(\|v+r\|^2\) and using \(2\langle v,r\rangle\le t\|v\|^2+t^{-1}\|r\|^2\) gives the weighted inequality. If \(\|v\|\le(1-t)\|e\|\), \(0<t\le1\), then \((1+t)(1-t)^2\le1-t\). This is the scalar inequality proved in hf; it keeps a linear contraction in the squared error instead of doubling the leading term. The final identity rearranges \(\|v+r+b\|^2\) with its cross term paired against the final error, the form needed for convex-energy cancellation.

Weighted Young uses the free positive parameter to control a mixed term without doubling the leading error. Choosing that parameter as \(mh\) later makes \((1+mh)(1-mh)^2\le1-mh\) when \(mh\le1\). The remaining defect term is multiplied by \(1+(mh)^{-1}\). Keeping the integrated nonsmooth force in a separate inner product is essential because its energy contribution will cancel rather than be bounded by a large norm.

steps.title: Justify potential and quadratic expectations
steps.body:
For a globally \(K\)-Lipschitz scalar \(f\), center at \(f(0)\); its growth is at most \(K\|X\|\). Hence \(f(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\) on a probability space. The actual Hilbert-space \(L^2\) inner product gives \(\|X\|_2^2=\int\|X(\omega)\|^2dP\), without any arbitrary representative-dependent value.

For a value-Lipschitz observable \(f\), \(|f(X)|\le K\|X\|+|f(0)|\); hence an \(L^2\) state on a probability space gives \(f(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\). The first proof implements this by centering \(f\) at zero. The second identity uses the definition of the \(L^2\) inner product and \(\langle X,X\rangle=\|X\|^2\): \(\|X\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|X(\omega)\|^2dP\). These facts ensure that the energy expressions below are ordinary finite Bochner integrals.

Formal correspondence: integrable_lipschitz_compLp : Every globally Lipschitz scalar observable of an L2 random variable is integrable. lp_norm_sq_eq_integral : Exact second-moment identity for actual L2 random variables.

A Lipschitz scalar observable obeys \(|f(x)|\le|f(0)|+K\|x\|\). Its composition with an \(L^2\) state is therefore in \(L^2\), and on a probability space it is also integrable. Quadratic differences of two \(L^2\) states are integrable by the norm triangle inequality. Thus both energy expectations and squared distances in the subsequent inequality have ordinary finite values.

steps.title: Integrate the actual deterministic energy premise
steps.body:
Suppose \(\|T(x)-y\|^2\le\|x-y\|^2-2h(f(x)-f(y))+C\), with \(T,f\) Lipschitz. Apply it pointwise to \(S,Y\in L^2\). The composition representative agrees almost everywhere with \(T(S)\), and every term is integrable. Monotonicity and linearity of the integral yield

\[\|T(S)-Y\|_2^2\le\|S-Y\|_2^2-2h(\mathbb E f(S)-\mathbb E f(Y))+C.\]

Apply the deterministic premise at \((S(\omega),Y(\omega))\). The representative facts for lpDrift and subtraction identify its left side almost everywhere with \(\|T(S)-Y\|^2\). The local facts hn, hfS, hfY prove integrability of both quadratic norms and both potential values. Only then does integral_mono_ae integrate the inequality and distribute its finite terms: \[\|T(S)-Y\|_2^2\le\|S-Y\|_2^2-2h(\mathbb Ef(S)-\mathbb Ef(Y))+C.\] The constant remains \(C\) because \(P\) has mass one.

Formal correspondence: lp_energy_of_pointwise : Lift a proved deterministic energy inequality to actual L2 random variables. This is an integration lemma; the particle instantiation below proves its pointwise premise from the genuine proximal minimization problem.

Apply the pointwise inequality to representatives of the two random states on their common full-measure event. The Lipschitz composition represents the proximal output almost surely. With finite integrability already established, integral monotonicity and linearity give the same energy inequality in \(L^2\). The additive constant is unchanged because the source has mass one, and no unproved exchange of infinite terms is involved.

steps.body:
Convex differentiability gives \(\langle S-Y, abla e(Y) angle\le e(S)-e(Y)\) pointwise. Integrate to obtain the same inequality for the \(L^2\) inner product. The gradient composition and state difference lie in \(L^2\), making their pairing integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. Integrating therefore yields the corresponding Hilbert-space inner-product inequality. ProximalLangevin/IndependenceHelpers.lea.title: Regroup genuinely independent source blocks
ProximalLangevin/IndependenceHelpers.lea.summary:
The Brownian splitting argument groups previously independent source blocks into the initialized past and the future increment. These measure-theoretic lemmas justify that regrouping at the level of joint laws. They retain the full joint-independence hypotheses, which are stronger than unrelated pairwise independence statements.

These measure-theoretic lemmas reorganize supplied joint independence. They do not infer joint independence from pairwise independence.

steps.title: Two independent variables form a Boolean family
steps.body:
Given \(X\perp Y\), define \(Z_{\rm false}=X\), \(Z_{\rm true}=Y\). The finite-family intersection criterion has four possible index subsets: the empty set, either singleton, or both indices. Probability mass one handles the empty case, the singletons are identities, and the two-element case is exactly \(P(X\in A,Y\in B)=P(X\in A)P(Y\in B)\).

An independent family is defined by factorization for every finite set of indices. For a Boolean index there are four possibilities: neither variable, only \(X\), only \(Y\), or both. The singleton identities are tautological; the empty family has probability one because \(\mu\) is a probability; the two-variable case is exactly the assumed independence of \(X\) and \(Y\). The two membership case splits in Lean exhaust these four possibilities explicitly.

Formal correspondence: iIndepFun_bool_of_indepFun : Two independent random variables form an independent family indexed by Bool . The probability assumption supplies the empty-family identity.

For two variables, independence is the factorization of probabilities of simultaneous membership in measurable sets. Encoding them with a two-element index family adds no further condition, because every finite subfamily contains zero, one or two variables. The empty subfamily uses source mass one, the singleton cases are identities, and the two-variable case is exactly the supplied factorization.

steps.title: Regroup a jointly independent triple
steps.body:
Assume \(X\perp(Y,Z)\) and \(Y\perp Z\), with measurable variables. The joint pushforward is \(\mu_X\otimes(\mu_Y\otimes\mu_Z)\). Use the measurable product-associativity equivalence to rewrite it as \((\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y)\otimes\mu_Z\). Projection also proves \(\mu_{(X,Y)}=\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y\), so \((X,Y)\perp Z\). The joint independence premise is essential.

The hypotheses say that \(X\) is independent of the whole pair \((Y,Z)\), and that \(Y\) and \(Z\) are independent. Therefore the triple law is \(\mu_X\otimes(\mu_Y\otimes\mu_Z)\). Product associativity rewrites it as \((\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y)\otimes\mu_Z\), proving independence of \((X,Y)\) and \(Z\). The proof uses equality of pushforward measures under the measurable associator, so this is joint independence; pairwise independence of three unrelated variables would not suffice.

Formal correspondence: indepFun_prodMk_left_of_indepFun : Regroup a jointly independent triple from X | (Y,Z) into (X,Y) | Z . Independence of Y and Z is essential; pairwise independence alone is insufficient.

Write the law of the triple explicitly and use the supplied independence to factor it into three marginal laws. Reassociating the product measure groups the first two marginals together. Their product is the joint law of \((X,Y)\), so the regrouped factorization proves \((X,Y)\perp Z\). The proof uses equality of measurable pushforwards, ensuring the conclusion remains valid for path-valued source blocks.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingOrthogonality..title: Derive Brownian future orthogonality from the actual past
ProximalLangevin/SplittingOrthogonality..summary:
The key cross term vanishes because the reference observable is measurable from the actual initialized Brownian past, whereas the future increment is independent and centered. The argument constructs this past/future independence from full scalar-path independence and the adapted integral solution. The orthogonality is in expected inner product, rather than a samplewise identity.

Let the scalar Brownian coordinates have independent full paths, measurable evaluations, and initialization independent of the whole Brownian family. The actual Langevin integral solution is measurable from initialization and the stopped noise past.

steps.title: Assemble independent vector past and shifted future
steps.body:
Each scalar Brownian path has independent shifted future \(B_i(T+s)-B_i(T)\) and stopped past \(B_i(\min(t,T))\). Encode these as a Boolean pair for each coordinate. Full-path independence makes the coordinate rows independent; flatten the rows and Boolean columns, then take the disjoint sets of past and future indices. Regrouping proves independence of the entire vector path families.

The stopped past records each coordinate path up to time \(t\), while the future block records increments after \(t\). Brownian independent increments give this separation within each scalar coordinate. Independence of the whole coordinate paths permits regrouping the coordinatewise pairs into one vector past and one vector future. This is a statement about the generated product sigma-algebras, so it remains valid when the future vector is paired with any measurable function of the entire past.

Formal correspondence: brownian_future_past_independent : The complete shifted future and the stopped past of independent scalar Brownian coordinates are independent vector-valued path families.

Within each scalar Brownian path, independent increments separate the stopped past from all shifted future increments. Independence of complete coordinate paths lets these coordinatewise pairs be assembled into one jointly independent family. Disjoint selection then groups all past coordinates on one side and all future coordinates on the other. This yields independence of entire vector-valued path blocks, enough for every measurable past observable.

steps.title: Relate concrete noise to its L² representative
steps.body:
Define the pointwise vector \(\mathcal B_t=\sqrt2(B(t_+)-B(0))\), using the nonnegative-time conversion \(t_+=\max(t,0)\). The \(L^2\) Brownian-noise construction agrees almost everywhere with this formula. Each coordinate evaluation is measurable, so finite vector assembly, subtraction and scaling prove measurability of the raw representative.

Formal correspondence: rawBrownianNoise : The pointwise vector presentation of the Langevin noise from time zero.

The raw noise at a fixed time is a finite vector of measurable scalar evaluations, differences and a fixed scale factor. Its coordinate second moments make it square integrable. The constructed \(L^2\) noise and this pointwise vector agree almost surely, so computations of means, laws and independence can be transferred between them. The nonnegative time convention only specifies the domain of Brownian evaluation.

steps.title: Add the independent initialization to the stopped past
steps.body:
The stopped noise path and a future increment are independent. Initialization is independent of their joint pair, so the regrouping lemma proves that initialization together with the stopped past is independent of the future. An auxiliary result then compares sigma-algebras: every variable almost everywhere strongly measurable for the natural initialization/noise past inherits this independence. Almost everywhere replacement transfers the result to actual \(L^2\) representatives.

The initialized natural past contains both the initial state and the stopped Brownian path. Independence of initialization from the entire Brownian source, together with past/future Brownian independence, permits the triple regrouping \((\text{initial},\text{past})\mid\text{future}\). An almost-strongly-measurable past variable can be replaced by a measurable representative without changing its law or independence. This is the role of the representative arguments: independence is transferred through almost-everywhere equality, rather than assumed for the later integral solution.

Formal correspondence: brownian_future_independent_initial_past : A future Brownian increment is independent of the initialization and all earlier actual L2 Brownian-noise representatives. naturalPast_independent_of_aestronglyMeasurable : Every random variable measurable from the natural initialization/noise past inherits its independence from a supplied future source variable.

Initialization is independent of the complete noise source, including both stopped past and future. Combining this fact with Brownian past/future independence gives independence of the pair consisting of initialization and past from the future increment. A variable measurable from that initialized past inherits the same independence by composition. Almost-sure replacement preserves both the law and this factorization, allowing actual square-integrable representatives to be used.

steps.title: Centering and independence imply Hilbert orthogonality
steps.body:
Every scalar Brownian coordinate has mean zero. Commute the finite coordinate projections through the Bochner integral to get \(\mathbb E B_t=0\), then subtract and scale for \(\mathbb E\mathcal B_t=0\). For independent \(L^2\) variables \(X,W\), bilinear integration gives \(\langle X,W\rangle_{L^2}=\langle\mathbb E X,\mathbb E W\rangle\). If \(W\) is centered this is zero.

Formal correspondence: brownianCoordinates_integral_zero : The finite-dimensional Brownian vector has zero mean. brownianNoise_integral_zero : The actual L2 additive Langevin noise is centered at every real time. independent_centered_lp_inner_zero : Binary independence and zero mean imply genuine L2 orthogonality.

For independent square-integrable vectors, their inner product is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. Independence and bilinearity factor its expectation as the inner product of their means. A Brownian increment has mean zero coordinatewise, and finite vector assembly preserves that zero mean. Therefore its expected pairing with any independent square-integrable past vector vanishes exactly, without estimating the size of either vector.

steps.title: Apply adaptedness of the constructed integral solution
steps.body:
The invariant-subspace construction for the actual integral equation proves that \(Y_t\) is measurable for the natural past. A Lipschitz observable \(b(Y_t)\) remains past measurable and in \(L^2\). The preceding independence and zero-mean results therefore prove

\[\langle b(Y_t),\mathcal B_h-\mathcal B_t\rangle_{L^2}=0,\qquad0\le t\le h.\]

This essential cancellation is a conclusion of the Brownian and integral-equation construction.

The constructed solution is adapted to the initialized natural past, so the Lipschitz observable \(b(Y_t)\) is measurable there. The future Brownian increment is independent of this past and has zero mean. Both variables belong to \(L^2\), hence their inner product is integrable, and independence factors its expectation as \[\mathbb E\langle b(Y_t),B_h-B_t\rangle=\left\langle\mathbb E b(Y_t),\mathbb E(B_h-B_t)\right\rangle=0.\] The \(L^2\) inner product is precisely this integral. Thus the final orthogonality input of the splitting proof follows from adaptedness, centering and the constructed Brownian law.

Formal correspondence: lp_langevin_future_inner_zero : A Lipschitz function of the actual Langevin solution is orthogonal to every later Brownian increment. Adaptedness is derived from the integral equation by the existing invariant-subspace construction.

The integral-equation construction ensures the reference state at time \(t\) depends only on initialization and noise up to \(t\). Composing with a Lipschitz drift observable preserves that measurability and square integrability. Apply initialized-past independence to the future increment over \([t,h]\), then use its zero mean. The resulting cancellation removes the otherwise order-\(\sqrt{h-t}\) contribution from the splitting cross-energy estimate.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingProcess.lean.title: Local smooth drift defect and the future cross term
ProximalLangevin/SplittingProcess.lean.summary:
The reference integral equation controls increments by a drift part of order time and a Brownian part of order square root of time. Only the smooth component's Lipschitz constant is used to bound its local defect. For the nonsmooth cross term, future-noise orthogonality is used before a norm bound, retaining a smaller time-order remainder.

Let a continuous Hilbert-valued reference satisfy \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t g(Y_s)ds+B_t\), with \(\|g(Y_t)\|\le G\) and \(\|B_t\|\le\sigma\sqrt t\). Only the smooth-part Lipschitz constant enters the local defect.

steps.title: Integrate the smooth drift increment
steps.body:
The integral equation implies \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le Gt+\sigma\sqrt t\). If \(a\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(0\le t\le h\), then \(\|a(Y_t)-a(Y_0)\|\le L(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)\). Integrating over an interval of length \(h\) yields

\[\left\|\int_0^h(a(Y_t)-a(Y_0))dt\right\|\le Lh(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h).\]

For the integral solution \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t g(Y_s)ds+B_t\), assume \(\|g(Y_s)\|\le G\) and \(\|B_t\|\le\nu\sqrt t\) in the Hilbert space under consideration. Then \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le tG+\nu\sqrt t\). If only the smooth part \(a\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \[\left\|\int_0^h(a(Y_t)-a(Y_0))dt\right\|\le Lh(Gh+\nu\sqrt h).\] The code first bounds the integrand uniformly for \(0\le t\le h\), using monotonicity of \(t\) and \(\sqrt t\), and then applies the interval-integral norm inequality. The Lipschitz constant of the full drift ensures regularity but does not enter this numerical bound.

Formal correspondence: splitting_localDefect_bound : A coarse local smooth-drift defect bound uses only the smooth part's own Lipschitz constant and the total reference drift moment.

Taking the norm of the integral equation gives \(\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le Gt+\sigma\sqrt t\). Smooth-force Lipschitzness multiplies this increment by \(L\). For \(t\in[0,h]\), replace \(t\) and \(\sqrt t\) by their endpoint upper bounds, then multiply by the interval length. This proves the local defect estimate without using the full smoothed score's inverse-scale Lipschitz constant.

steps.title: Cancel future noise before estimating the remainder
steps.body:
Subtract the reference equations at \(t,h\) and use adjacent-interval additivity:

\[Y_t-Y_h=\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds-(B_h-B_t).\]

If \(\|b\|\le K\) and \(\langle b,B_h-B_t\rangle=0\), the noise term cancels exactly. Cauchy–Schwarz and the drift bound give \(\langle Y_t-Y_h,b\rangle\le(h-t)GK\). This avoids an order-\(\sqrt{h-t}\) loss.

Subtract the two integral equations and split the integral at \(t\): \[Y_t-Y_h=\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds-(B_h-B_t).\] Pair this identity with \(b\). The explicit orthogonality assumption cancels the future-noise contribution before any norm estimate, leaving \[\langle Y_t-Y_h,b\rangle\le\left\|\int_t^h g(Y_s)ds\right\|\|b\|\le(h-t)GK.\] In the probabilistic application this is an inner product in \(L^2\), so orthogonality means the expected inner product is zero; it is not a samplewise cancellation of Brownian increments.

Formal correspondence: reference_future_inner_le : Future-noise orthogonality turns the reference increment cross term into a drift integral of order h-t , rather than a Brownian norm of order sqrt(h-t) .

Subtracting the equations at \(t\) and \(h\) expresses their difference using only the future drift integral and future noise increment. Pair with the past-measurable bounded force before applying Cauchy–Schwarz. Orthogonality removes the noise term exactly. The drift integral has norm at most \((h-t)G\), giving the remainder \((h-t)GK\), of first order in the remaining time.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingCrossEnergy.le.title: Cancel the original nonsmooth energy in expectation
ProximalLangevin/SplittingCrossEnergy.le.summary:
Convex support turns the nonsmooth reference-force pairing into expected envelope energies. Stationarity aligns its time-dependent reference energy with the endpoint energy, and a finite value gap compares the envelope with the original nonsmooth potential. This cancels the original energy appearing in the actual proximal estimate, leaving controlled gap and drift remainders.

Let \(e\) be convex and differentiable, let \(e\le f\le e+\delta\), and let \(Y_t\) be a stationary reference for the smoothed energy with the actual integral equation and future-noise orthogonality. Lipschitz value bounds ensure all expectations exist.

steps.title: Integrate a one-sided uniform value gap
steps.body:
If \(f(x)\le e(x)+\delta\) pointwise and both functions are Lipschitz, their compositions with any \(L^2\) variable \(X\) are integrable. Integral monotonicity and total mass one give \(\mathbb E f(X)-\mathbb E e(X)\le\delta\). This is the precise one-sided expectation lemma used in the cross-energy argument.

If \(f\le e+\delta\), the two Lipschitz observables of an \(L^2\) state are integrable. Thus \(\mathbb Ef(X)\le\mathbb Ee(X)+\delta P(\Omega)=\mathbb Ee(X)+\delta\). The proof checks this integrability before splitting the integral. This comparison will be used once at the algorithm's intermediate state with \(e\le f\), and once at the reference endpoint with \(f\le e+\delta\).

Formal correspondence: expectation_gap_le : A finite uniform value gap controls its actual expectation.

Because the two observables are Lipschitz, composition with a square-integrable state gives integrable potential values. Integral monotonicity may therefore be combined with ordinary linearity. The constant gap integrates to \(\delta\), since the source probability has mass one. This elementary bound is applied to actual finite expected energies, with no differentiation of the original nonsmooth potential.

steps.title: Combine convex support, stationarity and the future estimate
steps.body:
The integrated convex support bounds \(\langle S-Y_h, abla e(Y_t) angle\) by \(\mathbb E e(S)-\mathbb E e(Y_t)+\langle Y_t-Y_h, abla e(Y_t) angle\). Stationarity replaces \(\mathbb E e(Y_t)\) by \(\mathbb E e(Y_h)\). Orthogonality and bounded drift/score give the remaining term at most \(hGK\). Commute the fixed inner-product functional through the time integral. Finally the gap \(e\le f\le e+\delta\) changes the two expected energies by at most \(\delta\), proving

\[2\left\langle S-Y_h,\int_0^h abla e(Y_t)dt ight angle-2h(\mathbb E f(S)-\mathbb E f(Y_h))\le2h\delta+2h^2GK.\]

For \(b_t= abla e(Y_t)\) in \(L^2\), convex support and the future-increment estimate imply \[\langle S-Y_h,b_t angle\le\mathbb Ee(S)-\mathbb Ee(Y_t)+(h-t)GK.\] Stationarity replaces \(\mathbb Ee(Y_t)\) by \(\mathbb Ee(Y_h)\). Integrate on \([0,h]\); continuity of \(b_t\) justifies moving the bounded linear inner-product functional through the Bochner integral. This yields an upper bound \(h[\mathbb Ee(S)-\mathbb Ee(Y_h)]+h^2GK\).

The two value comparisons give \([\mathbb Ee(S)-\mathbb Ee(Y_h)]-[\mathbb Ef(S)-\mathbb Ef(Y_h)]\le\delta\). Multiply by \(2h\) and combine to obtain the displayed \(2h\delta+2h^2GK\) remainder. In Lean, hpoint is the pointwise-in-time estimate, hi its integral, and hsum the finite value-gap cancellation. The conclusion never substitutes \(\operatorname{Lip}( abla e)\) into this remainder.

Formal correspondence: splitting_cross_energy_le : The integrated reference-gradient cross term cancels the original nonsmooth energy up to a finite value gap and a drift error of order h² . The orthogonality premise is instantiated by the actual Brownian construction in lp_langevin_future_inner_zero , not by a convergence assumption.

Split \(S-Y_h=(S-Y_t)+(Y_t-Y_h)\). Convex support controls the first pairing, and future orthogonality plus drift bounds control the second. Stationarity replaces \(\mathbb E e(Y_t)\) by \(\mathbb E e(Y_h)\). Integrating over time gives an envelope-energy difference. At \(S\) use \(e\le f\), and at \(Y_h\) use \(f\le e+\delta\), leaving only one \(\delta\) in the difference.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingOneStep.lean.title: Derive the synchronous one-step splitting bound
ProximalLangevin/SplittingOneStep.lean.summary:
The synchronous one-step estimate is derived by decomposing the error into a contracted smooth forward difference, a local smooth defect and an integrated envelope force. The actual proximal energy inequality and the stationary cross-energy comparison cancel the nonsmooth energy. Weighted Young then leaves a linear squared-error contraction with an explicit finite forcing.

In a Hilbert \(L^2\) space, let \(f_1\) be \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let the actual Lipschitz map \(T\) satisfy the nonsmooth energy inequality for \(f\). The reference solves the actual stationary smoothed integral equation for \(f_1+e\), where \(e\le f\le e+\delta\).

steps.title: Keep every local forcing term explicit
steps.body:
For \(m,h>0\), drift moment \(G\), noise moment factor \(\sigma\), bounded nonsmooth score \(K\) and value gap \(\delta\), define

\[\mathcal F=(1+(mh)^{-1})[Lh(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)]^2+2h\delta+2h^2GK+h^2K^2.\]

The four terms are the weighted smooth local defect, the envelope value gap, the drift cross term, and the genuine proximal energy remainder.

Formal correspondence: splittingCouplingForcing : Explicit local forcing in the synchronous splitting proof.

The smooth local defect is squared only after multiplying by the weighted factor \(1+(mh)^{-1}\). The remaining three contributions come from the finite envelope gap, the reference drift crossed with the bounded envelope score, and the actual proximal remainder. Separating these four terms records their different sources and permits a later scalar estimate showing that their sum is second order in the step.

steps.title: An exact decomposition makes the energy cancel
steps.body:
Let \(S=X-h abla f_1(X)+B_h\), \(v=(X-h abla f_1(X))-(Y_0-h abla f_1(Y_0))\), \(R=\int_0^h[ abla f_1(Y_t)- abla f_1(Y_0)]dt\), and \(H=\int_0^h abla e(Y_t)dt\). The integral equation gives the exact identity \(S-Y_h=v+R+H\). Expand its square using the rearranged identity; integrate the actual proximal energy inequality for \(T(S)\). The cross-energy lemma cancels the resulting expected \(f\)-difference. Sharp smooth-step contraction and weighted Young inequality bound \(\|v+R\|^2\), while the local-defect lemma bounds \(R\). Discarding \(-\|H\|^2\le0\) yields

\[\|T(S)-Y_h\|_2^2\le(1-mh)\|X-Y_0\|_2^2+\mathcal F.\]

Here \(m\le L\) and \(h\le2/(m+L)\) imply \(mh\le1\). Every reference premise is later supplied by the canonical construction.

Set \(a= abla f_1\), \(b= abla e\), \(S=X-ha(X)+B_h\), \(v=[X-ha(X)]-[Y_0-ha(Y_0)]\), \(R=\int_0^h[a(Y_t)-a(Y_0)]dt\), and \(H=\int_0^h b(Y_t)dt\). Splitting the actual reference integral equation gives the exact identity \(S-Y_h=v+R+H\). The norm rearrangement is \[\|S-Y_h\|^2=\|v+R\|^2+2\langle S-Y_h,H angle-\|H\|^2.\]

Apply the genuine proximal energy estimate to \(T(S)\), then control \(\|v+R\|^2\) using the weighted inequality with \(t=mh\). Strong smooth convexity gives \(\|v\|\le(1-mh)\|X-Y_0\|\), and the step restriction proves \(mh\le1\). The local smooth drift estimate bounds \(\|R\|\), while the preceding cross-energy theorem cancels the original nonsmooth potential difference up to \(2h\delta+2h^2GK\). Discarding \(-\|H\|^2\le0\) leaves exactly the four displayed terms in splittingCouplingForcing. The facts hdecomp, hweighted, hRweighted and hcross correspond to these four stages.

Formal correspondence: splitting_one_step_of_integral_solution : One splitting step compared with an actual smooth stationary reference. The pointwise energy premise is proved for the actual averaged joint proximal map; the reference hypotheses are discharged by its canonical Brownian construction. No stochastic error recurrence is assumed.

The decomposition is exact because the same additive noise appears in the algorithm's forward step and the reference integral equation. After applying the proximal energy inequality, the integrated envelope-force pairing cancels its original potential difference up to the cross-energy remainder. Weighted Young preserves factor \(1-mh\) in the old squared error. Dropping the nonpositive integrated-force square leaves the stated forcing, without a separate stochastic recurrence assumption.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingCanonical.lean.title: Construct a stationary Brownian coupling for one true transition
ProximalLangevin/SplittingCanonical.lean.summary:
The analytic one-step premises are realized on the product of an arbitrary finite-cost initial coupling and a canonical Brownian source. The reference is the actual stationary Langevin solution for the smoothed Gibbs potential. Its law, moment bounds and future orthogonality are constructed, while the Brownian endpoint identifies the algorithm's exact independent-Gaussian transition law.

The generic splitting map is \(\mathcal T_h(x,\xi)=T(x-h\nabla f_1(x)+\sqrt{2h}\xi)\). The reference target is the actual Gibbs law of \(F=f_1+e\). Assumptions concern potentials, true energy, bounded gradients and a finite input coupling.

steps.title: Measurable update and exact gradient additivity
steps.body:
The map is the composition of the measurable Gaussian forward update with the Lipschitz map \(T\). Differentiability proves \( abla(f_1+e)= abla f_1+ abla e\). Almost everywhere representative identities then prove additivity of the corresponding \(L^2\) drift maps, as an equality of actual \(L^2\) elements.

Formal correspondence: splittingUpdate : The actual forward, noise, backward splitting transition. lpDrift_gradient_add : The lifted drift of an actual sum is the sum of its lifted gradients.

The smooth forward map is continuous jointly in state and Gaussian input, and the energy map is Lipschitz. Their composition is therefore measurable and defines a transition probability. Differentiability of both potential components gives the sum of their gradients. Composing with square-integrable states respects this equality almost surely, so the reference drift is exactly the score of the sum potential.

steps.title: Extend any finite-cost coupling by canonical Brownian noise
steps.body:
Start with any coupling \(c\) between \(\mu\) and the Gibbs target, with finite quadratic cost. Extend it by the canonical independent Brownian source. The initial reference has the exact Gibbs law and finite moments; the constructed Langevin integral solution stays stationary. Its natural-past measurability and Brownian independence prove the future orthogonality. Uniform moments give

\[G=\sqrt{2L^2d/m+2K^2}+K,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{2d}.\]

Use the Brownian increment over \([0,h]\) as the Gaussian update noise; its independence gives the exact Markov marginal. Apply the derived analytic one-step theorem. The explicit output pair is a finite coupling and proves

\[W_2(\mu\mathcal T_h,\pi)^2\le(1-mh)\operatorname{cost}(c)^2+\mathcal F(m,h,L,G,\sigma,K,\delta).\]

The construction discharges stationarity, Gaussian laws, finite moments and orthogonality; they are not extra convergence hypotheses.

Start from an arbitrary finite-cost coupling \(c\) between the input law and \(\pi\propto e^{-(f_1+e)}\). Extend it by an independent canonical Brownian source, producing square-integrable initial states \(X,Z\) with the required marginals. The actual Lipschitz integral equation constructs \(Y_t\) from \(Z\), and the Gibbs stationarity theorem proves \(\operatorname{Law}(Y_t)=\pi\) throughout the interval.

The bound on the total reference force is \[G=\sqrt{2L_1^2d/m+2K^2}+K,\] combining the proved smooth-score Gibbs moment with the uniformly bounded envelope score. The Brownian moment gives \(\|B_t\|_2\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\). Adaptedness and future-increment independence prove horth; stationarity proves equality of the envelope expectations in hstationary. These facts discharge the analytic one-step theorem's stochastic inputs.

Finally, the normalized Brownian increment \(V\) has the standard Gaussian law and is independent of \(X\). The representative identity hX'coe identifies the updated random variable with \(T(X-h\nabla f_1(X)+\sqrt{2h}V)\); hX'law proves its law is the actual independent-Gaussian Markov step. The pair \((X',Y_h)\) therefore provides a finite transport coupling. This proves both output finiteness and the squared estimate for the original arbitrary \(c\).

Formal correspondence: splitting_markov_step_coupling_bound : A genuine canonical coupling estimate for one actual independent Gaussian splitting step. All stochastic inputs of the analytic one-step theorem are constructed here from the potential assumptions.

Under the product source, the first initial marginal has the input law and the second has Gibbs law. Independent Brownian noise evolves the latter by the constructed Langevin equation, whose stationarity theorem preserves the Gibbs law. The normalized endpoint increment is fresh standard Gaussian noise for the former. Their updated pair is thus a finite-cost coupling of the actual transition and the target, to which the derived analytic bound applies.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingTransport.lean.title: Take the infimum of squared finite coupling estimates
ProximalLangevin/SplittingTransport.lean.summary:
A squared coupling estimate with common nonnegative coefficients can be passed to Wasserstein distance without selecting an optimal plan. Finite input distance supplies finite approximating couplings. The greatest-lower-bound argument below keeps the additive forcing outside the coupling infimum and justifies all real-valued squares.

Assume \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\), \(q,c\ge0\), and \(W_2(\mu', u')^2\le q\operatorname{cost}(p)^2+c\) for every finite-cost coupling \(p\) of \(\mu, u\). No optimal coupling is needed.

steps.title: Use the greatest lower bound characterization
steps.body:
If \(q=0\), one finite coupling already gives the result. If the target square is at most \(c\), the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise set \(r=\sqrt{(W_2(\mu', u')^2-c)/q}\). Each coupling estimate implies \(r\le\operatorname{cost}(p)\); infinite-cost couplings also satisfy this extended inequality. Hence \(r\le\inf_p\operatorname{cost}(p)=W_2(\mu, u)\). Square this nonnegative inequality and multiply by \(q\) to obtain

\[W_2(\mu', u')^2\le qW_2(\mu, u)^2+c.\]

Finiteness justifies every extended-to-real conversion.

Write \(A=W_2(\mu', u')^2\), and suppose every finite-cost input coupling satisfies \(A\le qC^2+c\). If \(q=0\), one finite-cost coupling already proves \(A\le c\). If \(A\le c\), the result is immediate from \(q\ge0\). Otherwise set \(r=\sqrt{(A-c)/q}\); then every finite coupling has cost at least \(r\), and infinite-cost couplings also satisfy this lower bound in the extended order.

The operation le_iInf now proves \(r\le W_2(\mu, u)\) directly from the definition as an infimum. The finite-distance hypothesis justifies passing to real values. Squaring and multiplying by \(q\) gives \(A\le qW_2(\mu, u)^2+c\). This is why the proof does not need existence of an optimal transport plan.

Formal correspondence: wasserstein2_sq_bound_of_finite_couplings : A uniform squared estimate for actual finite-cost couplings passes to the square of the genuine Wasserstein distance.

Equivalently, choose input couplings with costs tending down to the finite infimum. Their squared costs tend to \(W_2(\mu, u)^2\) by continuity of squaring on nonnegative real numbers. The same output bound holds for every such coupling, so taking the limit gives the displayed inequality. The explicit case split handles zero coefficient and a nonpositive residual before dividing, avoiding hidden positivity assumptions.

ProximalLangevin/SplittingRate.lean.title: A finite coefficient for the splitting error floor
ProximalLangevin/SplittingRate.lean.summary:
The local forcing can be bounded by \(mh^2C\) when the envelope value gap is at most \(hK^2/2\). The explicit coefficient uses curvature, smooth-score regularity, drift and noise moments, and a uniform nonsmooth-score magnitude. It contains no inverse envelope gradient constant, enabling a vanishing small-step transport floor.

The derived forcing uses no inverse envelope gradient constant. This scalar estimate turns it into an \(O(h^2)\) one-step squared error when the value gap is \(\delta\le hK^2/2\).

steps.title: Define and sign the explicit coefficient
steps.body:
For \(m>0\), \(G,K\ge0\), define

\[C(m,L,G,\sigma,K)=\frac{4L^2}{m^2}\left(\frac{G^2}{m}+\sigma^2\right)+\frac2m(GK+K^2).\]

Squares and positive denominators prove \(C\ge0\). This constant may be conservative but remains finite under its stated scalar assumptions.

Formal correspondence: splittingRMSConstant : A finite coefficient for the squared splitting error floor. splittingRMSConstant_nonneg : The coefficient is nonnegative under the actual moment-bound hypotheses.

Every summand of \(C\) is nonnegative under \(m>0\) and nonnegative magnitude constants. The coefficient is finite because its only denominators are powers of the positive curvature. This separates numerical conservativeness from analytic validity: the constant need not be optimal to yield a finite-step convergence guarantee, but all its dimension and particle factors remain explicit.

steps.title: Bound the exact local forcing
steps.body:
For \(h\le1/m\), use \((Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)^2\le2G^2h^2+2\sigma^2h\le2h(G^2/m+\sigma^2)\) and \(h+1/m\le2/m\). The weighted defect is then at most \(4L^2h^2(G^2/m+\sigma^2)/m\). The gap contributes \(2h\delta\le h^2K^2\). Adding the remaining \(2h^2GK+h^2K^2\) proves \(\mathcal F\le mh^2C\). Thus iteration can produce the squared floor \(hC\).

The local defect contains \((Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)^2\). First use \((u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2\) and \(h\le1/m\) to obtain \[(Gh+\sigma\sqrt h)^2\le2h(G^2/m+\sigma^2).\] Next, \((1+(mh)^{-1})h^2\cdot2h=2h^2(h+1/m)\le4h^2/m\).
