This module contains explicit mathematical certificates. Each claim is limited to its stated algebraic example or implication; these certificates do not claim that every stronger result in the reference paper is false.

steps.title: The quadratic proximal expansion has positive second order
steps.body:
On page 15, v3 equation (22) prints a negative second-order term in the proximal expansion. Differentiating \(p+\lambda\nabla g_2(p)=x\) gives a positive second derivative contribution. The scalar quadratic supplies an exact certificate:

\[ \operatorname{prox}_{u^2/2}^\lambda(x) =\frac{x}{1+\lambda} =x-\lambda x+\lambda^2x-\frac{\lambda^3x}{1+\lambda}. \]

The negative second-order expression leaves an error at least \(\lambda^2\) when \(x=1\), so it cannot be that quadratic's third-order expansion. This diagnoses the displayed algebra; the quadratic is not globally Lipschitz and is not by itself a counterexample to the full final theorem under A3.

Separately, twice differentiability almost everywhere and the stated moment bound do not supply a uniform integrable third-order remainder. The original \(O(\lambda)\) minimizer claim is therefore not reproduced here. The proved uniform-gap argument replaces it with \(\sqrt{\lambda K^2/m}\). A proof gap does not establish that the stronger conclusion is false.

Formal correspondence: quadratic_prox_minimizes : The proximal point of u ↦ u²/2 is x/(1+lam) . The difference of objectives is a nonnegative square; no differentiability of an argmin map is assumed. quadratic_prox_expansion : The second-order coefficient in the proximal expansion has a positive sign. This exact identity diagnoses the opposite sign in v1 equation (25) and v3 equation (22). negative_second_order_residual : The negative second-order term printed in v1 equation (25) / v3 equation (22) leaves an error of order lam² , already for the scalar quadratic.

For \(f(u)=u^2/2\), minimizing gives \((1+\lambda)p=x\), hence the exact resolvent. Long division produces a positive \(\lambda^2x\) coefficient and the explicit third-order remainder. A negative coefficient therefore fails already in this smooth scalar calculation. The example diagnoses the expansion's algebra; it does not itself satisfy a global value Lipschitz assumption and so is not a counterexample to every theorem using that assumption.

steps.title: Squared scaling and the geometric endpoint
steps.body:
Norm homogeneity gives \(\|Ng\|^2=N^2\|g\|^2\). The numerical case \(N=2,\|g\|=1\) disproves linear squared-gradient scaling. Substituting \(\lambda=\gamma/(1-\mu\gamma)\) gives \(1-q=0\). Lean’s total real division has \(1/0=0\); the numerical certificate \(1\not\le0+1/(1-1)\) shows why an unguarded formula at that endpoint cannot express an error floor.

Formal correspondence: squared_gradient_scaling : Scaling a gradient by N scales its squared norm by N² , not N . This corrects v1 Corollary A.5; v3 Corollary A.12 already uses this scaling. linear_squared_gradient_scaling_fails : A numerical witness to the invalid NC bound from the valid C bound when the gradient is multiplied by N . endpoint_denominator_zero : The geometric-series denominator is zero at the upper endpoint allowed in v1 Corollaries A.4--A.6 and v3 Corollaries A.11--A.13. A finite error floor requires a strict inequality. endpoint_error_floor_fails : At q=1 , the recurrence e(n+1)=e(n)+1 has linear growth. Interpreting real division by zero cannot rescue the printed error floor.

Norm homogeneity applies before squaring, so multiplying a gradient by \(N\) multiplies its squared norm by \(N^2\). Separately, a unit recurrence multiplier gives a finite sum of \(n\), not a bounded geometric floor. Both observations are exact numerical facts. They identify why particle factors and positive-denominator guards must be preserved in any proposed transport or energy estimate.

steps.title: The proximal deficit carries an inverse step factor
steps.body:
If \(\langle x-y,p(x)-p(y)\rangle\le(1-\mu)\|x-y\|^2\), expand the residual difference \(R(x)-R(y)=\gamma^{-1}[(x-y)-(p(x)-p(y))]\). For \(\gamma>0\), this proves \(\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle\ge(\mu/\gamma)\|x-y\|^2\). The modulus is \(\mu/\gamma\), rather than \(\mu\).

Formal correspondence: proximal_displacement_strong_monotonicity : If the proximal displacement satisfies the paper's assumption B1, the envelope gradient inherits the constant mu/gamma .

Expanding the residual difference gives \(\langle x-y,R(x)-R(y)\rangle=\gamma^{-1}(\|x-y\|^2-\langle x-y,p(x)-p(y)\rangle)\). Substituting the proximal deficit gives \((\mu/\gamma)\|x-y\|^2\). The inverse step is unavoidable because the residual is divided by \(\gamma\). This coefficient must therefore be used in any subsequent strong-monotonicity or curvature inference.

steps.title: A shared parameter prevents the lifted-proximal identity
steps.body:
Use the convex pair function \(g(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\) and unit proximal parameter. The actual pair objectives show that inputs \((1,0)\) and \((1,4)\) have minimizers \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((2,3)\). Averaging their parameter outputs gives \((5/4,1/2,3)\). The shared lifted objective is

\[\tfrac12(|\theta-x_1|+|\theta-x_2|)+\tfrac12(\theta-1)^2+\tfrac14(x_1^2+(x_2-4)^2).\]

Direct absolute-value inequalities certify the two pair minima. Exact arithmetic shows that the competitor \((1,1,3)\) has strictly smaller shared objective than the averaged output. Therefore averaged pairwise proximity is not in general the proximal map of the lifted sum.

The final counterexample keeps a single parameter shared across two pair objectives. Minimizing each pair separately allows two different parameter choices; averaging them afterwards need not solve the single shared-parameter minimization problem. The explicit absolute-value objectives make each pair minimizer and the failed shared optimality test computable. This is why the main splitting proof uses summed pairwise energy and Jensen, rather than treating its averaged map as a lifted proximal minimizer.

Formal correspondence: pairAbsObjective : The pair objective for the convex, globally Lipschitz penalty g₂(theta,x)=|theta-x| with smoothing parameter one. pairAbs_first_prox : At pair input (1,0) , the true proximal point is (1/2,1/2) . pairAbs_second_prox : At pair input (1,4) , the true proximal point is (2,3) . sharedAbsObjective : The two-particle lifted objective in physical particle coordinates. The quadratic penalty uses precisely the scaled state norm with N=2 . averaged_pair_prox_not_lifted_minimizer : Averaging the two true pairwise proximal outputs gives parameter 5/4 and particles (1/2,3) . A feasible competitor (1,1,3) has strictly smaller lifted objective. Thus the pairwise average cannot be a lifted proximal minimizer, even for a convex globally Lipschitz penalty.

Each pair minimization is allowed its own proposed parameter, while the lifted objective has one shared parameter. Averaging the proposed parameters need not minimize that shared objective. In the displayed absolute-value example the pairwise output has objective \(51/32\), whereas a feasible shared comparator has value \(3/2=48/32\). This strict inequality disproves the minimizer identity and motivates the valid Jensen-and-energy route.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldDrift.lean.title: The actual mean-field force is Lipschitz in W₂
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldDrift.lean.summary:
The mean-field parameter force is the actual integral of the parameter block of the joint gradient. Linear growth from global gradient Lipschitzness makes this integral well defined for finite-second-moment latent laws. Comparing integrands on arbitrary couplings gives a Wasserstein continuity estimate with the correct split-envelope regularity constant.

For a pair potential \(V\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, define \(b_V(\theta,\mu)=\int\nabla_\theta V(\theta,x)\mu(dx)\). The measures are probability laws with finite second moments. Every Bochner expectation and every finite real transport distance is justified.

steps.title: A Lipschitz observable preserves L² and controls expectation differences
steps.body:
Center an observable \(\phi\) at \(\phi(0)\); its norm growth is bounded by \(K\|x\|\), so \(\phi(X)\in L^2\subset L^1\). Given any finite-cost coupling \(c\) of \(\mu, u\), pushforward integration and Cauchy–Schwarz give

\[\left\|\int\phi\,d\mu-\int\phi\,d u ight\|\le K\left(\int\|x-y\|^2dc ight)^{1/2}.\]

Taking the actual coupling infimum yields the bound \(K W_2(\mu, u)\), with finiteness supplied by the second moments.

The nonzero value \(\varphi(0)\) must be retained when proving integrability. Write \(\varphi(X)=[\varphi(X)-\varphi(0)]+\varphi(0)\). The first term is in \(L^2\) because its Lipschitz map vanishes at zero; the second is a constant in \(L^2\) on a probability space. This proves memLp_lipschitz_observable, including the offset.

For the transport estimate, take any coupling \(c\) of \(\mu, u\). Its marginal identities pull the given second moments onto its two coordinate random variables. Applying the observable lemma to both coordinates proves their \(L^2\) membership and hence their Bochner integrability. The fact hid then changes variables using those marginals and combines the two integrals:

\[\int\varphi\,d\mu-\int\varphi\,d u=\int[\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)]\,dc(x,y).\]

The successive inequalities in hfamily are the integral triangle inequality, the probability-space comparison \(\|F\|_1\le\|F\|_2\), and the pointwise Lipschitz bound \(\|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)\|\le K\|x-y\|\). They give the same upper bound \(K\,\operatorname{cost}(c)\) for every coupling. Taking the infimum in the extended nonnegative reals proves hbound. Finite input second moments already imply finite \(W_2\), so the product \(KW_2\) is finite and the final conversion to real numbers preserves the inequality.

Formal correspondence: memLp_lipschitz_observable : A Lipschitz observable with a nonzero offset still preserves finite second moments on a probability space. integral_lipschitz_wasserstein2 : Actual expectations of a Lipschitz observable are Lipschitz in W₂. Both input probability laws have finite second moment; infinity is never removed by an unguarded real conversion.

A Lipschitz observable can have a nonzero value at the origin, so its integrability estimate must include that constant. After establishing integrability, write the expectation difference as a single coupling integral. The observable's Lipschitz constant bounds its integrand by the pair distance. The probability-space inequality \(\|\cdot\|_1\le\|\cdot\|_2\) then bounds it by quadratic coupling cost, and taking the infimum gives the Wasserstein estimate.

steps.title: Project the true joint gradient to its parameter block
steps.body:
The bounded linear map \(P_\theta\) keeps the parameter coordinates. Its squared norm is a sub-sum of the full Euclidean square, hence \(\|P_\theta z\|\le\|z\|\). Define \(\phi_\theta(x)=P_\theta\nabla V(\theta,x)\), then define the mean-field force as its actual Bochner integral. These definitions use the existing joint potential, with no arbitrary force field substituted for its gradient.

Formal correspondence: jointParameterCLM : The parameter block of a parameter/latent joint vector. parameterGradient : The parameter component of the actual joint gradient. meanFieldDrift : The actual averaged parameter drift, as a Bochner integral.

Orthogonal parameter projection cannot increase the joint gradient difference. Thus the parameter-gradient observable inherits the joint gradient's Lipschitz and affine-growth bounds. Integrating this actual block, rather than a separately postulated force, fixes the mean-field equation's relationship to the underlying potential. Its expectation exists because finite latent second moment also gives finite first moment.

steps.title: Control joint parameter and latent perturbations
steps.body:
Decompose a joint pair difference into its two coordinate inclusions, giving \(\|(\theta,x)-(\theta',x')\|\le\|\theta-\theta'\|+\|x-x'\|\). Gradient Lipschitzness and the nonexpansive parameter projection imply

\[\|\phi_\theta(x)-\phi_{\theta'}(x')\|\le L(\|\theta-\theta'\|+\|x-x'\|).\]

Fixing \(\theta=\theta'\) proves that the latent observable itself is \(L\)-Lipschitz.

Decompose the pair difference into a pure parameter displacement and a pure latent displacement. Their orthogonal inclusions have norm one; the triangle inequality gives their sum as an upper bound for the joint norm. Applying the joint score Lipschitz estimate and then parameter projection yields the displayed two-block estimate. Fixing either block gives the corresponding separate regularity bound.

steps.title: Separate the parameter change from the law change
steps.body:
For a differentiable potential \(V\), define

\[ b_V(\theta,\mu)=\int \nabla_\theta V(\theta,x)\,\mu(dx). \]

Assume \(\nabla V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu,\nu\) are probability laws with finite second moment. Coordinate projection has norm at most one, so the integrand is Lipschitz and grows at most linearly. Its Bochner expectation is therefore integrable. For any finite-cost coupling, compare its two integrands, apply the norm-of-integral inequality, and use Cauchy–Schwarz. Taking the infimum of actual coupling costs gives

\[ \|b_V(\theta,\mu)-b_V(\theta',\nu)\| \le L\bigl(\|\theta-\theta'\|+W_2(\mu,\nu)\bigr). \]

With the genuine split envelope \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), the proved constant is \(L_1+1/\eta\). The paper’s \(1/\eta\) constant applies to a full envelope, not to this split expression in general. This is a corrected W₂ version of Lemma C.1: its right-hand side is weaker than the paper’s W₁ statement, and the distinction is explicit. Propositions C.2–C.3 are not consequences formalized by this lemma alone.

Fix an arbitrary coupling \((X,Y)\) of the two latent laws. Split the force difference into a parameter change at fixed law and a law change at fixed parameter. Nonexpansive parameter projection and the full score's \(L\)-Lipschitz property give \(\|\nabla_\theta U(\theta,x)-\nabla_\theta U(\vartheta,y)\|\le L(\|\theta-\vartheta\|+\|x-y\|)\). Integrability of this observable follows from the latent second moments. Integrate, use Cauchy–Schwarz on \(\mathbb E\|X-Y\|\), and take the coupling infimum to obtain \[\|b(\theta,\mu)-b(\vartheta,\nu)\|\le L\|\theta-\vartheta\|+LW_2(\mu,\nu).\] The Moreau specialization substitutes the already proved score constant \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\).

Formal correspondence: meanFieldDrift_lipschitz_wasserstein2 : Corrected W₂ version of Lemma C.1 for an actual gradient-Lipschitz joint potential and actual finite-second-moment latent probability laws. moreau_meanFieldDrift_lipschitz_wasserstein2 : For split Moreau smoothing, the actual averaged drift has coefficient L₁+1/eta ; the finite moments and all integral guards remain explicit.

Add and subtract \(b_V(\theta',\mu)\). The parameter change is bounded by \(L\|\theta-\theta'\|\), using the same latent law and source mass one. The law change is bounded by \(LW_2(\mu,\nu)\), using arbitrary couplings. Adding yields the result. For split Moreau smoothing, both scores contribute, so its constant is \(L_1+1/\eta\), rather than the full-envelope constant alone.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldProcess.lean.title: Construct the mean-field L² integral equations
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldProcess.lean.summary:
A mean-field process can be constructed as an ordinary integral equation in the complete space of square-integrable random joint states. A bounded linear averaging operator replaces only the parameter score by its expectation. Lipschitzness of the actual gradient permits Picard construction, and projection then derives a deterministic parameter path coupled to the actual latent law.

Work on a probability space \(Q\), with \(H=L^2(Q;\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x})\). A potential \(V\) with globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient defines the actual mean-field drift. Its continuous finite-horizon integral solution is constructed by the Banach-space Picard theorem.

steps.title: Expectation is a bounded linear map from L²
steps.body:
The norm-of-integral inequality and \(\|X\|_{L^1}\le\|X\|_{L^2}\) on a probability space give \(\|\mathbb E_Q X\|\le\|X\|_2\). Bochner additivity and scalar linearity therefore define a bounded linear map \(\mathcal E:H\to E\) with operator norm at most one. The evaluation lemma records that its value is the actual integral.

Formal correspondence: norm_lp_expectation_le : On a probability space, the actual expectation is bounded by the L² norm. lpExpectationCLM : Actual Bochner expectation as a bounded linear map out of L².

Bochner integration is linear on square-integrable random variables, since probability normalization implies integrability. The norm bound follows from the norm-of-integral inequality followed by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus expectation is continuous with norm at most one. As a bounded linear map, it commutes with later continuous time integrals, which is needed when extracting the deterministic parameter equation.

steps.title: Coordinate projections and a parameter inclusion
steps.body:
Define \(P_x(\theta,x)=x\) and \(I_\theta(\theta)=(\theta,0)\). Their coordinate identities follow by evaluating the definitions. The Euclidean square identity \(\|(\theta,0)\|^2=\|\theta\|^2\), followed by nonnegative square-root cancellation, proves that \(I_\theta\) is an isometry.

Formal correspondence: jointLatentCLM : The latent component of one parameter/latent joint vector. jointParameterInclusionCLM : Embed only a parameter block into the joint space.

The parameter inclusion inserts zeros in all latent coordinates. The latent projection forgets the parameter coordinates. Expanding the Euclidean square shows that the inclusion preserves norms and the projection does not increase them. These coordinate maps act pointwise on square-integrable variables and retain their bounded linearity, giving precise control of the projected integral equations.

steps.title: A true latent mask erases all parameter coordinates
steps.body:
Set \(M_x=I-I_\theta P_\theta\). Its parameter block is zero and its latent block is unchanged. Expanding the Euclidean squared norm shows \(\|M_xz\|^2\le\|z\|^2\), since the discarded parameter square is nonnegative. Thus the mask is nonexpansive and remains bounded after composition on \(L^2\).

Formal correspondence: jointLatentMaskCLM : The actual latent-coordinate projection on the joint space.

The mask \(M_x\) removes the orthogonal parameter part and keeps the latent part. Its squared norm is exactly the sum of latent coordinate squares, bounded by the full sum. Therefore masking preserves square integrability and continuity of an \(L^2\)-valued input. In particular it produces a latent-only Brownian input whose parameter projection is identically zero.

steps.title: Average exactly the parameter block
steps.body:
Construct the bounded linear map

\[\mathcal M X=\operatorname{const}(I_\theta P_\theta\mathbb E_QX)+M_xX.\]

The expectation estimate and coordinate contractions bound each term by \(\|X\|_2\), so \(\|\mathcal M X\|_2\le2\|X\|_2\). Linearity then proves \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal M)\le2\). This is a conservative sufficient constant.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldAverageCLM : Average the parameter coordinates and retain the latent coordinates as actual random variables. This is a bounded linear map, not an assumed drift.

The averaging operator maps \((\Theta,X)\) to \((\mathbb E\Theta,X)\), with the expected parameter viewed as a constant random variable. Its two terms are bounded linear, so the sum has the stated sufficient norm bound two. This operator averages the parameter score only; it does not replace each latent force by its expectation. That distinction produces the intended interacting parameter–latent mean-field dynamics.

steps.title: Define the actual drift and apply Picard
steps.body:
Set \(\mathcal A_V(X)=\mathcal M(\nabla V(X))\). The Nemytskii map for the actual Lipschitz gradient preserves \(L^2\) and has constant \(L\), so \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_V)\le2L\). For any continuous \(H\)-valued input \(B\) with \(B_0=0\), and any \(T\ge0\), Picard constructs continuous \(Y\) with \(Y_0=Y^{\rm in}\) and

\[Y_t-Y^{\rm in}=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_V(Y_s)ds+B_t,\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The proof is an existence theorem in the actual complete Banach space \(H\).

The averaging operator retains the latent gradient pointwise and replaces the parameter gradient by its expectation as a constant random variable. Expectation is a bounded linear map \(L^2\to H\) of norm at most one on a probability space, and the coordinate masks are orthogonal contractions. Thus the averaged drift is globally Lipschitz once the true joint score is Lipschitz. Picard's theorem applies in the complete Hilbert space of square-integrable joint states to a continuous additive input, constructing the actual integral solution on every finite horizon.

Formal correspondence: lpMeanFieldDrift : The actual mean-field drift: expected parameter force and pointwise latent force. lpMeanFieldDrift_lipschitz : A conservative global Lipschitz constant for the constructed drift. exists_lp_meanField_integral : Picard constructs the continuous mean-field L² integral solution from its actual gradient and a continuous L² additive input on every finite horizon.

A Lipschitz score defines a Lipschitz composition map on \(L^2\) and has affine growth, so it is everywhere defined on the state Hilbert space. Composing with the averaging operator gives constant at most \(2L\). For a continuous additive input, subtracting that input reduces the problem to a standard nonautonomous Lipschitz integral equation. Picard yields a continuous finite-horizon solution and the stated integral identity.

steps.title: Verify the intended block formulas in L²
steps.body:
Almost everywhere representative equalities show

\[(\mathcal M X)(\omega)=(\mathbb E_Q P_\theta X,\,P_xX(\omega)).\]

Applying parameter projection gives the constant random variable \(\operatorname{const}(P_\theta\mathbb E_QX)\); applying latent projection gives \(P_xX\). The proofs explicitly combine the almost everywhere addition, constant and composition identities, so they are equalities in \(L^2\).

Formal correspondence: meanFieldAverageCLM_coe : The averaging map has exactly its intended pointwise block action. meanFieldAverageCLM_parameter : Averaging makes the parameter block a constant random variable. meanFieldAverageCLM_latent : Averaging leaves the actual latent random variable unchanged.

The coordinate formula can be checked on representatives: the included expectation contributes only a constant parameter block, and the mask contributes only the original latent block. Their sum has exactly the displayed components almost surely. Projecting removes the other block without error. These identities show that the abstract averaging construction implements the intended parameter expectation while leaving latent randomness intact.

steps.title: Identify the parameter force with the true marginal integral
steps.body:
Define \(a_V(X)=P_ heta\mathbb E_Q abla V(X)\), a continuous map on \(H\). The drift blocks are \(\operatorname{const}(a_V(X))\) and \(P_x abla V(X)\). If \(P_ heta X=\operatorname{const}( heta)\), reconstruct \(X=( heta,P_xX)\) almost everywhere. Commute the bounded projection through expectation and use the pushforward integral formula to prove

\[a_V(X)=\int abla_ heta V( heta,x)\,\mathcal L_Q(P_xX)(dx).\]

Formal correspondence: lpMeanFieldParameterForce : The actual expected parameter force of a square-integrable joint vector. lpMeanFieldDrift_parameter : The parameter projection of the actual drift is its expected force. lpMeanFieldDrift_latent : The latent projection of the actual drift is pointwise latent gradient. lpMeanFieldParameterForce_eq_meanFieldDrift : The expected force equals the actual mean-field drift integral whenever the input parameter is deterministic. The latent marginal is its actual law.

If the parameter block is deterministic, the joint state equals \(( heta,P_xX)\) almost surely. Evaluate the actual joint score on this representation, project its parameter block, and commute projection through expectation. Changing variables by the latent pushforward law then gives the marginal integral defining \(b_V\). This law is derived from the current random state, rather than introduced as an independent curve of measures.

steps.title: Project the integral equation and construct a deterministic parameter
steps.body:
Suppose the initial parameter is constant \(\theta_0\) and \(P_\theta B_t=0\). Bounded linear maps commute with the Bochner time integral, so projecting the constructed equation gives \(P_\theta Y_t=\operatorname{const}(\theta_t)\), where \(\theta_t=\theta_0-\int_0^t a_V(Y_s)ds\). The continuous primitive proves continuity of \(\theta\). Set \(\mu_t=\mathcal L_Q(P_xY_t)\) and insert the force identity:

\[\theta_t-\theta_0=-\int_0^t b_V(\theta_s,\mu_s)ds,\qquad P_xY_t-P_xY_0=-\int_0^tP_x\nabla V(Y_s)ds+P_xB_t.\]

Both identities hold in their stated deterministic or \(L^2\) sense on the finite horizon.

Project the constructed joint equation onto the parameter and latent blocks. Continuous linear maps commute with the Bochner time integral. Since the additive input has zero parameter block, its parameter coordinate remains a constant random variable, represented by a deterministic continuous path \(\theta_t\). The force identity replaces expectation of the joint parameter score by its integral under the actual latent pushforward law \(\mu_t\), giving \[\theta_t-\theta_0=-\int_0^t\left[\int\nabla_\theta V(\theta_s,x)\,d\mu_s(x)\right]ds.\] The latent projection yields the corresponding drift-plus-noise equation. The parameter law is therefore derived from the constructed process, not introduced as a free auxiliary measure path.

Formal correspondence: lp_meanField_parameter_equation : Projection of the constructed equation preserves a deterministic parameter and gives its genuine integral equation. lp_meanField_latent_equation : The latent component satisfies the actual projected gradient equation. exists_lp_meanField_equations : The constructed solution has a continuous deterministic parameter, its actual latent marginal, and both mean-field integral equations. No solution trajectory or law evolution is assumed in this existence statement.

The additive parameter input vanishes and the initial parameter is constant. The projected drift is also constant as a random variable at each time. Hence its time integral is constant, proving the parameter remains deterministic. Its continuous path is defined by the parameter integral equation. Substituting the preceding force identity expresses it in terms of the actual latent law, while latent projection retains the Brownian-driven integral equation.

steps.title: Construct a continuous latent-only Brownian input
steps.body:
Apply the latent mask to the actual coordinate Brownian \(L^2\) noise. Brownian second moments prove its continuity in \(L^2\) and its zero value at time zero. Masking makes its parameter projection zero at every time. No separate continuity assumption on a stochastic error process is used.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldBrownianNoise : Actual Brownian-coordinate inputs, with only their latent coordinates retained, give a concrete continuous L² input. Noise continuity and its zero initial value are conclusions of the Brownian laws.

For the coordinate Brownian vector, \(L^2\) increments have norm proportional to the square root of the time increment, proving \(L^2\) continuity. Multiplication by the bounded latent mask preserves continuity and makes the parameter block zero. Its value at time zero is zero because the Brownian increment from zero to zero vanishes. These facts verify the general input assumptions by construction.

steps.title: Specialize to Brownian input and to the split envelope
steps.body:
The constructed Brownian input satisfies all hypotheses of the general integral existence theorem, so substitution gives the Brownian-driven \(L^2\) solution. For \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), the actual proximal calculus supplies the Lipschitz gradient constant \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\), which is included as a derived witness in the conclusion. These results establish continuous \(L^2\) integral equations; they do not assert a pathwise strong-SDE or a Fokker–Planck PDE theorem.

Formal correspondence: exists_lp_meanField_integral_of_brownian : Genuine finite-horizon mean-field L² existence with a Brownian input. All stochastic input continuity is derived from the coordinate Brownian laws; no pathwise strong-SDE, independence or adaptedness assertion is made. exists_lp_moreau_meanField_integral : Split Moreau smoothing supplies the actual globally Lipschitz gradient needed by the mean-field construction. Its coefficient is L₁+1/eta .

Use the actual latent-only Brownian input in the finite-horizon Picard theorem, then use the proximal calculus to specialize the potential to \(g_1+g_2^\eta\). The sum has gradient constant \(L_1+1/\eta\), so all analytic drift hypotheses have already been proved. The conclusion is an \(L^2\)-valued continuous integral solution with a deterministic parameter equation; stronger pathwise or PDE conclusions require additional arguments.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldSmoothing.lean.title: Finite smoothing comparison for actual mean-field equations
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldSmoothing.lean.summary:
With the additional smoothness of the original nonsmooth-designated component, proximal optimality identifies the envelope score with the original score evaluated at the proximal point. A finite displacement bound then gives a uniform linear-in-scale score defect. Constructing both integral systems with common input lets that input cancel, and Grönwall controls their uniform timewise square-integrable difference.

For this module the convex bounded-below \(g_2\) is additionally differentiable, with \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient and global value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The finite-horizon comparison uses the same initialization and additive input for the original and split-smoothed systems.

steps.title: At differentiability points subgradients equal the gradient
steps.body:
A supporting vector \(s\) makes \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle s,x angle\) globally minimized at the support point \(p\). Its derivative there is zero, so \(s= abla f(p)\). Apply this to the genuine proximal residual to obtain the exact identity \( abla f^\eta(x)= abla f(P_\eta(x))\).

Formal correspondence: IsSubgradient.eq_gradient : A supporting subgradient of a differentiable function is its actual gradient. gradient_moreau_eq_gradient_prox : The actual Moreau score is the original smooth score at the true proximal point.

If \(s\) supports a differentiable convex function at \(p\), the function \(f(x)-\langle s,x angle\) has a global minimum at \(p\). Its derivative there vanishes, so \(s= abla f(p)\). Apply this to the actual proximal residual and the established envelope gradient formula. This proves an exact identity at every input, rather than an approximation to the score.

steps.title: Smoothness gives a finite score defect
steps.body:
Compose \( abla f\), which is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz, with the nonexpansive map \(P_\eta\). The envelope gradient therefore has constant \(L_2\), independent of \(\eta\). The actual proximal displacement bound \(\|x-P_\eta(x)\|\le\eta K\) gives

\[\| abla f(x)- abla f^\eta(x)\|\le L_2\|x-P_\eta(x)\|\le\eta L_2K.\]

This is a finite inequality, without a Taylor remainder.

When the original convex function is differentiable, a subgradient at a point equals its gradient; evaluate support along both signed directions and take the directional derivative. Proximal optimality therefore gives \( abla f^\eta(x)= abla f(P_\eta x)\). If \( abla f\) is \(L_2\)-Lipschitz and \(f\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz, then \[\| abla f^\eta(x)- abla f(x)\|\le L_2\|P_\eta x-x\|\le\eta L_2K.\] This finite score defect is the numerical forcing in the smoothing comparison.

Formal correspondence: smooth_moreau_gradient_lipschitz : Smoothness of the original score is preserved by the actual Moreau envelope. gradient_moreau_defect_le : The uniform score defect is derived from proximal optimality and displacement. Its coefficient is independent of the smoothing parameter.

The gradient of the envelope is \( abla f\circ P_\eta\). ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldVariance.lean.title: Exact iid variance and the empirical parameter force

Square-integrability justifies expansion of the finite double sum, and independence cancels all off-diagonal terms after centering. Specializing the observable to the actual parameter gradient supplies the quantitative empirical mean-field force fluctuation.

On a probability space, square-integrable Hilbert-valued variables have integrable inner products. On the actual finite product law, independent centered samples yield an exact \(1/N\) variance identity.

steps.body:
Realize the supplied \(L^2\) functions as \(L^2\) elements; Cauchy–Schwarz gives integrable pairwise inner products. Expand

\[\mathbb E\left\|\sum_iX_i\right\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\mathbb E\langle X_i,X_j\rangle.\]

For \(i\ne j\), independence factors the expectation into \(\langle\mathbb E X_i,\mathbb E X_j\rangle=0\). The diagonal terms are \(\mathbb E\|X_i\|^2\). Finite sums and established integrability justify the expansion.

Expand the Hilbert square as \(\|\sum_iX_i\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\). Each mixed product is integrable by the \(L^2\) inner-product bound, which justifies moving the finite double sum through the integral. For \(i\ne j\), independence factors \(\mathbb E\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) into \(\langle\mathbb EX_i,\mathbb EX_j\rangle=0\). For \(i=j\), it is \(\mathbb E\|X_i\|^2\). steps.title: The exact variance of an independent sample mean

The proof centers \(\phi\), expands the squared Hilbert norm, and uses independence and zero mean to cancel every off-diagonal inner product. The exact result is

\[ \mathbb E_{\mu^{\otimes N}} \left\|\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\right\|^2 =\frac1N\mathbb E_\mu\|\phi-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\|^2. \]

Taking square roots proves the \(N^{-1/2}\) sampling factor. The actual parameter-gradient observable is square integrable under finite-P₂ latent laws, so the formula applies to the mean-field force.

The source’s exchangeability premise alone does not cancel these covariances. A quantitative chaos estimate needs controlled initialization, such as the actual iid construction used here. This exact sampling identity is a proved ingredient; by itself it is not a propagation-of-chaos theorem.

steps.body:
Each coordinate difference is bounded by the product-state norm. The joint-pair estimate therefore gives \(\|\nabla V(J_i z)-\nabla V(J_i w)\|_2\le2L\|z-w\|\). ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCopies.lean.title: Actual iid L² copies and their exact drift residual
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCopies.lean.summary:
A genuine finite product of the reference probability space realizes independent copies of the mean-field state. Its deterministic parameter is shared exactly, while its latent coordinates are copied independently. Bounded linear copy maps commute with the reference integral equation, and their exact drift residual is the centered empirical parameter force with \(N^{-1/2}\) norm.

Starting from one mean-field random pair on \(Q\), construct copies on the actual finite product \(P=Q^{\otimes N}\). When its parameter is deterministic, all copies share that parameter and their latent coordinates are iid.

steps.title: Measure-preserving coordinate pullback is a bounded linear copy map
steps.body:
For product coordinate \(\omega_i\), define \(C_iX=X\circ\omega_i\). Evaluation is measure preserving, so pullback is an \(L^2\) isometry and a bounded linear map. Its representative equals \(X(\omega_i)\) almost everywhere. Coordinate substitution proves \(C_i(CX)=C(C_iX)\) for bounded linear \(C\), and \(C_i(\operatorname{const}x)=\operatorname{const}x\).

The coordinate evaluation \(\omega\mapsto\omega_i\) has pushforward \(Q\), so the integral of \(\|X(\omega_i)\|^2\) equals the original second moment. Pullback is therefore a linear isometry on \(L^2\). It preserves constants and commutes with fixed coordinate projections because these equalities hold pointwise on representatives. This gives a concrete copy operation rather than a distribution-only assertion.

steps.title: Center and compute the true empirical fluctuation norm
steps.body:
For \(N>0\), define \(\mathcal C X=X-\operatorname{const}(\mathbb EX)\) and \(\Delta_N(X)=N^{-1}\sum_iC_iX-\operatorname{const}(\mathbb EX)\). Almost everywhere finite-sum identities identify its representative with the genuine sample mean. The exact iid variance formula gives

\[\|\Delta_N(X)\|_{L^2(P)}^2=\frac1N\|\mathcal C X\|_{L^2(Q)}^2,\qquad\|\Delta_N(X)\|_2=\frac{\|\mathcal C X\|_2}{\sqrt N}.\]

The coordinate pullback \(X\mapsto X(\omega_i)\) is a linear isometry because coordinate evaluation preserves \(Q\). It therefore commutes with continuous linear coordinate projections and retains constants. Center the original variable by its actual Bochner expectation, then form the empirical fluctuation of these genuine iid copies. The representative theorem identifies this \(L^2\) object with the usual centered sample average. Substituting the exact product variance identity gives \[\|\text{empirical fluctuation}\|_2^2=\frac{\|X-\mathbb EX\|_2^2}{N},\] and nonnegative square roots give its precise \(N^{-1/2}\) norm.

Centering subtracts the actual Bochner expectation, producing a square-integrable zero-mean variable. Its copies are independent under the product measure, so the exact variance identity applies to their average. Taking square roots gives the residual norm divided by \(\sqrt N\). The result uses the centered force's true norm, with no assumed independence of the later interacting particle states.

If \(P_\theta X=\operatorname{const}\theta\), the parameter block of \(\mathcal R_N(X)\) is exactly \(\operatorname{const}\theta\). The coordinate lemmas are direct evaluations of this bounded linear construction.

The product maximum norm and exact fluctuation identity therefore give residual norm \(\|\mathcal C(P_ heta abla V(X))\|_2/\sqrt N\). This equality is the source of the particle comparison rate.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldForcing.lean.title: Grönwall comparison with an extra continuous noise input

Two integral equations can be compared when their common continuous input is supplemented by a small extra input in one system. Subtracting the extra input before applying Grönwall avoids differentiating Brownian paths. The bound is linear in a common inverse sampling scale, so drift fluctuation and parameter noise can be combined in one \(N^{-1/2}\) estimate.

steps.title: Subtract the extra input before applying integral Grönwall
steps.body:
Suppose \(\|A_t\|\le a\), \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C\), and

\[X_t-x=-\int_0^tF(X_s)ds+B_t+A_t,\qquad Y_t-x=-\int_0^tG_sds+B_t.\]

The inputs \(B,A\) may be continuous Brownian paths in \(L^2\); differentiating them would be invalid. Instead set \(D_t=X_t-Y_t-A_t\). Subtracting the two actual integral equations cancels \(B\) and \(A\), leaving \[D_t=-\int_0^t[F(X_s)-G_s]ds,\quad D_0=0.\] Continuity of the integrands proves that this remainder has derivative \(-F(X_t)+G_t\).

Let \(D=X-Y-A\). The difference of the two equations is a time integral, so \(D\) is differentiable even if \(A\) and the common input are not. Since \(X-Y=D+A\), the drift bound is \(L\|D\|+La+C\). The explicit zero-initial-error Grönwall function is linear in its forcing coefficient, including its \(L=0\) branch. Thus \(\operatorname{GB}(0,L,C/r,T)=\operatorname{GB}(0,L,C,T)/r\). If \(r>0\), \(\|A_t\|\le a/r\) and \(\|F(Y_t)-G_t\|\le C/r\), substitute into the preceding theorem and factor:

steps.title: Pull back Brownian coordinates and define their scaled L² noise
steps.body:
Coordinate evaluation on the finite product is measure preserving, so each pulled-back scalar process retains its standard Brownian law. Define \(A_t=N^{-1/2}\sqrt2(B_t^\theta-B_0^\theta)\) as an actual \(L^2\) element. The Brownian-noise construction proves continuity in \(L^2\) and value zero at time zero; scalar multiplication preserves both facts.

Choose copy zero on the finite iid product, which exists because \(N>0\). Coordinate evaluation is measure preserving, so pulling back each supplied standard Brownian coordinate preserves its Brownian law. Multiply its Langevin noise \(\sqrt2W_t\) by \(N^{-1/2}\), producing the actual common parameter input. The \(L^2\)-valued Brownian construction proves continuity in time and zero initial value; neither property is assumed for a newly introduced noise process.

Formal correspondence: empiricalParameter_preBrownian : Each coordinate of the common parameter source has the actual Brownian law after pullback to the finite iid product. empiricalParameterNoise : The actual parameter Brownian input, with the particle scaling.

A coordinate of the finite product has exactly the original source law. Pulling the parameter Brownian paths through that coordinate therefore preserves their scalar Brownian distributions. The vector construction sums their finite second moments and multiplies by \(\sqrt{2/N}\). Continuity in \(L^2\) and zero initial value are inherited from the constructed Brownian increment process and fixed scalar multiplication.

steps.title: Derive the exact norm and its N-independent horizon coefficient
steps.body:
The coordinate second moments sum to \(d_\theta t\). Consequently

\[\|A_t\|_2=\frac{\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt t}{\sqrt N}\le\frac{\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt T}{\sqrt N},\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The theorem follows by the exact Brownian norm identity and monotonicity of the square root. The canonical specialization uses the already constructed Gaussian time-indicator Brownian source, so it supplies a concrete instance rather than postulating one.

Each parameter Brownian coordinate has variance \(t\), so the vector Langevin noise has squared \(L^2\) norm \(2d_\theta t\). Scalar multiplication by \(N^{-1/2}\) gives the exact identity \[\|A_N(t)\|_2=\frac{\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt t}{\sqrt N}.\] Monotonicity of the square root gives the uniform horizon bound with \(\sqrt T\). The canonical corollary merely substitutes the already constructed Gaussian time-indicator Brownian source, thereby discharging existence of a source with these moments.

Formal correspondence: empiricalParameterNoise_norm : The exact Brownian second-moment scale of the actual parameter input. empiricalParameterNoise_bound : A finite-horizon bound with an explicit coefficient independent of N . canonical_empiricalParameterNoise_bound : A concrete source exists: the Brownian coordinates are the already constructed independent Gaussian time-indicator processes.

The squared norm is \((2/N)\sum_{j=1}^{d_\theta}\mathbb E|B_t^j-B_0^j|^2=2d_\theta t/N\). Its nonnegative square root gives the exact formula. For \(t\le T\), monotonicity yields the horizon coefficient \(\sqrt{2d_\theta T}\), independent of \(N\). This is the additional-input constant inserted into the scaled Grönwall comparison.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldBrownianFamily.title: An independent Brownian family for all actual particle coordinates
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldBrownianFamily.summary:
The actual particle input needs one common parameter Brownian block and a separate latent Brownian block for each particle. Selecting distinct tagged coordinates from independent source copies constructs all these paths with joint independence. The first source copy may supply both blocks because parameter and latent coordinate tags are disjoint.

On \(Q^{\otimes N}\), choose parameter Brownian coordinates from copy zero and latent coordinate \((i,j)\) from copy \(i\). Injective selection proves independence of complete selected coordinate paths.

steps.title: Select distinct copy/coordinate pairs
steps.body:
Map a parameter index \(j\) to \((0,\mathrm{parameter}\ j)\), and a latent index \((i,j)\) to \((i,\mathrm{latent}\ j)\). The parameter/latent tags make the two kinds disjoint, and equality within either kind forces equality of the original indices. This proves injectivity. Define the family by evaluating the corresponding source Brownian coordinate in the selected copy; the displayed coordinate identities unfold the selection.

The index map sends a parameter coordinate \(j\) to \((0,\theta_j)\) and a latent particle coordinate \((i,j)\) to \((i,x_j)\). These are distinct even for the first particle because the parameter and latent coordinates use different summands of the joint index. The injectivity proof checks the four parameter/latent cases explicitly. The two evaluation lemmas then identify the selected paths with the intended common parameter noise and each particle's own latent noise.

Formal correspondence: particleBrownianIndex : Select a distinct base-copy/coordinate pair for every particle-noise coordinate. particleBrownianIndex_injective : The common parameter uses copy zero; latent blocks use their respective copies. particleBrownianFamily : The actual joint Brownian source for the interacting particle coordinates.

A parameter coordinate is selected from copy zero with a parameter tag, while particle \(i\)'s latent coordinate is selected from copy \(i\) with a latent tag. Equality of two selected indices forces matching tags and matching original coordinates. Thus the selection is injective even when a parameter coordinate and the first particle share source copy zero. No scalar Brownian coordinate is reused.

steps.title: Each selected process retains its Brownian law
steps.body:
Pullback along product evaluation is measure preserving, so every selected scalar process is standard pre-Brownian. If all source evaluations are measurable, composition with the selected coordinate map proves every new evaluation measurable as well.

Formal correspondence: particleBrownianFamily_preBrownian : Every selected coordinate is an actual standard pre-Brownian motion. particleBrownianFamily_measurable : Measurable source evaluations remain measurable after selecting a copy.

Each selection is a composition of measure-preserving product evaluation with a supplied scalar Brownian coordinate. Its one-process law remains standard Brownian. Measurability of its evaluations is preserved by the same composition. These statements verify the individual path properties before joint independence is established by the separate full-family argument.

steps.title: Flatten independent rows and select an injective subfamily
steps.body:
The finite product makes the complete Brownian rows independent. Inside each row, the supplied full coordinate paths are independent. The product-family independence theorem flattens these into independent variables indexed by \((i,j)\). Precomposing with the injective selection proves independence of all particle coordinates, including parameter and first-particle latent blocks. The canonical Brownian source supplies both the row laws and full-path independence, yielding an explicit complete family.

First pull each whole Brownian row from the source to one coordinate of the finite product; distinct rows are independent by the product measure. Within a row the supplied coordinate paths are independent, and measure-preserving evaluation retains their joint law. The helper iIndepFun_uncurry' flattens these two levels into a jointly independent family indexed by all copy/coordinate pairs. Finally, precomposition with the injective index map selects the intended subfamily and preserves independence. This proves independence of full coordinate paths, including the parameter path and the first particle's latent path; it does not assert independence of interacting particle states.

Formal correspondence: particleBrownianFamily_paths_independent : Full coordinate-path independence is derived on the actual finite product. There is no assumption of independent particles after interaction. canonical_particleBrownianFamily : The concrete canonical Gaussian time-indicator construction supplies all selected scalar Brownian laws and their full-path independence.

Different product coordinates give independent complete source rows. Within each row the scalar coordinate paths are jointly independent by hypothesis. Flattening the row-coordinate pairs therefore gives one jointly independent family, and injective selection preserves independence. This proves independence of the full selected paths, stronger than independence at one time, and supplies the exact common parameter and individual latent Brownian inputs.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldInitialSource..title: Concrete independent initialization and Brownian paths
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldInitialSource..summary:
Primitive initial data consist of a deterministic parameter and a latent law with finite second moment. Their product with a canonical independent Brownian source constructs the actual square-integrable joint initialization, the complete noise family and initialization/noise independence. This discharges probabilistic existence assumptions before constructing mean-field and particle solutions.

Given a latent probability law \(\mu\) with finite second moment and a deterministic \(\theta_0\), use the product \(Q=\mu\otimes Q_B\), where \(Q_B\) is the canonical joint Brownian source. This constructs all initialization and source hypotheses from primitive data.

steps.title: Product source and its measurable Brownian evaluations
steps.body:
The source is the actual product law \(\mu\otimes Q_B\). Brownian coordinates use only its second factor, so measure-preserving second projection transfers their standard Brownian laws. Coordinate measurability assembles into full-path measurability. The joint path pushforward remains exactly its canonical product law, proving independence of the complete coordinate paths after initialization is added.

Probability normalization follows from the product measure identity \(Q(\Omega)=\mu(X)Q_B(\Omega_B)=1\cdot1=1\). This records normalization of the constructed source before any law or expectation is used.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldInitialSource : The supplied latent initialization law times the explicit Gaussian Brownian source. meanFieldInitialBrownian : Brownian coordinates use the independent second factor of the source. meanFieldInitialBrownian_preBrownian : Each coordinate has the actual standard Brownian law on the product source. meanFieldInitialBrownian_paths_independent : The entire coordinate paths remain independent after adding initialization.

The product probability has total mass one because both factors do. Brownian coordinates depend only on the second factor, whose projection preserves its source law. Hence adding the independent latent initialization leaves both the individual Brownian laws and their joint coordinate independence unchanged. Measurable evaluation at every time also transfers through this projection.

steps.title: Build the square-integrable pair initialization
steps.body:
The map \(x\mapsto(\theta_0,x)\) is nonexpansive because its parameter difference vanishes. The latent first-factor variable has finite second moment under the product law. Lipschitz composition therefore proves that \((\theta_0,X_0)\) is square integrable, and its actual \(L^2\) representative defines the initialization.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldInitialPair_lipschitz : Holding the parameter fixed embeds latent vectors isometrically into pairs. meanFieldInitial_memLp : A fixed parameter and the actual latent initialization form an L² joint vector. meanFieldInitialLp : The actual square-integrable initialization used by the integral constructors.

The initialized pair is \((\theta_0,X_0)\). Its squared norm is \(\|\theta_0\|^2+\|X_0\|^2\), so the deterministic parameter contributes a finite constant and the latent assumption supplies the remaining finite moment. The pair map is measurable and Lipschitz in the latent input. Thus it determines an actual element of the joint \(L^2\) state space.

steps.title: Retain the exact parameter, latent law and source independence
steps.body:
The representative equals \((\theta_0,\omega_1)\) almost everywhere, so its parameter projection is \(\operatorname{const}\theta_0\), and its latent pushforward is exactly \(\mu\). The whole initialization depends only on the first factor while all Brownian paths depend only on the second. Product independence, followed by the almost everywhere representative substitution, proves independence of initialization and the entire Brownian family.

The source is the product of the supplied latent initial law and the canonical joint Brownian source. The initialized pair is \((\theta_0,x)\), a Lipschitz function of the first coordinate; its square integrability follows from the given latent second moment. The noise paths depend only on the second coordinate. Product independence therefore proves initialization/noise-path independence, while the projection identities prove that the parameter is the constant \(\theta_0\) and the latent law is exactly the supplied \(\mu\). This construction discharges the probabilistic inputs without asking for a pre-existing process on the user's probability space.

Formal correspondence: meanFieldInitialLp_parameter : The parameter block is exactly the constant initial parameter in L². meanFieldInitialLp_latent_law : Its latent marginal is exactly the supplied finite-second-moment law. meanFieldInitialLp_independent_paths : Initialization is independent of every Brownian coordinate at every time.

The first product coordinate has exactly the supplied latent law, and the parameter coordinate is the fixed \(\theta_0\). All Brownian paths depend only on the independent second factor. Their joint input law therefore factors exactly between initialization and complete noise family. Replacing random variables by almost-surely equal square-integrable representatives preserves these laws and their independence.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticles.lean.title: Constructed iid particle comparison with uniform timewise L² control
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticles.lean.summary:
A continuous mean-field reference is first constructed independently of particle count. On each finite product source its iid copies satisfy the reference equation with a drift defect equal to an empirical centered parameter force. Compact-horizon continuity bounds that force, while the additional parameter Brownian input has the same inverse-square-root particle scale. Grönwall then controls every tagged timewise \(L^2\) error.

For a potential with globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, compare a constructed mean-field solution with actual finite-particle coordinate solutions on the iid product source. The coefficient is chosen before all particle counts and the norm is the supremum of timewise \(L^2\) errors.

steps.title: The actual centered force is continuous and bounded on a finite horizon
steps.body:
Define \(\mathcal C_V(X)=P_\theta\nabla V(X)-\operatorname{const}\mathbb E[P_\theta\nabla V(X)]\) using bounded linear centering and the actual Lipschitz drift. This composition is continuous. For continuous \(Y_t\), the image of compact \([0,T]\) is compact; its centered-force norm therefore has a finite bound \(C\ge0\). This \(C\) depends on the reference and horizon and is chosen independently of \(N\).

Formal correspondence: centeredMeanFieldForce : The centered actual parameter force of one mean-field copy. exists_centeredMeanFieldForce_bound : Continuity of the constructed reference supplies a finite force coefficient on a compact horizon. This coefficient is independent of particle count.

The actual centered parameter score is a continuous function of the reference \(L^2\) state: score composition is Lipschitz, projection is bounded linear and expectation is continuous. The reference path is continuous, so its centered-force norm attains a finite bound on compact \([0,T]\). This bound is chosen before constructing any \(N\)-particle product and is therefore independent of particle count.

steps.title: Copies inherit the actual equation by bounded linearity
steps.body:
The copy map \(\mathcal R_N\) is bounded linear, so it commutes with the Bochner time integral and preserves differences. Apply it to the mean-field equation to get the exact copied-reference forcing. Define

\[C_T=2\big[(C+2Lb)\Psi(2L,T)+b\big].\]

Here \(C\) bounds the actual centered force and \(b/\sqrt N\) bounds the extra parameter input. The factor two converts the coordinate maximum norm into the sum of parameter and one latent error.

Formal correspondence: iidMeanFieldCopies_integral_equation : The actual iid reference inherits its integral equation by a bounded linear map, so its forcing is constructed from the mean-field solution. meanFieldParticleConstant : Finite-horizon coefficient in the tagged-coordinate L² comparison. C bounds the actual centered reference force, and b bounds the parameter Brownian input after multiplication by sqrt N .

Applying the bounded linear reference-copy map to the time integral commutes with integration. The copied process consequently satisfies an exact integral equation with copied mean-field drift. Its difference from the particle drift is controlled by the empirical residual theorem. The extra factor two in the final coefficient bounds the sum of the parameter and one latent coordinate error by twice the maximum product norm.

steps.title: Construct the particle solution and use the exact iid residual
steps.body:
For each \(N>0\), Picard constructs the actual particle solution \(Z\) with copied latent input and any continuous extra parameter input \(A\) bounded by \(b/\sqrt N\). The copied mean-field reference has drift residual norm exactly \(\|\mathcal C_V(Y_t)\|_2/\sqrt N\le C/\sqrt N\). Apply the forcing-comparison theorem to the \(2L\)-Lipschitz particle drift. Both tagged coordinate errors are at most the product-state norm, hence

\[\|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\le C_T/\sqrt N,\qquad0\le t\le T.\]

The theorem retains the constructed integral equation and exact iid initial state. It does not assume the final rate.

Continuity of the single-copy centered force along the constructed mean-field path implies a finite bound \(C\) on the compact interval \([0,T]\). Construct the actual particle process by Picard with copied latent input and the extra parameter input \(A_N\). The copied reference equation follows by commuting its bounded linear copy map through the time integral. Its drift defect is at most \(C/\sqrt N\), by the exact iid residual theorem, and \(\|A_N\|\le b/\sqrt N\).

The scaled integral-forcing theorem, with particle Lipschitz constant \(2L\), yields \[\|Z_t-R_t\|\le\frac{\operatorname{gronwallBound}(0,2L,C+2Lb,T)+b}{\sqrt N}.\] Each parameter or tagged-latent difference is bounded by the maximum product norm; their sum is therefore at most twice this expression. This accounts for the factor two in meanFieldParticleConstant. The reference and \(C\) are chosen before \(N\), making the coefficient independent of particle count.

Formal correspondence: exists_particle_comparison_of_meanField_solution : The constructed particle solution is uniformly close, in each coordinate L² norm, to the genuine iid copies of an actual mean-field integral solution. The reference force coefficient is finite and independent of N .

Construct the actual particle solution with the copied initialization and prescribed additive input. The copied reference has drift residual at most \(C/\sqrt N\), while the extra parameter input is at most \(b/\sqrt N\). The particle drift is \(2L\)-Lipschitz. The scaled forcing theorem gives the maximum-norm error, and each tagged coordinate is bounded by that norm. The coefficient is fixed by the reference and horizon, not by \(N\).

steps.title: Construct both systems with actual Brownian inputs
steps.body:
The actual centered reference force is a continuous L²-valued function of time. Compactness of \([0,T]\) supplies a finite \(C\ge0\) such that

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\| \nabla_\theta V(Y_t)-\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)\|_2\le C. \]

This \(C\) is chosen before the quantifier over all particle counts; it depends on the reference potential, initial law and horizon, not on \(N\). Subtract the common latent input and the extra parameter Brownian input in the actual integral equations. The proof applies Grönwall to the remaining drift integral, so it never differentiates Brownian noise. Define

\[ \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0,\end{cases} \qquad C_T=2\big[(C+2Lb)\Psi(2L,T)+b\big]. \]

For every \(N>0\), the theorem constructs the actual particle integral solution with the prescribed iid initialization and proves, for every tagged particle \(i\),

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\left( \|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N}. \]

For the actual split-smoothed potential \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\), use the derived constant \(L=L_1+1/\eta\). The coefficient can depend on \(\eta\); uniformity in smoothing is not claimed. This is a constructed iid propagation-of-chaos replacement in uniform timewise L² norm. It does not move the time supremum inside the expectation, as in printed Proposition C.2; the expected path-supremum norm is stronger; the proved uniform timewise L² estimate does not establish it.

Formal correspondence: exists_brownian_meanField_particle_comparison : Both the mean-field reference and finite-particle coordinate processes are constructed from actual Brownian-coordinate inputs. The parameter-noise N-¹/² bound is proved from those laws by empiricalParameterNoise_bound . The conclusion controls each time's L² norm uniformly over the horizon.

The Brownian construction supplies \(b=\sqrt{2d_\theta T}\) and genuine independent latent and parameter coordinate paths. Substituting them gives actual mean-field and particle integral equations with the intended noise amplitudes. The estimate is uniform in time after taking \(L^2\) norms. A bound on the expectation of the samplewise time supremum would require an additional argument and is not obtained by exchanging these operations.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCanonical.lean.title: Canonical finite-particle comparison from primitive latent data
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldCanonical.lean.summary:
The canonical endpoint starts from a latent probability law with finite second moment, a deterministic initial parameter, a globally Lipschitz score and a finite horizon. Product sources supply all required independent Brownian coordinates. It constructs one mean-field reference and then actual particle solutions for every positive particle count, retaining their equations and uniform timewise square-integrable comparison.

Given a finite-second-moment latent law \(\mu\), deterministic \(\theta_0\), globally Lipschitz \(\nabla V\), and \(T\ge0\), the initialized canonical product source supplies concrete independent Brownian inputs and actual integral solutions for all \(N>0\).

steps.title: Discharge every scalar Brownian law and full-path independence
steps.body:
The initialized source already has the true Brownian coordinate laws and independent full paths. The injective particle-coordinate selection on its finite product preserves both properties. Thus the parameter coordinates and every particle’s latent coordinates form one independent standard Brownian family, including the first-copy overlap resolved by distinct coordinate tags.

Formal correspondence: initialized_particleBrownianFamily : Actual interacting-particle Brownian coordinates on the iid initialized canonical source: every coordinate is standard Brownian and all full paths are independent, including common-parameter and first-particle coordinates.

The initialized source has standard scalar Brownian coordinates independent as complete paths. Passing to a finite product creates independent source copies. The injective coordinate selection then supplies all common parameter and particle latent Brownian paths without duplication. Thus the individual Brownian laws, full-family independence and initialization independence needed in the endpoint all follow from the concrete source construction.

steps.title: Construct the reference once, then every particle process
steps.body:
Use the actual initial pair \((\theta_0,X_0)\) on \(\mu\otimes Q_B\), whose square integrability and deterministic parameter projection were proved. Substitute this source and the actual Brownian coordinate process into the Brownian comparison theorem. It constructs continuous \(Y,\theta\), a finite \(C\ge0\), and for every \(N>0\) a continuous actual particle solution \(Z^N\) with exact iid initialization. The equations retain latent noise \(\sqrt2 B^{x,i}\) and parameter noise \(\sqrt{2/N}B^\theta\), and prove

\[\sup_{0\le t\le T}\big(\|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\big)\le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N}.\]

The coefficient is selected before the quantifier over \(N\). This controls the supremum of \(L^2\) norms, without claiming an expected path supremum.

The primitive inputs are a latent probability law with finite second moment, a deterministic parameter, a globally Lipschitz joint score and a finite horizon. The initialized product source supplies all Brownian coordinate laws, their whole-path independence, and initialization/noise independence. Substitute these into the already proved Brownian comparison theorem to construct one mean-field reference, then a particle solution for every positive \(N\). The output retains both integral equations and the deterministic parameter equation alongside the bound. Its uniformity is \(\sup_{t\le T}\|Z_t-R_t\|_{L^2}\); no exchange of supremum and expectation is made.

Formal correspondence: exists_canonical_meanField_particle_comparison : From a latent probability law with finite second moment, construct the mean-field reference and actual interacting-particle processes for every positive particle count. The displayed constant is independent of that count; its existence follows from proved finite-horizon moments of the reference.

Construct the mean-field path and its finite centered-force horizon bound once. For each \(N>0\), copy the reference to the finite product, add the actual \(\sqrt{2/N}\) parameter Brownian input, and solve the empirical particle equation. The earlier residual and forcing estimates give the stated \(C_T/\sqrt N\) bound for every tag and time. The same reference-dependent \(C_T\) works for all particle counts.

ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleLaw.le.title: One-time Wasserstein convergence for actual tagged particles
ProximalLangevin/MeanFieldParticleLaw.le.summary:
The constructed tagged particle and its actual reference copy live on one probability space, giving an explicit finite-cost coupling of their one-time joint laws. The copy law is exactly the original mean-field law. Their coordinate \(L^2\) comparison therefore implies a Wasserstein rate while preserving the actual particle integral equation and noise construction.

The constructed particle/reference pair supplies an actual finite-cost coupling of tagged one-time laws. This module transfers the proved timewise \(L^2\) rate to \(W_2\), keeping the original integral equations and initialization.

steps.title: A measure-preserving copy has exactly the reference law
steps.body:
The copy representative equals \(X(\omega_i)\) almost everywhere. Product-coordinate evaluation pushes \(Q^{\otimes N}\) to \(Q\), so the pushforward composition formula proves \(\mathcal L_{Q^{\otimes N}}(C_iX)=\mathcal L_Q(X)\). The almost everywhere change of representative does not affect the law.

Formal correspondence: iidCopyCLM_law : An actual iid L² copy has exactly the original law.

The copy is obtained by evaluating the original variable on one product coordinate. That evaluation pushes the product source to the original source measure. Composing pushforwards consequently gives the same law as the original variable. Almost-sure representative changes do not affect this equality, so the copied reference in the eventual coupling has precisely the intended mean-field marginal.

steps.title: Use the actual tagged joint pair as a coupling
steps.body:
On the product space couple the actual pair \((\Theta^N,X_i^N)\) with the genuine iid copy of \((\theta,X)\). Both are \(L^2\), so the coupling has finite cost. The joint-pair norm bound gives

\[W_2(\mathcal L(\Theta^N,X_i^N),\mathcal L(\theta,X))\le\|\Theta^N-\theta\|_2+\|X_i^N-X_i\|_2.\]

Finiteness is established before converting the extended transport value to a real number.

On the finite product space use the explicit pair consisting of the actual tagged particle \((\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N})\) and the genuine joint iid reference copy. Measure-preserving coordinate evaluation proves that the latter has exactly the original mean-field law. This pair is an admissible finite-cost coupling because both random variables are in \(L^2\). Its cost is bounded by the sum of the parameter and tagged-latent \(L^2\) differences, yielding the displayed Wasserstein estimate. The public theorem inserts the constructed coordinate comparison and keeps the actual Brownian particle integral equation in its conclusion, so the law bound refers to the specified process.

Formal correspondence: tagged_particle_wasserstein_le : The actual tagged-particle pair and the genuine iid copy provide a finite transport coupling. This helper only translates coordinate L² distances.

Reconstruct the tagged joint pair from the common particle parameter and its \(i\)-th latent coordinate. Couple it with the corresponding iid mean-field pair on the same product source. Their joint distribution has the required two marginal laws and finite quadratic cost. The pair norm is bounded by the sum of coordinate norms; Minkowski gives the same inequality in \(L^2\), and transport is no larger than this explicit coupling cost.

steps.title: Retain the true Brownian input in the final law theorem
steps.body:
The joint pair \((\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N})\) has finite second moment, and each reference copy has exactly the actual law of \(Y_t=(\theta_t,X_t)\). Their constructed joint distribution is an admissible coupling. The pair L² norm is at most the sum of its coordinate norms, giving

\[ W_2\!\left(\mathcal L(\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N}),\mathcal L(\theta_t,X_t)\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N},\qquad 0\le t\le T. \]

The final endpoint retains the particle integral equation, the exact iid initial law and the actual Brownian input alongside this bound. The Wasserstein distance is proved finite before converting it to a real number. This proves convergence of actual tagged one-time laws; pathwise strong-SDE, expected path-supremum and gradient-flow PDE statements remain outside the established result.

The named particle input is the copied latent-only Brownian input plus the separately scaled parameter Brownian input. The final existential theorem retains that exact input and the actual empirical-gradient integral equation, while the tagged coupling converts the previously proved coordinate estimate to the displayed law bound for every \(N\), tag and time.

Formal correspondence: particleBrownianInput : The actual Brownian input in the particle coordinate equations. The parameter noise is scaled by 1/sqrt N ; every latent copy keeps its noise. exists_canonical_meanField_particle_law_comparison : From an arbitrary finite-second-moment latent law and independent canonical Brownian source, construct both integral solutions and prove the actual tagged-particle one-time Wasserstein bound, uniformly over the horizon. This uses a different process norm from the source's expected path supremum and does not establish that printed bound.

Insert the constructed coordinate error bound into the explicit coupling estimate at each fixed time. This proves finite \(W_2\) and the rate \(C_T/\sqrt N\) uniformly over the specified time interval and tag. The conclusion retains the empirical-gradient integral equation, copied iid initialization and actual Brownian input, so it refers to those processes rather than an arbitrary family of nearby probability laws.

ProximalLangevin/Check.lean.title: Assumptions and conclusions of the proximal arguments
ProximalLangevin/Check.lean.summary:
The proximal development combines actual convex minimization, exact particle updates, finite-moment Gaussian laws, stationary splitting couplings and constructed mean-field comparisons. An assumption audit ensures that numerical bounds are applied only after their analytic and probabilistic prerequisites have been established. It does not add a new convergence statement.

This module imports the proximal development and asks Lean to print the axioms used by its principal analytic, algorithmic and stochastic declarations. It is an audit entry point rather than a new mathematical assumption.

steps.title: Analytic prerequisites and mathematical scope
steps.body:
Run lake build ProximalLangevin +ProximalLangevin.Check from the repository root. Each #print axioms command reports the dependency closure of an already checked declaration, including proximal optimality, the three actual algorithm bounds, Brownian coupling and mean-field constructions. The file introduces no new theorem or definition. The audit complements compilation; it does not strengthen any theorem’s stated assumptions or turn conditional scalar statements into algorithm convergence results.

Each #check command asks Lean to elaborate the complete theorem type, retaining every displayed assumption. Each #print axioms command reports the transitive foundational dependencies of that theorem. Compile this module after the library build to inspect that report; these commands check the existing proofs and do not supply new mathematical hypotheses or conclusions.

The key mathematical distinction is between a scalar consequence of an assumed recurrence and a recurrence derived from an actual transition. The splitting endpoint uses the latter through its constructed stationary coupling. Likewise the mean-field endpoint retains actual integral equations and iid source constructions. Auditing these dependencies preserves their stated scope and prevents interpreting algebraic examples or conditional estimates as broader stochastic convergence theorems.

ProximalLangevin.lean.title: Proximal particle algorithms and mean-field comparisons
ProximalLangevin.lean.summary:
The development connects proximal optimality to the Moreau gradient, identifies concrete particle schemes and proves finite-time comparisons for their actual laws. The splitting route uses a genuine energy inequality and stationary Brownian cancellation, while the mean-field route uses Lipschitz integral equations and exact iid variance. The root module gathers proximal calculus, actual particle algorithms, corrected original-center bounds and constructed mean-field comparisons into one importable Lean library. Its imported theorems retain their exact assumptions and scope.

steps.title: Connect proximal calculus with particle convergence
steps.body:
Importing ProximalLangevin makes the checked public development available. The mathematical chain is true proximal minimization, residual/Moreau calculus, exact algorithm identities, genuine finite-moment Gaussian laws, concentration and transport, then the original-center comparison. The splitting chain additionally constructs Brownian stationarity and orthogonality; the mean-field branch constructs continuous \(L^2\) integral equations and actual iid comparisons. Run lake build ProximalLangevin +ProximalLangevin.Check. This umbrella has no local declarations; its proof content is in the linked imported modules.

This entry module assembles the named proof families through imports. The complete assumptions, intermediate estimates and final conclusions are stated in the dependency pages below. Building the entry module recompiles its imported dependencies and verifies that their interfaces agree.
